jute.types: Raw jute is traded as white jute (Corchorus capsularis) or tossa jute (Corchorus olitorius), and producing countries grade it into numbered classes by strength, color, luster, fineness, root content and defects such as specks and hard bark. Higher grades go into finer yarns for carpet backing, decor fabrics and blends, while lower grades and cuttings, the hard root ends, go into sacking and twine. At the mill, fiber is sold as sliver or spun yarn, measured by weight per unit length. Product classes include hessian (burlap), sacking, carpet backing cloth, jute felt and nonwovens, and jute geotextiles. Kenaf and roselle, species of Hibiscus, are traded as jute substitutes and can be mixed into jute goods.
jute.fabrics: Hessian, or burlap, is an open plain weave used for sandbags, upholstery foundations, crafts, plant wraps and decorative wall coverings. Sacking is heavier and denser, woven for coffee, cocoa, grain and sugar bags. Carpet backing cloth forms the secondary backing of tufted carpets, and jute twine and cordage are used in gardening and packaging. Jute rugs are braided, hand-knotted or flat-woven for a coarse, natural look. Jute geotextiles are laid on slopes and riverbanks to control erosion while vegetation establishes, then decompose. Diversified products include shopping bags, espadrille soles, blinds, and jute blended with cotton or viscose for home textiles.
jute.quality: For bags and hessian, look for an even, tight weave, consistent yarn thickness and minimal loose fiber and dust; excessive shedding suggests low-grade fiber or short cuttings. Heavier cloth for its width is generally stronger. Jute smells faintly of its batching oil; a strong petroleum odor can indicate mineral oil, which matters for food packaging, so food-contact sacks should be specified accordingly. Rugs should be tightly braided or woven with firm edges and a backing that does not stain floors. Burlap-look products may be polypropylene or paper yarn, which a label check or a burn test reveals. Coatings, laminations and plastic backings change disposal, so ask what is attached.
pros: It is inexpensive and strong in tension, suiting sacks, twine and backing fabrics.
It is largely rainfed in delta regions and is biodegradable at end of life when uncoated.
Its rough texture gives rugs and decor a natural look and good grip.
Jute geotextiles stabilize soil temporarily and then break down, leaving no persistent plastic.
cons: It is coarse and sheds loose fiber, so it is not comfortable next to the skin.
It yellows and weakens in sunlight and rots or mildews if kept damp.
Wet cleaning can shrink, distort or brown jute rugs and fabrics.
It wears quickly under repeated bending and foot traffic compared with wool or synthetic rugs.
jute.impact: Jute is mostly grown in rainfed delta farming systems of India and Bangladesh, but retting stems in ponds and ditches depletes oxygen and can pollute local water. A 2023 study by researchers at India's ICAR Central Research Institute for Jute and Allied Fibres, which counted carbon absorbed while the crop grows, reported net negative greenhouse gas emissions for jute and kenaf carrier bags and far higher emissions per kilogram for LDPE plastic bags; such cradle-to-grave results depend on carbon accounting choices and on how often each bag is reused. Batching oils, chemical softeners and plastic coatings reduce biodegradability. Farm and mill work is labor intensive, and public audit data on wages and conditions are limited, so social claims need supplier evidence.
jute.care: Keep jute dry. Vacuum rugs regularly without a beater bar, shake out small mats and rotate rugs to even out wear and sun fading. Blot spills immediately with a dry cloth, working from the edge inward, and avoid soaking, because water can cause brown stains and shrinkage; many jute rugs are dry clean only or spot clean only. For bags and hessian, brush off dust and spot clean with a barely damp cloth, then dry quickly in shade. Pressing is rarely needed; if the label allows, use steam through a cloth. Store in a ventilated, dry place away from direct sunlight, and check for mildew in humid seasons.
faq: Is burlap the same as jute?

Burlap is the North American name for hessian, a fabric rather than a fiber. It is traditionally woven from jute, sometimes from other bast fibers, and imitation burlap can be polypropylene or paper yarn. The fiber content on the label tells you which it is.
Can you wash a jute rug?

Usually not in water. Soaking jute can shrink it, distort its shape and leave brown water stains as the fiber releases colored compounds. Vacuum it, spot clean with minimal moisture, and follow the maker's instructions, which often call for professional dry cleaning.
Why does my jute rug shed?

Jute is made of short, stiff cells bonded together, so friction breaks loose fragments, especially in new rugs. Shedding usually lessens after a few weeks of regular vacuuming. Heavy continued shedding suggests low-grade fiber or placement in a high-traffic area.
Is jute biodegradable?

Plain, uncoated jute is biodegradable, which is why it is used for temporary erosion-control geotextiles. Latex or plastic backings, laminations and some finishes slow or prevent breakdown, so check what has been bonded to the jute before composting or landfill assumptions.
notable: Jute geotextiles are chosen for erosion control because they are expected to decompose once vegetation roots have stabilized a slope.
A 2023 life cycle study reported net negative greenhouse gas emissions for jute and kenaf carrier bags because it credited the carbon absorbed during crop growth.

polyester.types: Polyester is sold in two basic forms. Filament yarn is continuous; it leaves the spinning line as partially oriented yarn (POY), which is either fully drawn into flat, glossy fully drawn yarn (FDY) or false-twist textured into draw-textured yarn (DTY), the crimped, bulky workhorse of knits, fleece and stretch wovens. Air-textured yarn adds loops for a spun-like look. Staple fiber is cut into short lengths and spun, usually with cotton or viscose, into spun polyester, which feels more like cotton but pills more. Microfiber means filaments finer than about 1 denier (roughly 1 dtex), against about 3 to 5 denier for conventional filament. Other trade forms include hollow fiberfill, cationic-dyeable polyester, and recycled polyester (rPET), which in 2024 was about 12% of polyester output and was still made about 98% from bottles, according to Textile Exchange.
polyester.fabrics: Filament polyester dominates silk-look wovens: satin (a float weave for sheen), chiffon and georgette (sheer plain weaves from high-twist crepe yarns, georgette being heavier and grainier), taffeta (a crisp, tight plain weave for linings and formalwear) and pongee linings. Ripstop polyester adds heavier yarns in a grid to stop tears spreading, and is used for tents, flags and light jackets. Knits include jersey, mesh and interlock for sportswear, and fleece, a knit brushed and napped on one or both sides for warmth. Microfiber is made into peach-skin shirting, microsuede, cleaning cloths and sheets. Spun polyester blended with cotton gives polycotton shirting, workwear and bedding, and polyester fiberfill stuffs pillows and duvets.
polyester.quality: Start with the construction. A tight weave or dense knit with smooth filament yarn resists snagging and pilling better than a loose knit of spun staple. Fleece should feel even and springy, with no bald patches after brushing, and seams should lie flat without puckering. Rub a hidden area: fuzz balls on a new garment predict heavy pilling. Hold sheers up to light to judge evenness. Satin and chiffon labeled 'silky' are often polyester, so read the fiber line rather than the description. A recycled claim should name a percentage and be backed by a chain-of-custody certificate such as the Global Recycled Standard, because no routine test separates recycled from virgin PET. Very low prices usually reflect thin, loose fabric rather than the fiber itself.
pros: It keeps its strength when wet and dries quickly because it absorbs very little water.
Heat-set polyester holds pleats and resists creasing and shrinkage through repeated washing.
Filament fabrics resist abrasion and hold bright disperse-dye colors well.
It is inexpensive and made in an unusually wide range of yarn types, from sheer chiffon to lofty fleece.
Bottle-grade PET gives an established, if one-way, recycled feedstock.
cons: Spun and fleece polyester pills, and the strong fibers anchor the pills to the surface instead of letting them drop off.
Its low absorbency and oleophilic surface can hold body oils and odor, and it builds static in dry air.
It melts rather than chars, so hot irons glaze it and sparks can burn holes.
Washing and drying release microplastic fibers that persist in the environment.
Most recycled polyester comes from bottles, so it does not close the loop for textile waste.
polyester.impact: Polyester is a fossil-based plastic, and its best-studied problem after production energy is microfiber release. In a 2019 full-scale washing study, De Falco and colleagues measured about 124 to 308 mg of microfibers per kg of synthetic clothing washed, roughly 640,000 to 1,500,000 fibers per kg. Carney Almroth and colleagues (2018) found polyester fleece shed far more than other polyester knits, averaging 7,360 fibers per square meter per liter in one wash against 87. A 2022 study of vented tumble dryers found airborne releases comparable to those sent down the drain. Recycled content does not solve shedding: a 2026 Swedish study found fabrics whose recycled polyester had been mechanically reprocessed twice or three times shed about 4.3 and 6.2 times more than virgin controls. Tighter constructions and higher-twist yarns shed less in the same studies.
polyester.care: Most polyester washes well at 30 to 40 C with ordinary detergent; cooler, fuller, shorter cycles reduce both energy and fiber shedding, and a mesh bag or an in-line filter captures some fibers. Wash fleece and performance knits inside out and skip fabric softener, which can coat surfaces and reduce wicking. Tumble dry low or line dry; condenser and heat-pump dryers retain more fibers than vented dryers. Iron on a low to medium setting (the one- or two-dot symbol under ISO 3758, about 110 to 150 C), using a press cloth on satins to avoid shine. Treat oily stains promptly with a little dish detergent, since polyester binds oils. Remove pills with a fabric shaver rather than pulling. Polyester resists moths and mildew, but heat from radiators or dryers can distort it permanently.
faq: Is polyester the same as microfiber?

Not exactly. Microfiber describes fineness, filaments finer than about 1 denier, and can be polyester, nylon or a blend of both. Most microfiber cloths and peach-skin fabrics are polyester or polyester with nylon. Ordinary polyester filament is several times coarser. The fiber content line tells you the polymer; the word microfiber tells you only about filament size.
Is recycled polyester better than virgin polyester?

It reuses existing plastic, mostly bottles, instead of new petrochemicals, but it behaves the same in the garment and still sheds microfibers. Some studies found recycled polyester fabrics shed more, especially after repeated mechanical recycling. Its benefit depends on the documented feedstock and energy used. Look for a percentage and a chain-of-custody certificate rather than a general green claim.
Why does my polyester sweater pill so much?

Pills form when loose fiber ends on spun or brushed yarns tangle under friction. Because polyester fibers are strong, the tangled balls stay anchored instead of breaking away as they do on weaker fibers. Tighter knits, filament yarns and higher-twist yarns pill less. Wash inside out on gentle cycles and use a fabric shaver to remove pills.
Can you iron polyester?

Yes, at a low to medium setting, usually one or two dots on the care label (about 110 to 150 C). Too much heat glazes the surface or melts it, because polyester is thermoplastic. Use steam and a press cloth, especially on satin or dark colors, and test an inside seam first.
notable: Textile Exchange reports that about 98% of recycled polyester in 2024 still came from plastic bottles, and that recycled textiles made up under 1% of global fiber supply.
A 2022 laboratory study found that vented tumble dryers emit microfibers to the air in amounts comparable to those released down the drain during washing.
A factory study published in 2023 found that wet processing, mostly dyeing, released up to 25 times more microfibers than home laundering.

nylon.types: Textile nylon is almost always nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, and labels rarely say which; nylon 6,6 melts higher and is common in heavy-duty technical fabrics, while nylon 6 is generally easier to dye and is widely used in hosiery, swimwear and carpet. Yarns are sold by linear density: yarns range from the very fine deniers of sheer hosiery to the hundreds of denier used in bag and luggage fabrics. High-tenacity filament serves webbing, luggage and cordage. Air-jet textured nylon gives a cotton-like, matte surface; false-twist textured nylon gives stretch and bulk. Microfiber nylon is finer than about 1 dtex per filament, and bright, semi-dull and full-dull grades differ in delusterant content and sheen.
nylon.fabrics: Warp-knit tricot, smooth on one face and fine-ribbed on the other, is the base of lingerie, linings and, with elastane, swimwear. Tulle is a fine nylon net used for veils, petticoats and costume. Hosiery is circular knitted from fine nylon, often with covered elastane. Ripstop nylon interweaves reinforcing yarns in a grid and is used for tents, parachutes, kites and down jackets, often with a silicone or polyurethane coating. Heavy textured fabrics such as CORDURA Classic, which its producer describes as high-tenacity air-jet-textured nylon 6,6 in 330 to 1000 denier, and ballistic basketweaves go into packs, luggage and workwear. Nylon also makes taffeta shells, matte activewear knits and hook-and-loop fasteners.
nylon.quality: For bags and outerwear, compare denier (thread thickness) together with weave density, coating and seam construction; a tightly woven lighter fabric can outperform a loosely woven heavier one for some uses. A genuine ripstop grid should be visible as a regular pattern of heavier lines. Check coatings for tackiness or flaking, which signals hydrolysis of polyurethane. For hosiery, denier signals opacity: roughly 15 denier and under reads sheer, about 30 to 40 semi-opaque and 40 or more opaque, though brands vary. Look for reinforced toes, flat seams and a gusset. Branded fabric names are trademarks, so ask for the fabric specification sheet rather than trusting a logo. Yellowed white nylon on a shelf suggests old or light-exposed stock.
pros: Nylon combines high tenacity with exceptional abrasion and fatigue resistance, which suits bags, hosiery and ropes.
Its elastic recovery and smooth hand make fine, sheer knits that stretch and spring back.
Acid dyes give deep, bright colors on nylon.
It is light for its strength and dries fairly quickly.
cons: It yellows and weakens with prolonged sunlight unless UV-stabilized.
It readily picks up loose dye from other items in the wash, graying whites.
It is heat sensitive and melts under a hot iron or near flame.
Sheer knits ladder and snag, and smooth nylon builds static in dry air.
Nylon 6,6 relies on adipic acid, whose production can emit nitrous oxide unless abated.
nylon.impact: Nylon is made from petrochemicals, and the adipic acid route used for nylon 6,6 has historically been a significant industrial source of nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas, unless emissions are abated. Nylon garments shed microplastic fibers like other synthetics. In a 2019 study that washed individual cotton, acrylic, polyester and polyamide garments, Cesa and colleagues found releases peaked in the first three washes and that a standard machine filter let about 40 to 75% of fiber mass pass. Fabric design matters: a 2023 laboratory study reported about 60% less shedding from nylon 6 fibers blended with polydimethylsiloxane to lower surface friction. Because nylon 6 depolymerizes cleanly, it is a stronger candidate for closed-loop recycling than most synthetics.
nylon.care: Wash nylon cool to warm, about 30 to 40 C, with a mild detergent, and separate it from dark or bleeding items because nylon soaks up stray dye. Put hosiery and lingerie in a mesh bag or hand wash, and avoid chlorine bleach, which can yellow nylon and destroys any elastane in the blend. Line dry away from direct sun or tumble on low. Iron only at the lowest setting (one dot, about 110 C) and quickly, preferably through a cloth. Coated technical fabrics should never be dry cleaned or wrung; wash them with a technical cleaner and reproof as the maker directs. Store out of sunlight, and check coated gear for sticky, peeling polyurethane, which usually means the coating has hydrolyzed.
faq: What does 1000D mean on a nylon backpack?

It means the yarns used weigh about 1000 grams per 9,000 meters, so they are thick. Higher denier usually means more abrasion resistance and weight, but weave density, polymer type, coatings and seam quality matter as much. A tightly woven lower-denier ripstop can outperform a loose heavy fabric for some uses.
Is nylon or polyester better for a rain jacket?

Both work; the waterproofing comes from coatings or membranes, not the fiber. Nylon shells are usually stronger and more abrasion resistant for their weight, while polyester absorbs less water, resists sunlight better and dries a little faster. Check the fabric weight, the waterproof layer and the seam taping rather than the fiber alone.
Why did my white nylon turn gray or yellow?

Nylon attracts loose dye in wash water, so washing it with colored items grays it. Sunlight, chlorine bleach and some storage conditions also yellow nylon. Wash whites separately in cool water, avoid chlorine bleach and store garments out of direct light.
What denier tights are the most durable?

Higher denier tights generally last longer because each yarn is thicker. Sheer styles of about 15 denier or less snag and ladder easily, while opaque tights of 40 denier and up resist runs better. Reinforced toes and quality elastane covering also extend life.
notable: CORDURA's own technical sheet describes its Classic fabrics as high-tenacity air-jet-textured nylon 6,6 made in 330, 500, 700 and 1000 denier.
Blending a small amount of silicone polymer (PDMS) into nylon 6 during melt spinning cut laundry microfiber shedding by about 60% in a 2023 study.
Hosiery denier is a direct measure of yarn weight: grams per 9,000 meters of yarn.

spandex.types: Elastane is sold by denier and by how it is combined with other yarns. Bare elastane is knitted directly in circular and warp knits. Covered yarn wraps the elastane core with one or two helices of nylon or polyester filament (single or double covered), as in hosiery. Air-covered yarn entangles filament and elastane with an air jet, and core-spun yarn wraps staple fiber such as cotton around it, the standard route for stretch denim. Polymer grades also differ: polyether-based types dominate, while grades formulated for chlorine resistance or higher heat-setting temperatures target swimwear and polyester blends. Patents describe chlorine resistance achieved with additives such as finely divided zinc oxide. In training and competitive swimwear, PBT polyester stretch fabrics are used as elastane-free alternatives where pool chlorine is the main concern.
spandex.fabrics: Stretch denim typically contains about 1 to 3% elastane; a study in the Journal of the Textile Institute showed that the elastane ratio and finishing both shift the fabric's mechanical properties. Shirting, chinos and suiting use similar small amounts for comfort. Knit tops and jersey dresses often use somewhat more. Leggings, swimwear and activewear commonly pair nylon or polyester with roughly 15 to 25% elastane, and sports and medical compression garments may go higher. Hosiery, bras, shapewear, waistbands, cuffs and medical compression stockings all rely on it, and it is often invisible, carrying less than a tenth of the fabric weight.
spandex.quality: Stretch the fabric to its limit and release it: good recovery returns it flat within seconds without ripples or a lingering bulge, and knees or seats that stay bagged after a day of wear indicate poor recovery. In leggings, stretch over your hand to check opacity; see-through leggings usually mean a light fabric or thin elastane. For stretch denim, 1 to 2% gives comfort with a rigid look, while higher shares feel softer but can bag and wear at stress points. White glints or tiny broken elastic threads on the surface signal degraded elastane. Swimwear marketed as chlorine resistant should name the fiber or technology and give some test basis. The percentage must appear on the label, so check it before buying.
pros: A few percent adds stretch and shape retention without adding bulk.
It allows close-fitting garments with fewer darts, zips and closures.
It extends to several times its length and recovers quickly.
Compression garments rely on it to deliver graduated, repeatable pressure.
cons: Chlorine, heat, UV and time gradually break down its recovery, so swimwear and hot-dried garments sag.
Even small percentages make blended fabrics much harder to recycle.
It can bleed disperse dye in polyester blends, lowering wash fastness.
When it fails, garments bag at knees and seats and the fabric can pucker as broken filaments retract.
spandex.impact: Elastane is a fossil-derived polyurethane usually spun from an amide solvent such as dimethylacetamide, which plants recover and recycle; how completely varies by site and is not normally disclosed to consumers. Its footprint per garment is small by mass, but its larger effect is on end of life. Blending even a few percent of elastane into cotton, polyester or nylon interferes with mechanical recycling, because it interferes with shredding and respinning, and with chemical recycling, because it contaminates recovered polymer. That is why sorting projects are testing infrared methods to detect elastane and why dissolution routes to remove it are under study. Shorter garment lives caused by lost stretch, rather than worn fabric, also add to waste.
spandex.care: Heat is the main enemy. Wash stretch garments at about 30 to 40 C, turn them inside out, and air dry or use the lowest tumble setting. Never use chlorine bleach. Rinse swimwear in clean cool water promptly after pool or sea use, press out water in a towel rather than wringing, and dry it flat in the shade. Rotating swimsuits lets fibers recover between uses. Iron only on the lowest setting, quickly and through a cloth, or steam lightly. Some lotions and sunscreens can stain; rinse them out rather than letting them build up. Store knits folded, since long hanging can stretch them. When elastane ages, no treatment restores it: bagging, rippling and white sprouting fibers are permanent.
faq: Is spandex the same as elastane and LYCRA?

Yes, largely. Spandex is the US generic name, elastane is the name used in Europe and ISO standards, and LYCRA is a brand of elastane fiber. All describe segmented polyurethane fibers with at least 85% segmented polyurethane. A label may say spandex or elastane; LYCRA can appear only alongside the generic name.
How much spandex should jeans have?

Most stretch jeans contain about 1 to 3% elastane. Around 1 to 2% gives comfort while keeping a denim look; higher shares feel softer and hug more but can bag and lose shape faster. Recovery quality matters as much as percentage, so check that the fabric snaps back after stretching.
Why do swimsuits lose their stretch?

Pool chlorine, heat, sunlight and body oils gradually break the polyurethane segments that give elastane its recovery. Rinsing after each swim, drying in the shade and avoiding hot tubs slow this. Chlorine-resistant grades and PBT polyester swim fabrics last longer in heavily chlorinated pools.
Can clothing with spandex be recycled?

It is difficult. Small amounts of elastane disrupt mechanical recycling and contaminate recycled polymers, so many recyclers reject stretch blends. Researchers are developing solvents that dissolve elastane out of blends and sensors to sort stretch fabrics, but these are not yet routine.
notable: Patent literature describes chlorine-resistance tests in which elastane yarn is stretched to 150% of its length and soaked in water with about 3 ppm active chlorine.
Stretch denim's comfort usually comes from a cotton-wrapped core of elastane that makes up only about 1 to 3% of the fabric.
Chlorine-resistant elastane grades have been made by dispersing fine zinc oxide particles in the fiber.

acrylic.types: Most acrylic reaches shoppers as staple fiber spun into yarn. High-bulk acrylic mixes shrinkable and pre-relaxed fibers; when the yarn is steamed, the shrinkable fibers contract and push the others into loops, giving loft. Bicomponent acrylic combines two polymer compositions side by side so the fiber crimps like wool. Low-pill acrylics are modified so that pills break away more easily; as with low-pill polyester, a common approach is to reduce fiber strength. Solution-dyed acrylic has pigment added to the dope, giving strong lightfastness for awnings and outdoor cushions. Modacrylic, a separate generic name with 35 to 85% acrylonitrile, is more flame resistant and is used for faux fur, wigs and protective blends. Craft yarns are sold by weight class, such as fingering, worsted and bulky.
acrylic.fabrics: Acrylic is mainly knitted. Jersey and rib knits make sweaters, hats, scarves and gloves, often blended with wool, cotton or nylon to balance cost, warmth and durability. Raschel-knitted and brushed fabrics make blankets and throws. Deep-pile knits in acrylic and modacrylic imitate fur and shearling for coats, trims and toys. Solution-dyed acrylic canvas is used for awnings, boat covers and outdoor upholstery because it resists fading and mildew. Acrylic fleece and sweatshirt linings, socks and baby blankets are common, and hobby knitting and crochet consume a large share of acrylic yarn because it is inexpensive, washable and bright.
acrylic.quality: Acrylic's weak point is pilling, so judge the yarn and knit. Firm, tightly knitted fabric with smooth, well-twisted yarn resists pilling better than loose, lofty, low-twist knits. Rub a hidden area between your palms; if fuzz forms quickly, pills will follow. Blends help: acrylic with wool or nylon wears better than loose 100% acrylic. Descriptions such as 'cashmere feel' or 'wool touch' usually mean acrylic, so rely on the fiber content. Pilling ratings from tests such as ISO 12945-2 (Martindale) or ASTM D3512 (random tumble) use a 1 to 5 scale, 5 meaning no pilling; a supplier quoting grade 4 or better is a good sign. Check that seams are linked or overlocked neatly.
pros: It gives a light, warm, wool-like loft at low cost.
It is machine washable and does not felt or attract moths as wool does.
It takes bright, fast colors, and solution-dyed grades resist sunlight well.
It suits people who find wool itchy or who avoid animal fibers.
cons: Staple acrylic knits pill readily, and the strong fibers hold pills on the surface.
Heat can permanently relax and flatten knits, a change knitters call 'killing' acrylic.
It absorbs little moisture, so it can feel clammy and builds static.
It sheds microplastic fibers, and in some washing studies it shed more than polyester.
acrylic.impact: Acrylic's footprint combines fossil feedstock, solvent-based spinning and high fiber shedding. Napper and Thompson (2016) estimated that a 6 kg wash of acrylic fabric could release more than 700,000 fibers and found polyester-cotton shed significantly less than acrylic or polyester. In a 2024 study comparing acrylic, polyamide, polyester, recycled polyester and polypropylene, Akyildiz and colleagues recorded the highest count, about 2,405 fibers, from a woven acrylic sample, and found that an optional prewash released far more fibers than the main wash. Because acrylic garments often pill and look worn early, their service life can be short, which adds to waste. Recycling of acrylic textiles is still mostly at pilot scale.
acrylic.care: Wash acrylic knits inside out at about 30 C on a gentle cycle, with a mild detergent and a full load to reduce friction. Avoid hot water and hot tumble drying, which can stretch, shrink or flatten the knit; dry flat, reshaping while damp, or tumble on the lowest setting. Do not hang heavy sweaters, which lengthen. Ironing is rarely needed; if it is, use the lowest setting through a cloth and avoid direct steam unless you want to relax the fabric permanently. Remove pills with a fabric shaver or sweater comb rather than pulling them, which draws out more fibers. Acrylic is not eaten by moths but can pick up oily stains, which respond to pretreatment with a little dish detergent.
faq: Why does acrylic pill so much?

Acrylic is usually spun from short staple fibers that work loose and tangle under friction. The fibers are strong, so the tangled balls stay anchored instead of breaking off. Tighter knits, higher-twist yarns, low-pill fiber grades and blends with wool or nylon reduce the problem.
Is acrylic warm?

Yes. Its bulky, crimped fibers trap air, so an acrylic sweater can feel comparably warm to a similar wool knit in dry conditions. It absorbs much less moisture than wool, so it can feel clammy when you sweat and does not buffer humidity the same way.
Is acrylic yarn safe for baby blankets?

Acrylic is commonly used for baby items because it is soft, washable and inexpensive. It melts when exposed to flame rather than self-extinguishing like wool, so keep blankets away from heat sources, and check for loose fibers or pills that could come off. Follow the yarn maker's washing instructions.
What does 'killing' acrylic mean?

Knitters use the term for deliberately steaming or heating acrylic so the fibers relax permanently. The fabric loses bounce and gains drape, which suits lace or shawls. The same effect happens by accident in hot dryers, which is why acrylic sweaters can come out limp and stretched.
notable: In a 2016 washing study, polyester-cotton fabric consistently shed significantly fewer fibers than either acrylic or pure polyester.
Anti-pilling acrylic fibers have been patented, and low-pill grades generally work by letting pills break away instead of clinging.
A classic 1959 study of pilling showed that pills stay attached because anchoring fibers resist breaking, which is why strong synthetics pill more visibly than weaker fibers.

viscose.types: Viscose comes as staple, cut to cotton-type or wool-type lengths for spinning alone or in blends, and as continuous filament for linings, satin and dress fabrics. Regular viscose has modest wet strength; high-wet-modulus variants made by modified viscose routes include modal and the older polynosic fibers. Specialty grades include flame-retardant viscose for protective and upholstery uses, dope-dyed viscose colored before spinning, and hollow or trilobal cross-sections for bulk or luster. Feedstock labels such as bamboo, eucalyptus or beech describe the pulp, not a different fiber. Branded fibers such as LENZING ECOVERO are regular viscose with producer claims about pulp sourcing and emissions. Cupro, often confused with viscose, is made by a different cuprammonium process.
viscose.fabrics: Viscose challis is a soft, lightweight plain weave, often printed, for dresses and blouses. Viscose crepe, twill and satin give fluid drape for skirts and shirts, and filament viscose is used for linings and ribbons. Viscose jersey, usually with a few percent elastane, is common in T-shirts and dresses. Viscose velvet has a dense, lustrous pile. Blends with polyester (often sold as TR suiting) combine drape with wrinkle resistance, and slub viscose and viscose-linen blends imitate linen. Much viscose staple also goes into nonwovens such as wipes and hygiene products, where its absorbency is valued.
viscose.quality: Regular viscose loses much of its strength wet, so the main quality risks are shrinkage and distortion after washing. Look for fabrics described as prewashed or preshrunk, and for firm, tight weaves; loosely woven challis can show seam slippage, where yarns pull apart at stressed seams. Heavier crepe and twill hold shape better than thin challis. Run fabric between your fingers: viscose should feel smooth and cool without a papery crispness from stiffening finishes that wash out. On US labels the fiber must be named rayon or viscose; 'bamboo' alone is unlawful, although 'rayon made from bamboo' is acceptable. Pulp-sourcing and lower-impact claims need brand or certification evidence.
pros: It drapes fluidly and has a soft, cool hand at modest cost.
It absorbs moisture well and takes dyes to deep, bright shades.
It is made from renewable cellulose and its fibers have biodegraded in aerobic water tests.
It blends easily with cotton, polyester, linen and elastane to add softness and drape.
cons: It is weak when wet, so garments can shrink, stretch or distort in washing.
It creases easily and can show water spots on some finishes.
The viscose process uses carbon disulfide, so environmental and worker outcomes depend on plant controls.
Pulp can come from poorly managed or endangered forests unless sourcing is documented.
viscose.impact: Two issues dominate. The first is forests: Canopy, an environmental group, has warned that a significant share of the wood pulped for fabrics comes from ancient and endangered forests. Its CanopyStyle initiative, launched in October 2013, asks brands and fiber producers to exclude such sources, and its annual Hot Button Report ranks producers on sourcing risk. The second is chemistry: carbon disulfide and sulfur emissions and zinc-bearing effluent depend on recovery at the plant. A 2010 life cycle study by Shen, Worrell and Patel found Austrian viscose among the lowest-impact fibers assessed, while viscose produced in Asia was comparable to PET, showing that plant and region matter more than the fiber name. Bamboo branding does not make viscose greener.
viscose.care: Follow the label closely, because many viscose items are marked hand wash, cold wash or dry clean. When washing is allowed, use 30 C or cooler on a delicate cycle or by hand, with a mild detergent, and support the wet fabric rather than wringing or twisting it. Roll in a towel to remove water, then dry flat or on a padded hanger; avoid hot tumble drying, a common cause of shrinkage. Iron at medium heat, about 150 C (two dots), on the reverse while slightly damp or through a pressing cloth, since viscose can scorch and develop shine. Test stain removers on a hidden seam, and store folded knits so they do not stretch on hangers.
faq: Is bamboo fabric really rayon?

In most cases, yes. Soft bamboo apparel is usually viscose rayon made from bamboo pulp, and the chemistry is the same as wood-based viscose. The FTC requires such products to be labeled rayon or viscose, optionally 'made from bamboo', and has penalized retailers for calling them bamboo.
Why did my viscose shrink?

Regular viscose absorbs a lot of water, swells and loses much of its strength when wet, so agitation and heat can pull the fabric out of shape and shrink it. Cold, gentle washing, flat drying and avoiding the dryer prevent most problems; gentle steaming can recover some shrinkage.
Is viscose natural or synthetic?

Neither category fits exactly. Viscose is a manufactured fiber made from natural cellulose, usually wood pulp, which is chemically dissolved and regenerated. It is often called semi-synthetic or regenerated cellulose, and legally it is a manufactured fiber named rayon or viscose.
What is the difference between viscose and rayon?

In the United States, rayon is the generic name for regenerated cellulose fibers, and viscose is an acceptable name for fiber made by the viscose process. In the EU and much of the world, viscose is the standard label name. They usually describe the same fiber.
notable: In 2013 Amazon, Leon Max, Macy's and Sears agreed to pay a total of 1.26 million dollars in FTC civil penalties for labeling rayon textiles as bamboo.
In 2022 Kohl's and Walmart agreed to pay 2.5 million and 3 million dollars in civil penalties over bamboo claims, after FTC warning letters sent in 2010.
The FTC's 2010 warning letters on bamboo labeling went to 78 companies.

lyocell.types: Standard lyocell fibrillates when wet-abraded, and finishers either suppress this or exploit it for a peach-skin surface. Cross-linked low-fibrillation grades are treated during fiber production so that fabrics stay smooth through garment dyeing and home laundering, suiting knitwear and bright colors. Staple lyocell is made in several finenesses and cut lengths for cotton-type or wool-type spinning, including micro grades for very soft, dense fabrics, and some producers offer filament lyocell with a silk-like luster. Dope-dyed lyocell is colored before spinning. Lenzing sells lyocell under its TENCEL brand and, under the REFIBRA name, lyocell made partly from pulp that includes cotton scraps. Other producers make generic lyocell, so the brand tag, not the fiber name, identifies Lenzing fiber.
lyocell.fabrics: Lyocell is widely used in denim, alone or blended with cotton, where it adds drape, a cool touch and a soft, sometimes sueded surface after enzyme or stone washing. It is woven into shirting, chambray and twill trousers, and into sateen and percale sheets marketed for cool sleep. Jersey and interlock knits appear in T-shirts, dresses and underwear, and fibrillated finishes give sand-washed blouses. It is blended with wool, silk or linen for drape and with cotton through siro spinning, where two strands are spun together, for smooth yarns. Nonwoven lyocell is used in wipes and technical products.
lyocell.quality: Check for fibrillation on dark colors: a pale, frosted haze, especially along seams and folds, shows the finish was not controlled and will worsen with wear. A deliberate peach-skin fabric should look uniform. Smooth lyocell should feel cool, heavy and fluid rather than papery. Look at the generic name on the content line, since TENCEL can mean lyocell or modal, and treat pulp, recycling or solvent recovery statements as producer claims tied to specific fibers. For sheets, weave and yarn matter more than thread count, which is less meaningful for lyocell's smooth filaments and fine staple. Wrinkle recovery is better than viscose, but pure lyocell shirting still creases.
pros: It keeps most of its strength when wet, so it is more stable in washing than regular viscose.
It feels smooth and cool with a fluid drape and good moisture uptake.
Its solvent is recovered at a very high rate in a closed process, according to producers.
It blends well with cotton, wool and silk and suits both woven and knitted fabrics.
cons: Wet abrasion can fibrillate the surface, leaving a frosted, hairy look on dark colors.
Fabrics can stiffen after line drying and may need tumbling or steaming to soften.
It usually costs more than viscose and cotton of similar weight.
Brand names can obscure whether a product is lyocell, modal or a small-percentage blend.
lyocell.impact: Lyocell avoids carbon disulfide, and its NMMO solvent is recovered in a closed loop, so the main footprint questions are pulp sourcing and the energy used to evaporate and recover the solvent. In a 2010 life cycle assessment of Lenzing fibers published in Resources, Conservation and Recycling, Shen, Worrell and Patel ranked Tencel lyocell among the lowest overall impacts of the fibers studied, which also included viscose, modal, cotton, PET and polypropylene; results were specific to the plants, energy mixes and pulp supply of that producer. Canopy's Hot Button Report also covers lyocell producers' forest-sourcing risk. Lyocell made partly from cotton scraps reduces virgin pulp demand, but recycled content shares are producer claims.
lyocell.care: Wash lyocell at 30 C, or up to 40 C if the label allows, on a gentle cycle, inside out and in an uncrowded drum to limit the abrasion that causes fibrillation. Use a mild detergent without chlorine bleach. Tumble dry on low and remove promptly, or line dry and then soften briefly in the dryer or with steam, since line-dried lyocell can feel stiff. Iron at medium heat, about 150 C (two dots), preferably with steam or on the reverse for dark colors. Store as you would cotton. Once a frosted haze appears it cannot be reversed at home, so gentle washing from the start matters.
faq: Is TENCEL the same as lyocell?

Not exactly. TENCEL is Lenzing's brand name, used for both its lyocell and its modal fibers. Lyocell is the generic fiber name for cellulose spun from a direct organic solvent. Check the content label: 'TENCEL lyocell' and 'TENCEL modal' are different fibers.
Why does my dark lyocell shirt look frosted?

That haze is fibrillation. Wet lyocell fibers can split into fine surface fibrils when rubbed during washing, and the fibrils scatter light, making dark colors look pale. Washing inside out, on gentle cycles and in smaller loads slows it, but it cannot be fully undone.
Is lyocell good for sheets?

Many people find lyocell sheets smooth and cool, because the fiber absorbs moisture and drapes closely. They cost more than cotton and need gentle washing to avoid fibrillation. Comparative sleep-temperature claims come mostly from sellers and have limited independent testing.
Is lyocell eco-friendly?

It can have a lower footprint than viscose or conventional cotton because its solvent is recovered and it avoids carbon disulfide. Results depend on the producer's energy, pulp source and forest certification, so check producer documentation rather than relying on the generic name.
notable: A 2010 life cycle study found Lenzing's Tencel, along with its Austrian-made modal and viscose, among the lowest overall impacts of the fibers it compared.
Fibrillation, usually a flaw, is deliberately induced to create the soft peach-skin or sand-washed surface on some lyocell fabrics.

modal.types: Modal is defined as a high-wet-modulus regenerated cellulose: it is made by a modified viscose route so that it resists stretching when wet far better than regular viscose. Commercial forms include regular modal staple for cotton-type spinning, finer micro modal grades for very soft, light knits, and dope-dyed modal colored before spinning. Lenzing sells modal under its TENCEL brand, and other producers make generic modal. 'Beech modal' refers to fiber made from beech pulp, a producer-sourcing statement rather than a separate fiber. Polynosic fibers are an older related high-wet-modulus class. In lingerie and T-shirts, modal is often blended with cotton, and with a few percent elastane for stretch.
modal.fabrics: Modal is mostly knitted. Single jersey in T-shirts, camisoles and dresses, fine rib and interlock in underwear and lingerie, and French terry and fleece in loungewear show its softness and drape. Modal and cotton blends are common in T-shirts and sleepwear, combining modal's smoothness with cotton's structure, and modal and elastane blends are used for close-fitting underwear and base layers. Woven modal appears in sheets, pillowcases and shirting, often in sateen or twill. In towels and bath robes it is blended with cotton for softness, and it is also used in socks and scarves.
modal.quality: Good modal jersey feels smooth, cool and dense, with enough weight that it is not see-through when stretched; very thin, light knits cling and show wear quickly. Pilling is the most common complaint, especially in lower-quality blends and in areas of friction, so look for a smooth, tightly knit surface without loose fibers. Check the generic name on the content label: 'TENCEL' alone does not say whether the fiber is modal or lyocell, and 'micro modal' is a trade term. Recovery matters for underwear: a modal and elastane blend should spring back after stretching. Pulp and plant claims need producer or certification evidence.
pros: It is very soft and smooth, with a cool, silky touch against the skin.
It keeps shape and resists shrinkage in washing much better than regular viscose.
It absorbs moisture and takes dye well, keeping colors bright over many washes.
It drapes closely, suiting underwear, loungewear and fitted tops.
cons: It can pill in friction areas, especially in thin or loosely knitted fabrics.
Light jersey can cling and become see-through.
It is made by a viscose-type route that uses carbon disulfide, so plant controls determine its footprint.
It costs more than cotton or regular viscose jersey.
modal.impact: Modal shares the viscose chemistry of carbon disulfide and sulfuric acid, so its footprint depends heavily on chemical recovery, energy and pulp at the specific plant. In the 2010 life cycle assessment by Shen, Worrell and Patel of Lenzing fibers, modal made in Austria ranked with Tencel lyocell and Austrian viscose among the lowest overall impacts, while viscose produced in Asia was comparable to PET; those results cannot be transferred to modal from other producers. Forest sourcing is covered by Canopy's Hot Button assessments of fiber producers. Rayon knits shed fiber fragments in laundering, but laboratory tests have found rayon fragments biodegrade in aerobic water, unlike polyester.
modal.care: Wash modal at 30 to 40 C on a gentle cycle with mild detergent, inside out, and group it with smooth fabrics rather than towels or jeans to reduce pilling. Avoid chlorine bleach. Tumble dry on low or line dry; high heat stresses elastane blends and can cause some shrinkage. Most modal needs no ironing; if needed, use a low to medium setting, one or two dots, on the reverse. Remove pills with a fabric shaver rather than pulling them. Store knits folded, since heavy modal dresses can stretch on hangers. Follow the label for blends, which govern care.
faq: What is modal fabric?

Modal is a regenerated cellulose fiber made from wood pulp by a modified viscose process that gives it higher strength when wet. It is best known for soft, smooth jersey in underwear, loungewear and T-shirts, often blended with cotton or elastane.
Is modal better than cotton?

It depends on the use. Modal feels smoother and silkier, drapes more closely and keeps colors bright, while cotton is sturdier, cheaper, more breathable in heavier knits and pills less. Many garments blend the two to combine their strengths.
Does modal shrink?

Much less than regular viscose, because its high wet modulus keeps it from stretching and distorting in water. Some shrinkage can still occur with hot washes or high dryer heat, especially in blends, so gentle washing and low drying are safest.
Is modal the same as viscose or rayon?

Modal belongs to the rayon family of regenerated cellulose fibers, and in the United States it falls within the rayon definition. It differs from regular viscose in its production conditions and in its higher wet strength, and the EU lists it as a separate fiber name.
notable: A 2010 life cycle study ranked Lenzing's Austrian-made modal among the lowest-impact fibers it compared, alongside Tencel lyocell and Austrian viscose.
Laboratory laundering of knits found that cellulose-based fabrics shed more fiber by mass than polyester, yet the rayon and cotton fragments biodegraded in aerobic water tests.

ramie.types: Two botanical forms are grown: white ramie (Boehmeria nivea var. nivea), the China grass of temperate East Asia with silvery leaf undersides, and green ramie (var. tenacissima), adapted to the humid tropics. After decortication the raw ribbons are sold as china grass or decorticated ramie, and after degumming as clean fiber ready for spinning. Degummed fiber is combed into long top for fine, lustrous worsted-type yarns, while the short noil goes into coarser yarns or is cottonized for blending. Yarn quality is judged by fineness, the thoroughness of degumming, whiteness and hairiness. Traditional handwoven ramie cloths include Japan's Ojiya-chijimi and Echigo-jofu and Korea's Hansan mosi.
ramie.fabrics: Pure ramie is woven into crisp, lustrous plain weaves for summer shirts, dresses, table linen and traditional East Asian garments, where fine ramie gauze was valued for hot, humid summers. Blends are more common in Western retail: ramie and cotton knits for sweaters and T-shirts, ramie and linen shirting, and ramie with viscose or silk for drapier cloth. Ramie is also used in canvas, upholstery, fishing lines and nets, industrial sewing thread, and papers where high strength and wet resistance are needed. Its stiffness makes it useful in blends that must hold shape, such as structured jackets.
ramie.quality: Good ramie fabric is smooth, bright and even, without a prickly surface of protruding fiber ends, which indicates coarse or poorly degummed fiber. Rub it against the inside of your wrist to check. High luster and whiteness in undyed cloth reflect thorough degumming and bleaching. Check the content line, because ramie blends are often marketed as linen-look and ramie may not be called linen. In knits, ramie adds crispness but can lose shape and stretch at elbows if the ramie share is high. Heavier, tighter weaves resist the fiber's tendency to break at sharp creases better than loosely woven gauze.
pros: It is among the strongest plant fibers and is at least as strong wet as dry.
It has a natural luster that brightens dyed and undyed cloth.
It absorbs moisture and dries quickly, feeling cool in summer.
It holds its shape and resists shrinking in woven fabrics.
cons: It is stiff and inextensible, so it wrinkles readily and can crack at sharp, repeated folds.
Poorly degummed ramie feels prickly against the skin.
Degumming requires chemical or enzymatic processing with an environmental cost.
Pure ramie is a niche fabric, so supply and documentation can be limited outside East Asia.
ramie.impact: Ramie is a perennial that can be cut several times a year from the same roots, which reduces tillage, but its main environmental issue is degumming. Removing roughly a quarter to a third of the ribbon's mass as gums conventionally means boiling in alkali, then bleaching and washing, producing strong effluent that needs treatment; enzymatic and microbial degumming aims to cut those loads but is not yet the norm. Independent, dated life cycle assessments of ramie fabric are scarce, so claims of a low footprint should be treated with caution. China is the main producer and processor, which concentrates both expertise and supply-chain risk. Degummed ramie is nearly pure cellulose and biodegradable if not coated.
ramie.care: Wash ramie at 30 to 40 C with a mild detergent on a gentle cycle, and dry ramie and cotton sweaters flat so they do not stretch. Avoid wringing and heavy spinning, which set sharp creases that can crack the stiff fiber over time. Line dry woven pieces and remove them while slightly damp. Pure ramie takes a hot iron, about 200 C, best with steam while damp, much like linen; reduce the heat for blends. Avoid chlorine bleach on colors. Store garments hung or loosely rolled rather than folded tightly along the same lines, and keep them dry to prevent mildew.
faq: What is ramie fabric?

Ramie is a bast fiber from the stems of Boehmeria nivea, a nettle-family plant long grown in East Asia. It is spun into crisp, lustrous yarns similar to linen and is sold alone or blended with cotton, linen, viscose or silk.
Why were ramie and cotton sweaters so common in the 1980s?

Under US textile import quotas of the period, garments made mostly of ramie were not subject to quota limits, so importers used ramie-majority blends. Congress ended ramie's quota-free status in 1986, and ramie blends became less common afterward.
Is ramie scratchy?

Well-degummed, finely spun ramie feels smooth and cool. Coarse or insufficiently degummed ramie leaves stiff fiber ends protruding from the yarn, which can feel prickly. Blending with cotton and enzyme finishing reduce the effect.
Is ramie the same as linen?

No. Ramie comes from Boehmeria nivea and linen from flax, Linum usitatissimum. They look and behave similarly, but ramie is typically more lustrous and stiffer, and US and EU labeling rules require each to be named correctly.
notable: Garments of more than 50% ramie entered the United States without quota limits until legislation in 1986 ended ramie's quota-free status.
Ramie can be harvested several times a year from the same perennial rootstock.

recycled-wool.types: Recycled wool is classed by input. Pre-consumer material, such as spinning waste, knitting offcuts and cutting-room clippings, is clean and color-sorted; post-consumer material comes from worn garments sorted by hand for fiber and color. The older trade distinguished shoddy, torn from soft knitted or loosely woven goods and relatively long, from mungo, torn from hard-milled woven or felted cloth and shorter. Recovered fiber is usually blended with virgin wool for length or with polyamide or polyester for strength and spinnability. Certified grades follow Textile Exchange standards: the Recycled Claim Standard (RCS) applies from 5% recycled input, and the Global Recycled Standard (GRS) from 20%, with consumer-facing GRS labels requiring at least 50%.
recycled-wool.fabrics: Because the fibers are short, recycled wool is mostly carded and woollen spun rather than combed. It is woven into dense, fulled coatings such as melton and overcoat cloth, tweeds and flannels, and into blankets and throws. Knitters use it for chunky sweaters, beanies and scarves, often in heathered colors from mixed-shade fiber. Prato in Tuscany is known for regenerated carded wool cloth for coats and jackets. Recycled wool also goes into felts, upholstery fabrics, needle-punched nonwovens, insulation batts and padding, where length matters less than bulk and resilience.
recycled-wool.quality: Read the percentages: 'recycled wool' may be a minority share, blended with virgin wool, polyamide or polyester, and each must be listed by weight on US labels. Hairier, slightly harsher cloth and speckled or heathered color are normal. Pilling is the main durability risk, so choose dense, fulled weaves over loose knits for hard-wearing garments. Rub the surface: excessive loose fibers or dust point to short, over-processed fiber. Ask for a GRS or RCS certificate covering the product, not just the mill, and remember that no lab test can prove wool was recycled. Prices can be similar to virgin wool when inputs are carefully sorted.
pros: It keeps wool's warmth, moisture absorption and resilience.
It reuses fiber that would otherwise be discarded, avoiding new sheep farming for that share.
Color-sorted inputs can avoid redyeing, saving water, chemicals and energy.
Dense recycled wool cloth works well for coats, blankets and felts.
cons: Shorter fibers make yarns weaker and more prone to pilling than new wool.
Synthetic fibers are often blended in, making later recycling harder.
Mixed inputs can carry residues of previous dyes, finishes or stray fibers.
Recycled status cannot be verified in the finished fabric, so claims rely on certificates.
recycled-wool.impact: The main benefit of recycled wool is avoided virgin fiber: new wool carries land use, methane from sheep and scouring effluent, while mechanical recycling mainly needs sorting labor and electricity for tearing and carding. Where inputs are sorted by color, redyeing can be skipped. Prato has recycled wool since the mid-nineteenth century, with rag sorters called cenciaioli who could identify fibers by touch; the district is now the subject of academic case studies of circular textile networks. Independent, dated life cycle figures specific to recycled wool yarn are scarce, so percentage savings in marketing should be treated as producer claims. Blending with synthetics adds persistent microfibers and complicates end-of-life recycling.
recycled-wool.care: Care for recycled wool as for other wool, following the label for any blend. Air garments between wears, brush coats with a clothes brush, and spot clean small marks. When washing is allowed, use a wool or hand-wash cycle in cold or lukewarm water, about 30 C at most, with a wool detergent free of protease enzymes, and avoid agitation, which causes felting and shrinkage. Press water out in a towel and dry flat away from direct heat. Steam or iron at the wool setting, about 150 C (two dots), through a damp cloth. Remove pills with a comb or shaver. Store clean in breathable bags, with cedar or regular inspection against clothes moths and carpet beetles.
faq: Is recycled wool as good as new wool?

It is chemically the same wool, so it keeps warmth and moisture handling, but its fibers are shorter. That usually means more pilling and less strength, which is why it is often blended and used in dense coats, blankets and chunky knits rather than fine suiting.
How is wool recycled?

Garments and waste are sorted by fiber and color, stripped of buttons and zips, then torn and garnetted back into loose fiber. The fiber is blended, carded and spun into new woollen yarn or made into felts and nonwovens. Chemical recycling of wool is still at the research stage.
What do GRS and RCS mean on recycled wool?

They are Textile Exchange chain-of-custody standards. The Recycled Claim Standard verifies recycled content from 5% of input. The Global Recycled Standard applies from 20% recycled content, adds social, environmental and chemical requirements, and allows a consumer-facing product label only when the product contains at least 50% recycled material.
Why is recycled wool often blended with nylon or polyester?

Tearing shortens wool fibers, so spinners add longer, stronger synthetic fibers to hold the yarn together and reduce breakage and pilling. The trade-off is that a mixed-fiber product is harder to recycle again and sheds synthetic microfibers.
notable: Prato in Tuscany has recycled wool since the mid-nineteenth century, and its rag sorters, the cenciaioli, were known for identifying fibers by touch.
The old trade names shoddy and mungo distinguished longer fiber torn from soft goods from shorter fiber torn from hard-milled cloth.

recycled-polyester.types: Recycled polyester is classed by feedstock and route. Bottle-derived rPET, made from washed post-consumer bottle flake, dominates supply. Pre-consumer textile rPET comes from fiber, yarn and fabric production waste, and post-consumer textile rPET, from worn garments, is still a small niche. Mechanically recycled rPET is remelted and can carry impurities, while chemically recycled rPET is rebuilt from depolymerized monomers and can match virgin polymer. Product forms include filament yarn, flat or textured, for fleece and sportswear, staple fiber for blends, and hollow staple for fiberfill. Branded programs include Unifi's REPREVE and SEAQUAL yarn, which its initiative describes as including plastic recovered from the sea. Certified claims follow the RCS (from 5% recycled input) or the GRS (from 20%, with product labels from 50%).
recycled-polyester.fabrics: Recycled polyester appears wherever virgin polyester does. Knitted fleece, jersey and mesh are used in sportswear, base layers and sweatshirts; woven taffeta, ripstop and twill serve as jacket shells, linings, backpacks and luggage; and microfiber knits are used for towels and cleaning cloths. Hollow staple fiberfill insulates jackets, pillows and duvets. It is blended with cotton in T-shirts and with wool or viscose in suiting and knitwear, and used in carpets, upholstery and curtains. Performance finishes such as water repellents and wicking treatments are applied just as to virgin polyester.
recycled-polyester.quality: Recycled polyester should perform like virgin polyester of the same construction, so judge weight, weave or knit density and finish rather than the recycled label alone. Staple-fiber fabrics pill more than filament fabrics. Look for exact claims: '100% recycled polyester' differs from 'made with recycled materials', which may mean a small share, and the FTC Green Guides expect qualified claims when only part of a product is recycled. Ask whether feedstock was bottles or textiles, and for a GRS or RCS transaction certificate; hangtags from branded programs may be backed by tracer testing. No routine test can distinguish recycled from virgin PET in a finished garment.
pros: It performs like virgin polyester: strong, quick drying and resistant to shrinking and wrinkling.
A 2023 life cycle study found bottle-to-fiber polyester caused less environmental damage than virgin polyester fiber under every allocation method tested.
It uses an existing waste stream and reduces demand for new petrochemical feedstock.
Certified supply chains under GRS or RCS give buyers documentation for recycled content claims.
cons: Most comes from bottles, not old clothes, so it does little to solve textile waste.
Laundering still sheds polyester microfibers that persist in the environment.
Mechanically recycled PET can carry contaminants and loses chain length with each melt cycle.
Blends with cotton or elastane are difficult to recycle again.
recycled-polyester.impact: Life cycle studies generally credit recycled polyester with lower emissions and fossil resource use than virgin PET. A 2023 Thai assessment by Chairat and Gheewala in Environmental Research reported that producing bottle-grade resin and polyester fiber from waste bottles could cut greenhouse gas emissions by about 60% and fossil resource scarcity by about 85%, though the size of the benefit depended on the allocation method; the authors still favored bottle-to-bottle recycling to keep material at its highest value. Diverting bottles into clothing moves plastic into products that are rarely recycled again. Recycled content does not change shedding: in laundering tests polyester microfibers persisted in aerobic water while cotton and rayon fragments degraded.
recycled-polyester.care: Wash recycled polyester as you would virgin polyester: 30 to 40 C, inside out, on a regular or synthetic cycle. Polyester attracts oily soils, so pretreat collar and underarm grease with detergent before washing. Fabric softener can coat wicking and water-repellent finishes, so skip it on performance wear. Tumble dry on low or line dry; high heat can set wrinkles, damage elastane and melt prints. If ironing is needed, use the lowest setting, about 110 C (one dot), since polyester can glaze or melt. To reduce microfiber release, wash less often, in cooler water, and consider a filter or a fiber-catching wash bag, whose effectiveness varies.
faq: Is recycled polyester made from old clothes?

Usually not. Most recycled polyester fiber is made from plastic bottles, which are cleaner and easier to reprocess than garments with dyes, finishes and blended fibers. Textile-to-textile recycling exists but remains a very small share of supply.
Is recycled polyester better for the environment?

It usually has lower greenhouse gas emissions and fossil resource use than virgin polyester in life cycle studies. It does not stop microfiber shedding or make garments easier to recycle, and turning bottles into clothing takes them out of the bottle-to-bottle loop.
Does recycled polyester shed microplastics?

Yes. The polymer is the same PET, so recycled polyester sheds fibers in washing just as virgin polyester does, and those fragments persist in water. Cooler water, fewer washes and washing-machine filters can reduce but not eliminate release.
How can I tell if a garment is really recycled polyester?

You cannot tell by look, feel or routine lab test. Rely on documentation: a GRS or RCS certificate covering the product, a transaction certificate from the supplier, or a branded fiber program that uses tracer testing.
notable: A 2023 life cycle study found that bottle-to-fiber recycling scored well on circularity when fiber was made from 100% recycled PET, yet still recommended bottle-to-bottle recycling to keep the material at its highest value.
The Global Recycled Standard can be used business-to-business from 20% recycled content, but a GRS product label requires at least 50%.

mink.types: Mink is traded as pelts graded by sex, size, color, clarity and fur quality. Male pelts are larger with longer, coarser guard hair; female pelts are smaller, lighter and often finer, and garment makers choose between them for weight and drape. Farmed color types range from dark browns and blacks to paler mutation colors such as pastel and white, the product of generations of selective breeding. Pelts may be left natural, dyed, bleached, sheared to a velvety pile or plucked of guard hair. Construction also defines grade: full-skin garments, let-out garments in which pelts are cut into narrow diagonal strips and resewn to lengthen them, and cheaper pieced goods assembled from sections, paws or tails. Knitted mink uses narrow fur strips worked into a knit.
mink.fabrics: Mink is used as dressed skins rather than spun fiber. Full-length coats, jackets, stoles and capes are the traditional products, typically lined with silk or synthetic satin. Collars, cuffs and hood trims attach mink to wool or down outerwear, and pompoms and key chains use off-cuts. Sheared mink, trimmed to an even short pile, is used reversibly or with lighter linings. Knitted or woven mink cuts pelts into long thin strips that are knitted or woven with a yarn base, making lighter scarves and throws. Mink is also used in accessories such as hats, gloves and bag trims. Some cosmetic brushes and eyelash products have used mink hair, a separate market with its own labeling questions.
mink.quality: Quality shows in dense, even underfur that springs back when blown on, lustrous guard hairs of uniform length, and a soft, supple leather side that does not crackle. Tug gently: more than a few loose hairs suggests poor dressing or age. Matched color and seams that lie flat indicate careful construction; let-out work should show fine, even seams. Stiffness, odor, yellowing or tears in the leather indicate aging. In the US, the Fur Products Labeling Act requires labels to give the animal name, country of origin for imported fur, and whether the fur is dyed or bleached, pieced from paws, tails or bellies, or used. A missing or vague label is a red flag. Price depends heavily on construction and whether the pelts are whole.
pros: Dense underfur and guard hair give high warmth for weight and good wind resistance.
Well-dressed and stored mink garments can last many years and be remodeled.
The pelt surface sheds light rain and snow.
Mink is lighter and more supple than many longer-haired furs.
cons: Farming animals in cages raises welfare concerns that EFSA found could not be fully mitigated in current systems.
Sale and farming are restricted or banned in a growing number of jurisdictions.
It requires specialist cleaning and cool, ventilated storage.
Species and origin are hard for buyers to verify without documentation.
mink.impact: Mink impact debates center on animal welfare, disease and processing. The 2025 EFSA opinion found that key welfare consequences of cage systems could not be prevented within them, and experimental work shows farmed mink in non-enriched cages develop more stereotypic behavior, such as pacing, than those given enrichment. SARS-CoV-2 outbreaks on mink farms in 2020 showed how dense animal husbandry can create zoonotic risk. Environmentally, mink are carnivores fed on animal by-products, and pelts must be dressed and often dyed with chemical treatments; this review found no independent, peer-reviewed life cycle comparison of mink with faux fur, so claims on either side should be treated as contested. Legal context is shifting: California banned the sale of new fur products from 2023.
mink.care: Fur needs specialist care, and the label and a qualified furrier govern. Store mink on a broad, shaped hanger in a breathable cloth bag, never plastic, in a cool, dark, ventilated place; many owners use professional cold storage in warm months to protect against heat, humidity and insects. Keep it away from perfume, hairspray and shoulder-bag straps, which abrade and stain. If it gets wet, shake it out and hang it to dry at room temperature away from radiators; do not brush or use a hair dryer. Never iron, machine wash or home dry clean it. Have it professionally cleaned about once a year and small tears repaired promptly before they spread. Heat, light and dryness cause the leather to become brittle.
faq: How can I tell real mink from faux fur?

Part the hair at the base. Real fur grows from leather skin, while faux fur is attached to a knitted or woven fabric backing. Real hair tapers to a fine point and a singed hair smells of burnt hair, whereas acrylic faux fur melts. A label is required in the US for fur products.
Is it legal to sell mink in California?

Since 1 January 2023, California law (AB 44) has prohibited selling, offering, displaying for sale or manufacturing new fur products, with exceptions such as used or vintage fur, religious and tribal use, and certain species. Other jurisdictions have their own rules, so check the local law.
How long does a mink coat last?

With professional cleaning and proper cool storage, a mink coat can last for decades, and furriers can remodel or reline it. Heat, dryness and improper storage make the leather brittle and cause hair loss. Visible tears, stiffness or heavy shedding signal that the leather is deteriorating.
What does 'let-out' mink mean?

Letting out is a furrier technique in which each pelt is cut into narrow diagonal strips and sewn back together offset, making the skin longer and narrower. It creates long, flowing vertical lines in a coat and uses skilled labor, which is why let-out garments usually cost more than those made from whole or pieced skins.
notable: The US Truth in Fur Labeling Act of 2010 ended an exemption that had let fur items with less than $150 of fur go unlabeled.
Studies of farmed mink found that animals raised in barren cages show more stereotypic pacing and that enrichment reduces it.
California became the first US state to ban the sale and manufacture of new fur products, effective 1 January 2023.

fox.types: Fox fur comes from two farmed species in many color phases. Red fox, Vulpes vulpes, supplies natural red, silver and cross fox and other mutations; Arctic fox, Vulpes lagopus, supplies the trade's blue fox and its paler and shadowed variants, as well as white. Wild-caught red and gray fox pelts also enter the trade in some countries. Pelts are graded by size, color, density, guard hair length and damage. Fox is often dyed in bright colors, sheared or finished as long-haired pompoms. Cheaper products may be pieced from sections, paws or tails, which US labels must disclose. Because long fox hair can disguise species, farmed color names such as silver or blue fox do not substitute for the species name.
fox.fabrics: Fox is used mainly as trim: hood ruffs, collars, cuffs, headbands and pompoms on hats, shoes and bags. Its long, lofty pile makes dramatic stoles, boas and full coats, often in let-out or feathered constructions to control bulk. Fox tails and sections are sold as key chains and accessories. Dyed fox appears in fashion colors, and sheared fox gives a shorter, denser surface. Some products knit narrow fox strips into a yarn base to make lighter scarves and vests. Hood trims on down parkas are one of the largest volume uses, and on low-priced items the fur's species and origin are the least likely to be documented.
fox.quality: Good fox has long, glossy guard hairs of even length over a thick, soft underfur, with no bald or broken patches, and a supple leather side. Tug lightly at the hair: excessive shedding suggests poor dressing. Check that trims are sewn or clipped neatly and that the leather does not crack when flexed. On trims, part the hair to see skin rather than a knit backing to confirm real fur, and look for the label. In the US, the Fur Products Labeling Act and FTC rules require the animal name, origin of imported fur and disclosure of dyeing and pieced sections. In California, sale of new fur products has been illegal since 2023. Very cheap real fur trim warrants scrutiny of species and labeling.
pros: Very long, lofty hair gives a voluminous look and high insulation around the face.
Fox trims can be detached and reused on new garments.
It dyes readily in bright or natural shades.
Well-kept fox can be remodeled or reused.
cons: Farming in cages raises welfare concerns identified by EFSA in 2025.
Long hair tangles, mats and sheds with friction, especially on collars and cuffs.
Legal restrictions on fox farming and fur sales are expanding in several countries and states.
Species, origin and dyeing are hard for buyers to verify.
fox.impact: Fox fur's footprint is dominated by farming practice and legal and ethical debate. The 2025 EFSA scientific opinion identified restricted movement, inability to explore or forage, and species-specific problems such as locomotory disorders in Arctic foxes as consequences of current cages. Several countries have acted: Norway, once a notable producer of fox and mink pelts, completed a phase-out with compensation for farmers, and its ban took effect in February 2025. In the EU, the Fur Free Europe citizens' initiative gathered about 1.5 million signatures; the Commission requested an EFSA opinion and said it would decide on next steps after that, with its decision expected in 2026. Dressing and dyeing chemistry adds processing impacts, but independent life cycle data are scarce.
fox.care: Treat fox as a delicate pelt; follow the label and a qualified furrier. Store garments on wide, padded hangers in breathable cloth covers, never sealed plastic, in a cool, dark and ventilated space, and use professional cold storage in warm, humid climates. Remove fur trims from parkas before washing the parka. If the fur gets wet, shake it and let it dry naturally at room temperature, then gently shake again to restore loft; never use a hair dryer or radiator. Avoid friction from bags and seatbelts, and keep perfume and hairspray away. Do not iron, machine wash or brush heavily. Have the fur professionally cleaned periodically and inspect for moth or beetle damage during storage.
faq: What is the difference between silver fox and blue fox?

They are different species. Silver fox is a color phase of the red fox, Vulpes vulpes, with black fur tipped in silver. Blue fox is the trade name for farmed Arctic fox, Vulpes lagopus, typically in grayish-blue tones. Both are farmed in many mutation colors.
Is fox fur trim on a parka real?

It may be. Part the hair at the base: a leather skin means real fur, while a fabric knit means faux. In the US, fur trim must be labeled with the animal name and origin under the Fur Products Labeling Act. Real fur can also carry an EU notice on textile products that contain animal parts.
Where is fox farming banned?

Several European countries have banned or are phasing out fur farming, and Norway's ban took effect in February 2025. The EU was considering an EU-wide measure following the Fur Free Europe citizens' initiative. California bans the sale of new fur products. Rules change, so check current local law.
How should I clean a fox fur collar?

Do not wash it. Detach it from the garment if possible, shake out dust, and let a fur specialist clean it. If it gets wet, dry it naturally at room temperature and shake to restore the loft. Store it in a breathable bag in a cool, dark place.
notable: Norway, once home to nearly 300 fur farms, ended fur farming in February 2025 after a compensated phase-out.
The Fur Free Europe citizens' initiative collected about 1.5 million signatures asking the EU to end fur farming and the sale of farmed fur.
Blue fox is not a separate animal: it is the trade name for farmed Arctic fox.
