tanuki.types: Raccoon dog fur is sold under several names, which is itself the main buyer issue: tanuki (Japanese), Finnraccoon (Nordic farmed), and, in older US trade usage, Asiatic raccoon. Pelts come from farms in China and Finland and, less commonly, from wild animals. Farmed stock includes a wild-type grizzled gray-brown and several color mutations. Pelts are graded by size, density, guard hair length and color, and are frequently dyed or tipped to imitate other furs, or sheared. Because the raccoon dog is a canid, it is a different animal from the North American raccoon, Procyon lotor, and trade names should never replace the species name.
tanuki.fabrics: Raccoon dog fur is used above all as trim: hood ruffs on parkas and down jackets, collars, cuffs, and pompoms on hats, boots, bags and key chains. Its long, shaggy pile gives volume at low weight. Full coats, vests and stoles exist but are less common than trim. Dyed raccoon dog is used in bright fashion colors, including in low-cost accessories. Faux fur in acrylic or modacrylic imitates it for the same uses. Because trims and pompoms are small, they are easy to sell without clear species information, which is why labeling rules matter most here.
tanuki.quality: Check first that the item is labeled and names the species correctly. Parting the hair to find skin rather than a knitted backing confirms real fur; a faux pompom has a fabric base and hair that melts when singed. Good pelts have long, even guard hairs over dense underfur and supple leather without cracks or odor. In the US, the Fur Products Labeling Act requires the animal name and country of origin, and the Truth in Fur Labeling Act of 2010 removed an exemption that had let items with less than $150 of fur go unlabeled; the legislative record cites raccoon dog fur sold under other animal names. A cheap pompom described as faux but with a skin base is mislabeled.
pros: Long, voluminous guard hair gives a full, lofty trim at low weight.
It insulates well around hoods and collars.
It dyes readily in many colors.
It has usually been cheaper than fox or mink.
cons: Species confusion and mislabeling are documented, including sale under other animal names.
Welfare concerns in cage farming were highlighted by EFSA in 2025.
The species is listed as an invasive alien species of Union concern in the EU, which restricts keeping and breeding.
Long hair tangles and sheds, and dressed skins need specialist care.
tanuki.impact: Raccoon dog fur combines farm welfare issues with ecological and public health concerns. EFSA's 2025 opinion identified locomotory disorders and isolation stress among welfare consequences for caged raccoon dogs. Introduced populations have spread widely in Europe, and the EU added it to its list of invasive alien species of Union concern under Regulation (EU) No 1143/2014 through Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1262, with a transition period that allowed member states to seek authorization for continued farming. Mixed-species farms have also recorded viral infections in raccoon dogs. Processing adds dressing and dyeing chemistry, and independent life cycle data are lacking.
tanuki.care: Care follows general fur practice; the label and a furrier govern. Detach trims from parkas before washing the garment. Store items on padded hangers or flat in breathable cotton bags, never sealed plastic, in a cool, dark and ventilated place, and inspect them for moth and carpet beetle larvae. If the fur gets wet, shake it and let it dry at room temperature, away from heat, then shake again to restore the loft; never use a hair dryer or iron. Keep perfume and hairspray away. Have soiled pieces cleaned by a fur specialist rather than washing them. Pompoms can be fluffed by gently shaking; brushing tears long guard hairs.
faq: Is tanuki fur raccoon fur?

No. Tanuki is the Japanese name for the raccoon dog, Nyctereutes procyonoides, a member of the dog family. The North American raccoon, Procyon lotor, is an unrelated animal. US labels should use the correct animal name, and raccoon dog should not be described as raccoon.
How can I tell if a 'faux fur' pompom is real?

Part the hair at the base. Real fur is attached to leather skin; faux fur is attached to a knitted or woven fabric. You can also pull a hair or two and singe them carefully: real hair smells like burnt hair and curls to ash, while acrylic melts into a bead.
Is it legal to farm raccoon dogs in Europe?

The raccoon dog is on the EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern, which generally prohibits keeping and breeding. A transition period allowed member states to seek authorization for continued farming. National fur farming bans also apply in several countries, so rules depend on the country and date.
What is Finnraccoon?

Finnraccoon is a trade name for raccoon dog fur from farms in Finland. It refers to the same species, Nyctereutes procyonoides, as tanuki. Trade names should appear alongside, not instead of, the species name.
notable: The EU listed the raccoon dog as an invasive alien species of Union concern in 2019, with a transition period linked to requests to continue fur farming.
Congressional reports on the 2010 Truth in Fur Labeling Act described raccoon dog fur being sold as other animals or unlabeled because of a $150 exemption.
Despite its name and masked face, the raccoon dog is a canid, more closely related to foxes than to raccoons.

yangir.types: No standardized grades for yangir exist. Italian producer and brand pages describe it as the fine undercoat of the Siberian ibex, sometimes written Capra ibex sibirica, with a natural golden color, and at least one quotes an average diameter of about 13.5 microns. A peer-reviewed study by Tonin and colleagues (Textile Research Journal, 2002) described yangir as wild cashmere taken from wild goats hunted for meat and trophies, principally subspecies of Capra ibex, and used as a substitute for shahtoosh. Whether a given product comes from Capra sibirica or another wild Capra, and how pure it is, cannot be judged from the name. Trade forms include dehaired fiber, yarn and finished scarves or shawls, and the name also appears loosely in product listings mixed with other fibers.
yangir.fabrics: Yangir appears almost exclusively as luxury accessories and small-batch cloth: shawls, stoles and scarves, sometimes woven very fine in the manner of shahtoosh or pashmina, and occasional knitwear. Italian worsted and woollen mills and knitwear brands describe it as a premium noble fiber, and it is sometimes blended with cashmere or silk to extend a scarce supply. Garments are usually undyed or lightly dyed to preserve its natural tone. Because volumes are tiny and supply chains opaque, any specific product claim, including the fiber's share in a blend, should be treated as the seller's statement until supported by documentation or testing.
yangir.quality: A buyer has very little to go on beyond the seller's documentation. Genuine fine caprine down feels warm, very soft and slightly dry, with natural color variation if undyed. Ask for the species, country of origin, how the fiber was obtained and any permits required, plus a test report giving mean fiber diameter and species identification. Tonin and colleagues showed that scanning electron microscopy of cuticle patterns and differential scanning calorimetry could separate yangir from domestic cashmere and shahtoosh, so laboratory confirmation is feasible. Prices far above cashmere are expected; prices near cashmere suggest a blend or a mislabel. Any link to shahtoosh, which comes from the protected Tibetan antelope, is a serious red flag.
pros: Reported fiber fineness is comparable to fine cashmere.
Its natural golden tone can be used undyed.
Laboratory methods exist to distinguish it from domestic cashmere and shahtoosh.
In some cases it uses fiber from animals already hunted for other purposes, according to the 2002 study.
cons: It comes from wild animals, so supply, legality and sustainability depend on hunting controls.
There are no public grading standards, and claims are rarely independently verified.
Volumes are tiny and prices extreme, which invites substitution and mislabeling.
Like cashmere, it pills, felts and is attacked by moths.
yangir.impact: Yangir's footprint is small in volume but raises conservation questions. Tonin and colleagues warned in 2002 that, although legal, large-scale use of these fibers and hybridization of ibex with domestic goats to improve fiber yield could threaten wild ibex. The fiber has been promoted partly as an alternative to shahtoosh, whose trade drove poaching of the Tibetan antelope, but substitution only helps if yangir supply is itself legal and sustainable. How fiber is collected, from hunted animals, captive animals or shed coat, determines the welfare and ecological picture, and this review found no independent documentation of producers' collection methods. Dehairing and spinning follow cashmere practice, so processing impacts would be similar in kind, but no yangir-specific data were found.
yangir.care: Treat yangir like the finest cashmere and follow the maker's instructions. Hand wash cool, about 20 to 30 C, in a wool or cashmere shampoo, without rubbing or wringing; rinse at the same temperature to avoid felting. Press out water in a towel and dry flat away from heat and sunlight. Do not tumble dry. If needed, steam lightly or iron on the wool setting (two dots, about 150 C) through a damp cloth. Many owners prefer professional cleaning for fine shawls. Remove pills with a cashmere comb. Store clean, folded, in breathable cotton, with regular inspection for clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae, which target fine animal fibers.
faq: What is yangir?

Yangir is a trade name for the fine undercoat of wild ibex, described by sellers as Siberian ibex. A 2002 study called it wild cashmere taken mainly from wild goats hunted for meat and trophies and noted its use as a substitute for shahtoosh. It is rare, expensive and poorly documented, so product claims need evidence.
Is yangir finer than cashmere?

At least one seller quotes an average diameter of about 13.5 microns, which is within the range of fine cashmere, so it is comparable rather than clearly finer. Independent test data for commercial yangir are scarce. Ask for a laboratory report on the specific lot if fineness justifies the price.
Is yangir legal?

The 2002 study described it as legal at that time, but legality depends on the species, country of origin, hunting permits and any wildlife trade rules that apply. Ask the seller for species and origin documentation. Shahtoosh, the fiber yangir sometimes substitutes for, is banned in international commercial trade.
How can yangir be told apart from cashmere?

Specialist laboratories can compare cuticle scale patterns under scanning electron microscopy and measure thermal behavior with differential scanning calorimetry, methods shown to separate yangir, cashmere and shahtoosh. DNA or protein tests against authenticated reference fiber can add confirmation.
notable: A 2002 Textile Research Journal study showed that differential scanning calorimetry could distinguish yangir, cashmere and shahtoosh even after dehairing.
The same study warned that hybridizing ibex with domestic goats to improve fiber yield could threaten the conservation of wild ibex.

cervelt.types: Cervelt is a single proprietary fiber rather than a family of grades. Its website says it was developed by Douglas Creek Ltd, a New Zealand company, over about eight years, and describes it as the down of the New Zealand red deer, Cervus elaphus. The producer states a diameter of about 13 microns and that only about 20 grams of pure fiber can be collected per deer. These are producer claims and were not independently verified here. It is sold as dehaired fiber and as yarn, for example by New Zealand yarn and knitwear businesses, and in blends. Retail listings sometimes pair the name with other fibers, such as 'yangir cervelt', so the fiber content line matters more than the name.
cervelt.fabrics: Cervelt is used for small quantities of luxury knitwear and accessories: sweaters, stoles, scarves, beanies and socks, sometimes as 100% Cervelt and often blended with merino, cashmere or silk to extend supply and add strength. New Zealand knitwear makers sell Cervelt garments under their own labels, and a New Zealand newspaper reported Cervelt socks priced at $1,700 a pair. Yarn for hand knitting is sold in small skeins. Because output is limited, woven cloth is rare. The producer says the fiber has a wavy curl that spins into a resilient yarn and absorbs and releases moisture readily, which would suit next-to-skin knits, but these are marketing claims.
cervelt.quality: Buyers should ask for the fiber share, since blends are common, and for any laboratory report of mean diameter and species. Real fine down feels soft, warm and slightly springy; a harsh or slick hand suggests a different or treated fiber. Check knit density and seams as for cashmere: loose, lofty knits pill faster. Because deer is not a named specialty fiber under the US Wool Products Labeling Act, a US label would normally say deer hair or similar, and in the EU it falls under animal hair; a label reading only 'Cervelt' is incomplete. Extreme prices are expected, so a low price is a warning sign. Provenance can be checked with the maker and with DNA or protein testing laboratories.
pros: The producer reports fineness comparable to fine cashmere.
Its producer says the fiber's wavy curl spins into a strong, resilient yarn.
Blends with merino or cashmere can extend warmth and softness into lighter garments.
Published microscopy shows red deer underhair is structurally close to fine wool.
cons: Very limited supply makes it costly and hard to buy or verify.
Performance claims come mainly from the producer and sellers.
It is often blended, so the Cervelt share of a garment may be small.
Like other fine animal fibers, it pills, felts and attracts moths.
cervelt.impact: Cervelt's environmental and welfare profile cannot be independently assessed from public sources. It derives from New Zealand's farmed red deer industry, which raises deer mainly for venison and velvet antler, so the fiber would be a minor co-product of a pastoral system with its own land use and emissions. How the down is collected, whether by combing, shearing or from slaughtered animals, is not publicly documented in detail, and no life cycle assessment or welfare audit specific to Cervelt was found. At an estimated 20 grams per animal according to the producer, total volumes are tiny. A buyer interested in impact should ask the maker for collection methods, farm standards and any third-party audits.
cervelt.care: Treat Cervelt like fine cashmere unless the maker says otherwise. Hand wash in cool water, about 20 to 30 C, with a wool or cashmere detergent, without rubbing or wringing; rinse at the same temperature. Roll in a towel to remove water and dry flat, away from sunlight and radiators. Do not tumble dry. Steam lightly or iron on the wool setting (two dots, about 150 C) through a damp cloth if needed. Remove pills with a cashmere comb and store folded, clean, in breathable bags with regular checks for clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae. Blends with silk or merino follow the more delicate fiber's rules.
faq: What is Cervelt made from?

Cervelt is a trade name for the fine winter undercoat, or down, of farmed New Zealand red deer. According to its producer, it was developed by Douglas Creek Ltd, measures about 13 microns and yields only about 20 grams per deer. These are producer statements; independent test data are limited.
Is Cervelt softer than cashmere?

The producer claims it is lighter and softer than cashmere, and its stated 13 micron diameter is within the fine cashmere range. Independent comparative tests were not found. Softness also depends on spinning, knitting and finishing, so compare actual garments rather than fiber names.
Why is Cervelt so expensive?

Supply is very small: the producer says only about 20 grams of pure fiber can be collected per deer, and dehairing fine down from coarse deer hair is labor intensive. Luxury knitwear makers sell it in small batches. A newspaper report of $1,700 socks illustrates the price level.
How should Cervelt be labeled?

Cervelt is a trade name, not a generic fiber name. In the US a label would normally identify the animal, for example deer hair, with percentages; in the EU deer fiber falls under animal hair. The trade name can appear alongside, not instead of, that disclosure.
notable: According to its producer, only about 20 grams of pure Cervelt can be collected from a single deer.
A New Zealand newspaper reported socks made with Cervelt selling for $1,700 a pair.

abaca.types: Commercial abaca is sorted two ways: by plant variety and by fiber grade. Philippine breeders work with varieties such as Abuab, Inosa and Tangongon, and have developed Dioscoro 1, a backcross of the high-quality Abuab variety with Pacol, a wild Musa balbisiana that resists bunchy top virus. Fiber grades follow PNS/BAFS 180:2016 for hand-stripped and spindle-stripped fiber and PNS/BAFS 181:2016 for decorticated fiber. Letter grades such as S2, S3, I, G, H, JK and M1 reflect stripping cleanliness, color and texture. A machine-vision grading study describes I as pale yellow, G as dull and prone to bundling, H and M1 as dark brown to nearly black and used mainly for rope, and JK as going largely to pulp. Y1 is a residual grade for weak, stained or soiled fiber.
abaca.fabrics: Most abaca never becomes cloth. Much of it is pulped for strong, porous specialty papers such as tea bags and filters, and much of the rest becomes marine and industrial cordage. In apparel, abaca yarns appear in Philippine handloom fabrics, and barong makers sell abaca and jusi fabrics, describing jusi as woven from abaca or silk, so the actual fiber should be confirmed. Abaca pulp is also the base of some Japanese paper yarns: Oji Fiber states that its OJO+ yarn is made from Manila hemp paper slit into narrow tapes and twisted. Abaca also reinforces composites and is plaited or woven into bags, mats and hats.
abaca.quality: For raw fiber, ask for the PNS grade code and the extraction route, because hand-stripped, spindle-stripped and decorticated fiber are graded under different standards. Good fiber is long, lustrous, evenly colored and free of pulp residue, stains and mustiness; dark, brittle or dusty strands point to lower grades or poor drying. On finished goods, the label should say abaca, with Manila hemp at most as a synonym; a label saying only hemp misidentifies the plant. In handwoven cloth, even weft packing and neat joins signal careful work. Rope sold as manila should be checked for polypropylene imitations, which melt instead of charring.
pros: Abaca combines high tensile strength with good resistance to saltwater decay, the basis of its long use in marine rope.
Its long, low-lignin fibers make strong yet porous specialty papers, including tea bag and filter papers.
Like other Musa crops it is propagated from suckers and grown as a near-perennial plantation, so stands are harvested repeatedly without yearly replanting.
Paper yarns made from abaca pulp are light and low in shrinkage and, according to their producer, do not pill.
cons: Elongation at break of only about 2 to 4 percent makes abaca stiff and harsh against the skin.
Visual grading is subjective, and a 2012 study critically evaluated how well existing grades reflect measured fiber properties.
Abaca bunchy top virus damages plantations and makes supply volatile.
Apparel-grade abaca cloth is scarce and costly because most fiber goes to cordage, pulp and crafts.
abaca.impact: No peer-reviewed cradle-to-gate footprint for abaca fiber was found in this pass, so carbon-benefit claims, including Oji Fiber's statement that abaca absorbs carbon dioxide well, should be read as producer statements. What is documented is agronomic. Abaca is a Philippine smallholder crop propagated vegetatively, which lets viruses accumulate in planting material, and abaca bunchy top virus, described in 2007 as its own babuvirus species, is a major disease pressure. Breeders at the University of the Philippines Los Banos have responded with resistant backcross hybrids such as Dioscoro 1. PhilFIDA's Abaca Sustainability Manual sets out farm practices and explains Rainforest Alliance certification criteria for growers who seek it. Hand stripping is heavy, repetitive labor, and because grades set prices, poor tools and low grades cut farm income.
abaca.care: Most abaca products are handled rather than laundered. Dry abaca rope and cordage fully before storage, coil it loosely off concrete floors and keep it out of prolonged sun, since UV and repeated damp storage weaken cellulose fibers. For abaca or jusi barong fabric and other sheer handwovens, the label governs; general practice is gentle hand washing in cool water with a mild, neutral detergent, no wringing, and drying flat or on a padded hanger in shade. Iron while slightly damp at a medium to hot setting, with a pressing cloth over embroidery, and lower the heat if the fabric contains silk. Abaca creases sharply, so hang or roll garments rather than folding them tightly. Mold is the main storage risk in humid climates.
faq: Is Manila hemp the same as hemp?

No. Manila hemp is a trade name for abaca, the leaf-sheath fiber of Musa textilis, a close relative of the banana. True hemp is the stem fiber of Cannabis sativa. The plants, fiber structures and uses differ, so labels should name abaca rather than hemp alone.
What do abaca grade codes like S2 or JK mean?

They are Philippine grade designations under PNS/BAFS 180:2016 and 181:2016 that encode stripping cleanliness, color and texture. Pale, clean grades command higher prices and suit specialty pulp; dark grades such as H and M1 go mainly to rope, JK largely to pulp, and residual grades such as Y1 cover weak or stained fiber.
Why is abaca used in tea bags?

Its long, strong, low-lignin fibers form thin paper that holds together when wet yet stays porous enough for water to pass through. Wet strength also depends on papermaking conditions and any bonding agents, so the fiber is one factor among several in tea bag performance.
Can abaca fabric be washed?

Usually, gently. Hand wash sheer abaca or jusi cloth in cool water with mild detergent, avoid wringing, and dry in shade. Heavy or embroidered formal pieces are often safer with a professional cleaner. The garment's care label takes priority over general advice.
notable: The Philippine abaca hybrid Dioscoro 1 carries roughly 87.5 percent Abuab alleles and 12.5 percent alleles from Pacol, a bunchy-top-resistant wild banana.
Abaca bunchy top virus was formally described in 2007 as a new babuvirus, serologically distinct from banana bunchy top virus.
Some Japanese washi yarns sold for knitting are made from abaca pulp rather than from traditional kozo.

sisal.types: Sisal is traded as line fiber, short fiber and tow, yarn and twine, and woven floor covering, and each form has its own quality language. East African exporters sell line fiber under grade names such as 3L, UG and SSUG, which describe length, color and cleanliness: exporters describe 3L as long fiber of about 90 cm or more, whitish to yellowish and well brushed, while SSUG allows darker, blemished strands. Short fiber and brushing tow go to padding, pulp and composites. In floor coverings, sisal is sold by weave, yarn thickness and backing rather than by fiber grade. Products described as sisal-look or sisal-style may be wool, polypropylene or other plant fibers, so the fiber content line matters more than the name.
sisal.fabrics: Sisal's largest outlets are agricultural binder and baler twine, rope, and floor coverings such as tightly woven rugs, stair runners and wall-to-wall carpet. It is also used for brush bristles, buffing wheels for metal polishing, the compressed bristle of traditional dartboards, cat scratching posts, padding in upholstery and mattresses, and geotextiles. Chopped sisal reinforces cement, geopolymer and polymer composites, and sisal nanofibers are studied in films. Fine sisal yarns can be crocheted or woven into bags and hats, but the fiber's stiffness keeps it out of most apparel.
sisal.quality: A good sisal rug feels firm and slightly waxy, with even, tightly packed yarns, no loose ends and no backing showing through the weave. Color should be consistent; blotches or rings can indicate water exposure in storage. Read the label: sisal (Agave sisalana) differs from henequen, jute, coir and polypropylene look-alikes, and blends must be declared. A flame test on a snipped fiber separates plastic, which melts, from sisal, which chars. For twine and rope, ask for breaking load, length per kilogram and any oil or preservative treatment. Finer yarns and denser weaves cost more but show wear and stains less.
pros: Sisal is strong and abrasion tolerant, which suits rope, twine and floor coverings.
Its stiff, textured yarns give rugs a firm surface that resists crushing.
The plant grows in semi-arid regions, such as Bahia in Brazil, where few other crops yield a cash fiber.
Sisal twine is biodegradable and can replace plastic twine in agriculture.
cons: Water can shrink, distort and stain sisal floor coverings, so they suit dry rooms only.
The hard fibers feel scratchy underfoot and against the skin.
Stains are hard to remove because wet cleaning methods are ruled out.
Dust from sisal brushing and spinning has been linked to byssinosis and other respiratory symptoms in mill workers.
sisal.impact: A 2017 life cycle assessment in the Journal of Cleaner Production found that sisal fiber's greenhouse gas result depends strongly on local practice: wet disposal of leaf residues can release methane, and fertilizer use and transport distance also shift the outcome, so no single footprint figure applies to all sisal. Because only a small fraction of the leaf becomes fiber, residue management dominates the environmental picture. Occupational health is the best-documented social issue. A 1978 study of six Tanzanian sisal factories found byssinosis in about 5 percent of spinning workers but about 48 percent of brushing workers, linked to long exposure, heavy dust and smoking. A Croatian study of sisal textile workers recorded worsening respiratory symptoms at a 19-year follow-up.
sisal.care: Clean sisal rugs dry. Vacuum often, using suction only or a beater bar set high, and rotate the rug periodically to even out wear and sun fading. Blot spills at once with a dry white towel, working from the edge inward, and do not rub. Sellers of sisal floor coverings warn against steam cleaning and wet shampooing, which can shrink, distort, streak or discolor the fiber, and recommend dry-extraction compounds or professional dry cleaning instead. If a spot must be dampened, use as little water as possible and dry it quickly with moving air. Keep sisal out of bathrooms, kitchens, entryways and damp basements, where shrinkage and mold are likely. A rug pad reduces abrasion from grit.
faq: Can a sisal rug get wet?

Small spills are manageable if blotted immediately, but soaking is damaging. Sisal absorbs water readily, swelling and then shrinking or distorting as it dries, and water can leave brown streaks or rings. Sisal floor-covering sellers advise against steam cleaning and wet shampooing for this reason and recommend dry extraction methods.
Is sisal the same as henequen or jute?

No. Sisal is Agave sisalana and henequen is Agave fourcroydes; both are hard leaf fibers that look alike, and Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists them as separate fiber names. Jute is a softer stem fiber from Corchorus species and is used for different rugs and sacking.
Why do sisal rugs change color after cleaning?

Water applied to natural fiber floor coverings can draw out soluble plant matter and soil and leave streaks or color changes as it dries. That is why sisal sellers recommend dry extraction cleaning and blotting spills quickly rather than wet shampooing or steam.
Is sisal dust harmful?

For household rugs, ordinary vacuuming is not considered a special hazard. In factories, heavy sisal dust is a documented occupational risk: a 1978 Tanzanian study found byssinosis in nearly half of workers in brushing departments, and a Croatian study linked sisal textile work to declining lung function.
notable: In a 1978 study of six Tanzanian sisal factories, byssinosis affected about 48 percent of brushing-department workers but only about 5 percent of spinning workers.
A 2017 life cycle assessment found that whether sisal leaf residues are disposed of wet or dry can change the fiber's greenhouse gas result, because wet residues can release methane.

coir.types: Coir is first split by husk maturity. White coir comes from husks of coconuts harvested shortly before ripening; it is finer, softer and weaker, and is traditionally retted in water for months before being spun into yarn for mats, twine and rope. Brown coir comes from fully mature husks; it is thicker, stronger and more abrasion resistant, and goes into brushes, doormats, upholstery padding and rope. Both are further sorted by length: fibers about 20 cm or longer are bristle fiber, while shorter, finer fibers are mattress fiber. In India, hand-spun yarns carry regional names such as Anjengo, Aratory and Ashtamudi, the last a thick, shiny yarn used mostly for rope, and yarn and matting fineness is expressed in a unit called scorage.
coir.fabrics: Coir yarn is woven into matting, mats and runners; Coir Board specifications describe matting in scorages of roughly 12 to 20. Tufted and brush-cut doormats set stiff brown fiber on end, and rope and twine use thicker yarns. Curled mattress fiber is bonded with rubber latex into rubberized coir pads for mattresses and upholstery. Woven nets and needled blankets of coir serve as geotextiles for slope and riverbank erosion control while vegetation establishes. Coir pith, the spongy particles left after fiber extraction, is a separate product sold as a growing medium.
coir.quality: Doormats should feel dense and springy, with fiber packed tightly enough that the backing is hard to see; sparse tufts shed quickly. Brown coir should be evenly brown and stiff, while pale, soft white coir suits yarn goods but wears faster underfoot. Many mats have PVC backings, so check the label if you want an all-natural product. For geotextiles, specifications should state mass per square meter, open area and tensile strength. For growing media, ask whether the pith was washed or buffered, since growers use those steps to manage salt content. Dyed polypropylene bristle is a common look-alike and melts in a flame instead of charring.
pros: Brown coir is tough and unusually extensible for a plant fiber, so it survives constant scraping in doormats and brushes.
It resists microbial decay and seawater better than most cellulosic fibers.
It is a byproduct of coconut production, so no land is farmed for the fiber alone.
Coir geotextiles hold soil while plants establish and then biodegrade in place.
cons: It is too coarse and stiff for apparel or for bedding in direct contact with skin.
Traditional long retting in lagoons and backwaters releases polyphenols and organic load into the water.
Its high lignin content makes it darken in light and hard to bleach or dye to pale shades.
Doormats shed fibers, and mats with PVC backing are not fully biodegradable.
coir.impact: Because coir comes from husks, a byproduct of the coconut crop, its land and water footprint is largely attributed to coconut farming, but processing matters. Long retting of husks in Kerala's backwaters releases polyphenols and organic matter into the water, and researchers have studied cleaner routes such as mechanical defibering, steam explosion and microbial softening. Dry milling of green husks avoids months of retting but produces only mattress fiber, while mature husks in crushing mills need only about 7 to 10 days of retting. Many coir doormats are backed with PVC, which adds a fossil-based, hard-to-recycle layer. No comprehensive life cycle assessment covering the full coir supply chain was identified in this pass.
coir.care: Shake or beat coir doormats outdoors and vacuum them regularly, because embedded grit abrades the fibers. Brush out dried mud with a stiff brush rather than washing it in. Coir tolerates wetting better than most plant fibers, so a mat can be rinsed with plain water and a little mild detergent, but it must dry completely, standing on edge in airy shade; a mat left soggy on a hard floor can rot, stain the floor or grow mold. Avoid bleach, which weakens and blotches the fiber. Printed mats fade in direct sun. Rubberized coir mattress pads need ventilation and should not be soaked. Replace mats when the pile flattens and sheds heavily.
faq: What is the difference between brown and white coir?

Brown coir comes from mature coconut husks and is thick, strong and abrasion resistant, used for brushes, doormats and padding. White coir comes from husks harvested shortly before ripening; it is finer, softer and weaker, and is traditionally retted for months, then spun into yarn for mats, twine and rope.
Is coir the same as coco peat?

No. Coir fiber is the long strand from the husk, used for mats, rope, brushes and geotextiles. Coco peat, or coir pith, is the spongy dust and short particles left after the fiber is removed; it is used in potting mixes and should be washed or buffered by the supplier.
Can a coir doormat get wet?

Yes, more than most natural fiber mats, since coir resists rot and seawater comparatively well. The problem is drying: a mat that stays wet on a hard floor can mold or stain the floor. Stand it on edge in shade until fully dry before putting it back.
Why does my coir mat shed?

Brush-cut and tufted coir mats are made of short, stiff fibers set on end, and some loose ends work free with foot traffic, especially in the first weeks. Heavy, continuing shedding usually means low fiber density or worn tufts, and the mat is due for replacement.
notable: White coir from immature husks is traditionally retted in water for up to about ten months, while mature husks in crushing mills may need only 7 to 10 days.
Coir fibers at least about 20 cm long are classed as bristle fiber, while shorter, finer ones become mattress fiber.

kenaf.types: Kenaf is sold as two fractions of the same stalk with very different uses: long bast fiber from the outer bark and short, absorbent core fiber from the woody center, often called kenaf core. Bast fiber is judged by extraction route, fineness, color and cleanliness; water-retted fiber is finer and brighter than fiber from fast chemical or purely mechanical routes, which tend to be shorter or weaker. Buyers also meet kenaf as whole-stalk pulp for paper and as needle-punched or thermally bonded nonwoven mats. Cultivars differ in fiber yield and maturity, so seed choice depends on region. Trade statistics often group kenaf with jute and allied fibers, and EU labels may call it jute, which makes separate figures and products hard to trace.
kenaf.fabrics: Kenaf's biggest textile-adjacent market is technical. Nonwoven mats of kenaf, often combined with polypropylene or other binders, are heated and pressed into molded interior panels for vehicles and into composite boards. Traditional products are sacking, twine, rope and coarse burlap-like cloth. Spun kenaf can be blended with cotton for heavier fabrics, but its coarseness limits it to bags, upholstery and home textiles. The core fraction becomes animal bedding, oil and liquid absorbents, potting media and lightweight board, and whole stalks can be pulped for paper.
kenaf.quality: For fiber and yarn, look for long, clean strands with little adhering core or bark and an even cream to light tan color; dark specks and stiff patches usually mean incomplete retting. Water-retted fiber is generally finer and better for spinning. For nonwoven mats, ask for areal weight in grams per square meter, the fiber-to-binder ratio and moisture content, because kenaf absorbs water and moisture variation affects molding. Since EU rules can apply the jute name to kenaf, a jute label does not rule kenaf out. Claims about carbon capture or soil cleanup should be supported by data for the specific product.
pros: Kenaf is a fast-growing annual, giving a fiber harvest within a single season.
Its bast fiber is strong and stiff for its weight, which suits molded natural fiber composites.
The whole stalk is usable, with bast for fiber and core for absorbents and board.
Bast crops including kenaf are being studied for phytoremediation of metal-contaminated land.
cons: The fiber is coarse and variable, so apparel uses are limited to blends and heavy cloth.
It absorbs moisture, causing swelling and weak bonding in composites unless treated.
Kenaf grown on contaminated soil can take up cadmium, so metal content of such fiber should be tested.
It is often counted or labeled as jute, which makes species and origin hard to verify.
kenaf.impact: Kenaf is an annual crop grown mainly in India and China. A 2025 review in Science of the Total Environment grouped it with hemp, ramie, jute and flax as bast crops with potential for carbon uptake, use of marginal land and phytoremediation. That potential cuts both ways: hydroponic work shows kenaf roots accumulate cadmium, and a 2023 study found that intercropping kenaf with soybean on mining soil raised cadmium in kenaf leaves, so fiber from polluted land may carry metals. Water retting, which gives the best fiber, can load ponds and streams with organic matter, while chemical retting adds alkaline effluent. No widely accepted cradle-to-gate footprint for kenaf textile fiber was found, and sequestration claims usually describe growing biomass rather than long-term storage.
kenaf.care: Kenaf fabrics are usually coarse, jute-like home textiles, and the label governs. General guidance is to spot clean or hand wash in cool water with mild detergent, avoid long soaking, and dry flat in shade, because wet bast fiber is weaker and can shrink or distort. Iron on a medium to hot setting while slightly damp if needed. Keep kenaf goods dry in storage, since damp fiber mildews and smells. Sunlight yellows the lignin, so rotate upholstery and keep bags out of strong sun. Molded kenaf panels in cars need no care beyond cleaning the covering surface. Kenaf core absorbents and bedding are single-use and should be disposed of according to what they absorbed.
faq: Is kenaf the same as jute?

No. Kenaf is Hibiscus cannabinus, while jute comes from Corchorus species. Both give coarse bast fibers used for sacking and twine, and the jute definition in Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 extends to kenaf, so an EU jute label may cover it. Telling them apart in finished goods usually needs laboratory work.
Why is kenaf used in car interiors?

Kenaf bast is stiff and light, and nonwoven mats of kenaf with a thermoplastic binder can be heated and pressed into shaped panels. Research reviews name moisture sensitivity and fiber variability as the main technical hurdles, which surface treatments and binders are meant to address.
Does growing kenaf clean polluted soil?

Studies show kenaf tolerates and accumulates cadmium, which is why it is investigated for phytoremediation. That does not make every kenaf product a cleanup product, and fiber grown on contaminated land may contain metals that should be tested before it is used in consumer goods.
notable: Kenaf is a hibiscus, Hibiscus cannabinus, in the same genus as roselle and ornamental hibiscus.
In a hydroponic study, cadmium stress increased cell wall polysaccharides in kenaf roots, which may help hold the metal in the roots and limit its transport to shoots.

kapok.types: Kapok is sold mainly as loose, cleaned floss, judged by color, loft and the amount of seed and husk fragments left in it; well-cleaned floss is pale yellowish to cream, springy and free of dark specks. Beyond loose fill, kapok is sold as airlaid nonwoven batting bonded with a binder fiber, as a minority component in spun yarns blended with cotton or synthetics, and as an ingredient in insulating nonwovens and oil sorbents. Most traded kapok comes from Southeast Asia, especially Indonesia and Thailand, which are the only producers listed in FAO statistics, although Ceiba pentandra also grows in Africa and the Americas. Organic or untreated claims describe how the trees were grown and the floss cleaned, not its physical properties, and should be documented.
kapok.fabrics: Kapok's main products are fillings: pillows, cushions, mattresses, duvets, toys and upholstery, and historically life jackets and buoys. Because the fibers are too short, smooth and brittle to spin alone, kapok yarns are blends in which cotton or synthetic fibers carry the load. Airlaid kapok nonwovens bonded with low-melt binder fibers serve as insulating battings for bedding and clothing. Research uses include oil sorbent pads and booms, acoustic absorbers and carbon materials made from the hollow fibers.
kapok.quality: Good kapok fill is light, silky and springy, with a faint sheen and no musty smell. Squeeze a handful: it should rebound rather than stay matted. Dark flecks are seed or husk debris. Compare fill weight rather than volume; unlike down, kapok has no fill-power rating, so loft claims are hard to compare across brands. Check the label for blends with polyester fiberfill, which must be declared. Pillows need a tightly woven inner casing, ideally zippered for adjusting fill, because loose kapok is fine enough to work through open weaves. Treat hypoallergenic claims cautiously: allergy studies have found skin-test cross-reactions between aged kapok and mold and house dust extracts.
pros: Kapok is extremely light and buoyant because each fiber is a hollow, wax-coated tube.
Its waxy surface sheds liquid water, so fill does not readily wick moisture.
It is a plant-based alternative to down for people who avoid animal products.
It is gathered from long-lived trees, so fiber production needs no annual tillage.
cons: Kapok compacts with use, so pillows need regular plumping and occasional top-ups.
It cannot be spun alone, which confines it mostly to fillings and minor blends.
It is flammable like other light cellulosic floss.
Hypoallergenic claims are weakly supported, since aged kapok has cross-reacted with mold and house dust allergens in skin tests.
Soaked kapok clumps, dries slowly and rarely regains full loft.
kapok.impact: Kapok comes from tall, long-lived Ceiba pentandra trees, and pod collection and floss cleaning remain largely manual. FAO production estimates cover only Indonesia and Thailand, so global volumes and farm practices are poorly documented, and no peer-reviewed cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment of kapok fill was found in this pass. The main environmental argument is substitution: kapok can replace down, which raises animal welfare questions, and polyester fiberfill, which is fossil based and sheds synthetic microfibers. Seller claims that kapok trees need no pesticides or irrigation vary by farm and were not independently verified. Worker health evidence is limited but real: a 1994 case report documented occupational asthma in a worker exposed to kapok, with a positive bronchial challenge.
kapok.care: Most kapok pillows and cushions are not machine washable; the label governs. Remove and wash the outer cover separately. Plump the pillow daily to break up compacted fiber, and air it regularly in sunshine or a breezy, dry spot to drive out moisture. Spot clean the inner casing with a barely damp cloth and mild detergent, then let it dry completely. Do not soak the fill: wet kapok clumps and rarely regains its loft, and damp fill can grow mold. If the pillow has a zipper, tease clumps apart by hand and add fresh floss when it flattens. Keep kapok away from open flames and heaters, and store it dry in a breathable bag rather than sealed plastic.
faq: Is kapok better than down?

It depends on the use. Good down generally lofts more and recovers better after compression. Kapok is plant based, very light and supportive, but it compacts faster, needs regular plumping and cannot be washed the way down often can. Compare fill weight, casing quality and care requirements rather than assuming one is superior.
Is kapok hypoallergenic?

Not reliably. Kapok contains no animal proteins, but Thai allergy studies in the 1970s found skin-test cross-reactions between aged kapok and mold and house dust extracts, and a 1994 case report linked occupational asthma to kapok. People with dust or mold allergies should keep kapok clean, dry and encased.
Can you wash a kapok pillow?

Usually not in a machine. Soaking makes the floss clump, and it rarely recovers fully. Wash the removable cover, spot clean the inner casing, and refresh the fill by plumping it and airing it in sun and wind. Follow the maker's label if it says otherwise.
Why was kapok used in life jackets?

Each fiber is a hollow tube with a waxy, water-repellent surface, so packed kapok stays buoyant. When Southeast Asian supplies were cut off during the Second World War, the United States organized milkweed pod collection in 1944 to supply floss as a substitute.
notable: When wartime supplies of kapok from the East Indies were cut off, the United States organized a national milkweed pod collection in 1944 to fill life jackets.
A 1994 case report described what its authors called the first bronchoprovocation challenge with kapok, supporting but not proving that the fiber itself can be allergenic.

nettle.types: Textile nettle comes from several plants. European nettle fiber is Urtica dioica, grown from selected high-fiber clones rather than gathered from wild stands. Himalayan giant nettle, Girardinia diversifolia, known in Nepal as allo or puwa, grows in open forests and moist riverside sites at roughly 1,200 to 3,000 m and yields long, lustrous fibers; a 2024 study measured a fineness of about 1.9 tex, a moisture regain of about 9.5 percent and a cellulose content near 90 percent. Ramie, Boehmeria nivea, belongs to the same family and is sometimes marketed as nettle, but it is a separate crop and fiber. Commercially, nettle appears as hand-processed allo yarn and as industrially decorticated, refined fiber for blending.
nettle.fabrics: In Nepal, allo yarn is woven into bags, shawls, jackets and coarse cloth, and it is often blended with wool or cotton for a softer hand. European nettle is spun into linen-like yarns and usually blended with cotton, wool or other fibers in small collections of shirts, knitwear and accessories, since supply is limited. Fine, well-degummed nettle fiber suits lightweight woven fabrics similar to ramie or linen, while coarser grades go into nonwovens and composite trials, including automotive applications named in reviews.
nettle.quality: Most garments sold as nettle are blends, so read the fiber percentages; 100 percent nettle is rare and expensive. Pure nettle fabric looks and feels like linen or ramie, crisp with slubs and a slight luster. A very smooth, uniform, inexpensive nettle item may be mostly cotton or ramie. Himalayan allo cloth is coarser and more variable, and irregular yarn thickness is normal for hand spinning. Ask which species is used and where the fiber was processed. In the EU, nettle has no Annex I name and should appear as other fibres with a percentage, so a label listing only named fibers alongside a nettle claim deserves a question.
pros: Nettle is a perennial with low fertilizer and pesticide needs that grows across most European climate zones.
Its fiber gives a cool, linen-like hand with good moisture absorption.
Himalayan allo provides income from a wild plant in rural hill regions of Nepal.
Reviews highlight nettle's potential for growing on marginal land and supporting local biodiversity.
cons: Supply is tiny, so pure nettle cloth is scarce and expensive.
Like linen, nettle fabric creases readily.
Quality varies strongly with clone, retting and degumming, so fabrics are inconsistent.
Ramie is sometimes sold as nettle, and pure-nettle claims are hard to check without laboratory testing.
nettle.impact: Reviews describe Urtica dioica as a low-input perennial: once established, a stand can be harvested for several years, needs little fertilizer or pesticide, and can support local flora and fauna, and a 2024 review in Plants places nettle within circular bioeconomy strategies. It has also been proposed for restoring marginal and degraded land. The main footprint uncertainties lie in processing: water retting uses water and releases organic load, while chemical degumming uses alkali. No full life cycle assessment of commercial nettle fabric was found in this pass, so environmental claims should cite product-specific data. Himalayan allo is largely wild harvested and processed by hand in Nepal, with ash cooking and beating, which provides rural income but demands heavy labor.
nettle.care: Treat nettle fabric like linen of similar weight; the label governs. Machine wash cool to warm (about 30 to 40 C) on a gentle cycle with mild detergent, or hand wash blends containing wool in cool water with a wool-safe detergent. Avoid chlorine bleach, which weakens bast fibers. Reshape and line dry or dry flat, since tumble drying increases shrinkage and creasing. Iron while slightly damp on a medium to hot setting for pure nettle, and lower the heat for blends with wool or synthetics. Store clean and dry, folded loosely or rolled, and shift fold lines occasionally, because sharp creases in stiff bast fibers can weaken over time. Hand-spun allo pieces are best hand washed.
faq: Does nettle fabric sting?

No. The stinging hairs are on the living leaves and stems and are removed during harvesting and processing, while the textile fiber comes from the inner bast. A 2025 genome study identified genes likely encoding urthionin, a neurotoxic peptide thought to contribute to the sting, but finished fiber does not carry stinging hairs.
Is nettle fabric the same as ramie?

No. Both belong to the nettle family, Urticaceae, but ramie is Boehmeria nivea, a separate crop grown at scale in Asia. The fibers look similar under the microscope, so a nettle claim is best checked by asking for the species and, for expensive pieces, fiber testing.
What is allo?

Allo is the Nepali name for fiber from Himalayan giant nettle, Girardinia diversifolia, a wild perennial of mid-hill forests. Its long, lustrous fibers are stripped, cooked with ash, beaten and hand spun, then woven into bags, shawls and jackets, often blended with wool or cotton.
notable: A 2025 chromosome-level genome of stinging nettle found two gene copies putatively encoding urthionin, a neurotoxic peptide that may contribute to the plant's sting.
Himalayan giant nettle fibers measured in a 2024 study had a cellulose content near 90 percent and a moisture regain of about 9.5 percent.

banana.types: Banana fiber is a family of products rather than one grade. Coarse outer sheaths of the pseudostem give stiff fiber for rope, mats and paper, and finer inner sheaths give softer fiber for handloom yarn; Okinawan bashofu artisans select sheath layers by fineness for different cloths. Industrially, extracted fiber is cut to staple lengths, refined with enzymes or alkali and blended with cotton or regenerated fibers. Handmade paper and craft cordage use less refined fiber. Banana fiber is distinct from abaca, which is Musa textilis and has its own Philippine grades, even though both come from Musa plants. Yarns sold as banana silk are not silk and may be banana fiber, blends or regenerated cellulose, so composition should be stated.
banana.fabrics: The best-documented banana cloth is Kijoka bashofu from Ogimi village in northern Okinawa, a light, crisp plain-weave cloth used for summer kimono and other garments, with patterns woven from plant-dyed yarns. Elsewhere, banana fiber is made into handloom fabrics, rope, mats, bags and paper, and softened banana staple is blended with cotton or viscose for knit and woven fabrics sold as banana fabric. A 2016 study refined mechanically extracted fiber with a pectinase enzyme to make yarn intended for woven technical fabrics that reinforce composites.
banana.quality: Check the fiber percentage: most soft banana-fiber garments are blends, and the banana share may be small. Pure banana cloth is crisp and slightly stiff, with a papery rustle and natural slubs, and it softens with wear; a soft, drapey fabric labeled pure banana deserves a question. Kijoka bashofu is a designated Japanese traditional craft and is priced as a luxury textile, so very cheap bashofu is unlikely to be genuine. For yarns called banana silk, ask for the composition, since the name is a marketing term. Look for even color without dark streaks from sap staining or poor washing.
pros: Pseudostems remain after the fruit bunch is harvested, so fiber uses an agricultural residue.
Banana cloth is light, crisp and airy, which suits hot, humid weather.
Enzymatic refining can make banana fiber spinnable with milder chemistry than alkali cooking.
Small decorticators allow fiber extraction close to farms.
cons: Fiber diameter varies with sheath position, which makes consistent yarn difficult.
Pure banana cloth is stiff and wrinkles easily.
Traditional bashofu requires many labor-intensive steps and is very expensive.
Banana is easily confused with abaca, and blend percentages are often unclear.
banana.impact: Banana fiber is promoted as a residue product: much of the plant's biomass is left in the field after the bunch is cut, and turning some pseudostems into fiber adds income without new land. The benefit depends on processing. Mechanical decortication needs only modest power, but washing, degumming and bleaching may use alkali, and effluent handling is rarely documented. A 2016 Materials study refined fiber with a pectinase bath at 45 C and pH 4.5 for 6 hours to reach a spinnable textile grade, a lower-chemical route. No peer-reviewed life cycle assessment of banana fabric was found. Removing pseudostems also removes organic matter and nutrients that would otherwise return to the soil, a trade-off that is rarely quantified.
banana.care: Follow the label: banana-cotton blends often tolerate gentle machine washing, while pure banana cloth and bashofu need special handling. For pure or handwoven banana fabric, hand wash in cool water with a mild, neutral detergent, do not wring or twist, and dry flat or hanging in shade. The fabric is more vulnerable when wet, so support its weight while lifting it from the water. Iron while slightly damp at a medium setting under a pressing cloth. Valuable pieces such as bashofu kimono are best entrusted to a textile specialist. Store dry and away from light, and refold occasionally so that permanent crease lines do not form.
faq: Is banana fabric the same as abaca?

No. Both come from Musa plants, but abaca is Musa textilis, grown mainly in the Philippines for its strong leaf-sheath fiber, while banana fiber comes from pseudostems of fruit and fiber bananas. The fibers look similar under the microscope, so trade names alone do not prove the species.
What is bashofu?

Bashofu is Okinawan cloth woven from banana fiber. The Kijoka tradition in Ogimi village was recognized as an Important Intangible Cultural Property of Japan in 1974, and Toshiko Taira, who led its revival after opening her studio in 1963, was named a Living National Treasure in 2000.
Is banana silk real silk?

No. Silk comes from silkworm cocoons, while banana fiber is a cellulose plant fiber. Yarns sold as banana silk may be banana fiber, blends or regenerated cellulose. Ask for the stated fiber content, which covered textiles must disclose in the US and EU.
notable: Kijoka bashofu weaving in Ogimi, Okinawa, was recognized as an Important Intangible Cultural Property of Japan in 1974.
Toshiko Taira, who revived Kijoka bashofu, became a Living National Treasure in 2000 and died in 2022 at the age of 101.

pineapple.types: Pineapple leaf products fall into three families. Pina is the traditional Philippine handwoven cloth; in Aklan it is made from the leaves of a native pineapple called pinya Bisaya, whose fibers are extracted by hand. Blended pina fabrics include pina-seda, in which silk forms the warp and pineapple fiber the weft, and pina-jusi, a blend with jusi, a fabric described as abaca or silk; barong makers rank pure pina as the most expensive, followed by pina-seda and jusi. Industrial pineapple leaf fiber (PALF) is degummed, cut and blended for spun yarns or used in composites. Coated nonwoven sheets made from pineapple leaf fiber and sold as leather alternatives are a separate composite product, not woven pina.
pineapple.fabrics: Pina's signature use is the barong Tagalog, the Philippine formal shirt, along with women's formal blouses, handkerchiefs, veils and other fine clothing, often hand embroidered. The sheer, crisp cloth holds fine embroidery well. Pina-seda offers a similar sheer look with more strength and a lower price and is used for barongs, scarves and shawls. Industrial PALF has been ring spun into blended yarns and woven on power looms, and it reinforces composites. Nonwoven pineapple-leaf sheets bonded and coated with polymers are used for bags and shoes as leather alternatives.
pineapple.quality: Genuine pina is translucent, crisp and slightly stiff, with a soft luster and fine, slightly irregular yarns. Machine-perfect uniformity, a slippery hand or a low price suggests synthetics or blends sold as pina. Ask whether the cloth is pure pina, pina-seda or pina-jusi, since prices differ widely. Hand embroidery shows small irregularities and knots on the back, unlike machine embroidery. For Aklan pina, ask about the weaver or cooperative. A burn test on a single thread from a hidden seam allowance separates synthetic filament, which melts, from pineapple fiber, which chars, and silk, which smells of burnt hair.
pros: Pina is exceptionally fine and sheer for a plant fiber and has a natural luster.
Its crisp hand holds shape and supports detailed embroidery.
The fiber comes from pineapple leaves, a byproduct of the plant.
Aklan handloom weaving is a UNESCO-recognized living tradition that supports local livelihoods.
cons: Pure pina is costly because extraction, knotting and weaving are slow hand processes.
The cloth is delicate, creases sharply and can split along fold lines.
Undyed pina can yellow with age and light if stored poorly.
Blends and synthetics are often sold under the pina name, and composition is hard to judge by eye.
pineapple.impact: Pineapple leaves are a residue of the plant, so pina uses no extra land, and in Aklan the fiber comes from leaves of the native pinya Bisaya, harvested by farmers and extracted by hand. Hand scraping needs mainly labor and water rather than chemical degumming. The social dimension is central: UNESCO inscribed Aklan pina handloom weaving on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 6 December 2023, noting transmission within families and the spread of the craft from Kalibo to other provinces. Industrial PALF, by contrast, is degummed with alkali or enzymes before spinning, and the footprint of coated pineapple-leaf leather alternatives depends heavily on the polymer binders and coatings used.
pineapple.care: Pina and pina-seda garments are best hand washed or professionally cleaned; the label governs. To hand wash, use cool water and a small amount of mild, neutral detergent, swish gently without rubbing or wringing, rinse well, and roll the garment in a towel to remove water. Dry flat or on a padded hanger away from direct sun. Iron while slightly damp on a low to medium setting through a pressing cloth, working from the back of any embroidery; keep the heat low for pina-seda because it contains silk. Store in acid-free tissue in a cool, dry place, hung or rolled rather than tightly folded, because sharp folds can break fine fibers.
faq: What is pina-seda?

Pina-seda is a handwoven blend in which silk forms the warp and pineapple leaf fiber the weft. It keeps much of pina's sheer, crisp look while being stronger and less expensive than pure pina. Because it contains silk, it should be ironed at a low setting and washed gently.
How can I tell real pina from imitations?

Real pina is crisp, translucent and slightly irregular, with a soft luster rather than a plastic shine. Ask for the exact composition, whether pure pina, pina-seda or pina-jusi. A thread burned from a hidden seam should char like plant fiber; synthetic organza melts and beads.
Is Aklan pina weaving UNESCO listed?

Yes. Aklan pina handloom weaving was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 6 December 2023, at the Intergovernmental Committee session in Kasane, Botswana. The listing recognizes the craft knowledge and its transmission, not particular products or sellers.
Is pineapple leather the same as pina?

No. Pina is a woven cloth of hand-extracted pineapple leaf fiber. Pineapple leather alternatives are nonwoven sheets of leaf fiber bonded and coated with polymers, so their composition, durability and end of life differ, and their full composition should be requested from the producer.
notable: Aklan pina weaving was historically concentrated in the barangays of Old Buswang and New Buswang in Kalibo.
UNESCO inscribed Aklan pina handloom weaving in December 2023 at a committee meeting held in Kasane, Botswana.

bamboo-bast.types: Products called bamboo fall into distinct fiber types, and the label should say which. Mechanically processed bamboo bast is crushed, softened and separated culm fiber: rare, coarse and linen-like, and the only type that can be labeled simply bamboo in the US. Bamboo viscose or rayon, by far the most common, is regenerated cellulose made by dissolving bamboo pulp and spinning new filaments. Bamboo lyocell is regenerated cellulose spun from a solvent solution. Under US rules both regenerated types must be named rayon or lyocell, with made from bamboo allowed only when accurate. Bamboo also appears in split-cane mats, blinds and composites, which are not textile fiber products in the labeling sense.
bamboo-bast.fabrics: Mechanical bamboo fiber is spun into coarse, linen-like yarns, usually blended with cotton, for specialty woven fabrics and crafts, and is used as reinforcement in composites and cement. Most bamboo-labeled consumer textiles, including socks, underwear, sheets, baby clothing and towels, are made from regenerated cellulose derived from bamboo, often blended with cotton and elastane; these should be labeled rayon made from bamboo, viscose from bamboo or lyocell from bamboo depending on the jurisdiction. Split bamboo has a long history in plaited mats, baskets and blinds.
bamboo-bast.quality: Read the fiber content line first. In the US, textiles regenerated from bamboo pulp must be labeled rayon or lyocell; the FTC accepts wording such as rayon made from bamboo only when the product really was made from bamboo. A label reading 100% bamboo on a soft, silky, drapey knit is a red flag, because mechanical bamboo fiber is stiff and coarse. Genuine mechanical bamboo fabric feels crisp and linen-like, with slubs, and costs more. Claims that a bamboo fabric is eco-friendly, chemical-free or antibacterial need evidence for the finished product; the FTC has stated that turning bamboo into rayon uses toxic chemicals.
pros: Mechanically processed bamboo fiber is a true plant fiber, separated without dissolving the cellulose.
Bamboo is a fast-growing grass that regrows from its rhizomes after culms are cut.
Regenerated bamboo fabrics are soft, absorbent and drape well, as other rayons do.
Mechanical fiber keeps some lignin and stiffness, which suits durable, linen-like fabrics.
cons: Truly mechanical bamboo textile fiber is scarce, coarse and expensive.
Most bamboo textiles are rayon made by chemical processes that the FTC says involve toxic chemicals and hazardous pollutants.
Mislabeling has been widespread enough to draw US civil penalties.
Environmental claims tied to the growing plant often do not carry over to the finished fabric.
bamboo-bast.impact: The environmental case for bamboo textiles depends more on the processing route than on the plant. Bamboo grows quickly and regrows from its rhizomes, but converting it into rayon dissolves the pulp chemically; in April 2022 the FTC stated that this conversion requires toxic chemicals and results in hazardous pollutants, and it challenged Kohl's and Walmart for both mislabeling and deceptive environmental claims. The settlements carried civil penalties of 2.5 million US dollars for Kohl's and 3 million for Walmart under the Textile Act, made possible because both had received FTC warning letters in January 2010. For genuine mechanical bamboo fiber, impacts arise mainly from delignification chemicals, energy and effluent, and no product-level life cycle assessment was found.
bamboo-bast.care: Care depends on the actual fiber. For bamboo rayon or viscose, wash cool (about 30 C) on a gentle cycle, ideally in a mesh bag, with mild detergent; avoid wringing, because rayon is weaker when wet; reshape and line dry or dry flat, since tumble drying invites shrinkage and pilling. Iron inside out on a low to medium setting. Bamboo lyocell is sturdier when wet but still benefits from gentle washing. Mechanical bamboo bast fabric behaves like linen: machine wash warm on a gentle cycle, line dry, and iron while damp at a medium to hot setting. Avoid chlorine bleach on all types, and store garments dry, since cellulosic fibers mildew when damp.
faq: Is bamboo fabric really bamboo?

Usually not in the fiber sense. Most bamboo textiles are rayon, viscose or lyocell made by dissolving bamboo pulp and spinning new filaments. In the US, the FTC requires these fabrics to be labeled rayon or lyocell, optionally with made from bamboo. Only mechanically processed fiber can be labeled simply bamboo.
Why did the FTC penalize Kohl's and Walmart?

In April 2022 the FTC announced settlements under which Kohl's paid 2.5 million dollars and Walmart 3 million dollars in civil penalties for selling rayon textiles as bamboo, a Textile Act violation. It also challenged claims that the products were made with eco-friendly processes. Both firms had received warning letters in 2010.
Is bamboo fabric antibacterial?

Evidence for ordinary commercial fabrics is weak. Dissolving bamboo into rayon transforms the plant material, and laboratory results on specially modified bamboo fibers do not establish that everyday bamboo rayon resists bacteria. Any antibacterial claim should be backed by standardized testing of the finished fabric.
How can I spot mechanical bamboo fabric?

It is uncommon and priced accordingly. It feels crisp and linen-like, with slubs, rather than silky. Under a microscope it shows irregular bundles of lignified cells instead of uniform filaments. Ask the seller for documentation of the mechanical process and a fiber content test.
notable: The FTC described its 2022 case against Kohl's and Walmart as seeking its largest-ever civil penalty for bogus bamboo marketing.
Both retailers had received FTC warning letters in January 2010, and that prior notice is what allowed the agency to use its Penalty Offense Authority.

raffia.types: Natural raffia is the stripped leaf epidermis of Raphia palms. Madagascar, where Raphia farinifera grows, is the best-known source of export raffia for hats, bags and craft, and after harvest the strands are dried and graded by length, width and color. African cloth traditions use raffia from other Raphia species. Three substitutes share the name. Paper raffia is a continuous twisted paper ribbon, made from wood-pulp cellulose and sold on spools, typically about 5 mm wide and opening to roughly 25 mm when flattened. Synthetic raffia is usually polypropylene film ribbon for gift wrap and garden ties. Viscose raffia-look yarns are used in knitted bags and hats. A product called raffia can therefore be any of these.
raffia.fabrics: Natural raffia is woven, plaited, crocheted or knotted into sun hats, handbags, baskets, mats and embroidery, and loose strands serve as garden ties and gift binding. In Central and West Africa, raffia strips are woven on looms into cloth for wrappers, skirts and ceremonial textiles, sometimes decorated with embroidery. Paper raffia is crocheted or knitted into bags and hats that look like straw but are more uniform, and polypropylene raffia is woven into sacks, tarpaulins and inexpensive hats. Raffia fabric has also been tested as reinforcement in polyester and epoxy composites.
raffia.quality: Natural raffia has a matte, slightly irregular surface, strands of varying width and a faint hay-like smell. Perfectly even width, uniform color or a plastic sheen suggest paper or polypropylene. Check the composition on the label or listing: paper, polypropylene and viscose should be named, and paper hats are often sold as paper straw. In a hat, tight, even crochet or weave and a neatly finished brim edge indicate quality, while loose ends and uneven density suggest a hurried product. Handwork from Madagascar is labor intensive, so a very low price for pure natural raffia deserves skepticism.
pros: Natural raffia is a flexible ribbon that can be woven or crocheted without spinning.
It is light, breathable and packable, which suits sun hats and summer bags.
Natural raffia biodegrades, unlike polypropylene ribbon sold under the same name.
Raffia palms are multipurpose plants, so fiber harvest fits within a wider rural palm economy.
cons: It turns brittle and can crack when very dry, and it weakens and misshapes when soaked.
Natural variation in strand width makes the finish less uniform than paper or synthetic versions.
The name raffia is widely applied to paper and plastic substitutes, which confuses buyers.
Dyed raffia can bleed in rain and fade in strong sun.
raffia.impact: Natural raffia comes from palms that grow wild or semi-managed in wetlands and forests of Madagascar and tropical Africa, and hand harvesting of young leaflets can let a palm keep producing, although sustainability depends on how intensively leaves are cut. The Madagascar raffia trade supports rural stripping, weaving and crochet work; one Malagasy raffia business has written publicly about both fair trade practice and greenwashing within the market, and no independent certification specific to raffia was identified. Paper raffia carries a pulp-and-paper footprint, while polypropylene raffia is fossil based, persists in the environment and can fragment into microplastics. No life cycle assessment comparing these materials was found.
raffia.care: Keep natural raffia hats and bags dry and out of prolonged strong sun. Brush off dust with a soft brush and spot clean with a barely damp cloth; do not soak or machine wash. If a hat is crushed, mist it lightly or hold it in steam at a distance, reshape it by hand or over a bowl, and let it dry naturally. Store hats crown up or on a form, stuffed with tissue, in a breathable box rather than plastic, to prevent mold. Paper raffia needs even drier handling, since water softens and weakens paper, so clean it with a dry cloth only. Polypropylene raffia can be wiped with mild soapy water but softens with heat, so never iron it.
faq: What is the difference between raffia and paper raffia?

Natural raffia is the thin skin stripped from young leaves of Raphia palms, dried and split into strands. Paper raffia is a man-made twisted ribbon of wood-pulp paper, continuous and uniform, sold on spools in many colors. Paper raffia is more even but less durable, especially when wet.
Can a raffia hat get wet?

Light rain is survivable for natural raffia if the hat is reshaped and dried naturally, but soaking weakens and distorts it. Paper raffia hats are more vulnerable, since wet paper softens and can tear. Polypropylene hats tolerate water but can deform in heat.
Is raffia sustainable?

Natural raffia is a renewable, biodegradable palm product gathered largely by hand, but sustainability depends on harvest intensity and fair labor, and no raffia-specific certification was identified. Paper raffia depends on pulp sourcing, while polypropylene raffia is fossil based and can shed microplastics.
notable: Paper raffia is commonly sold as a twisted ribbon about 5 mm wide that opens to roughly 25 mm when flattened.
Textile raffia is not spun at all: the ribbon used for weaving is the thin epidermis peeled from young palm leaflets, split to the width the maker needs.

paper-yarn.types: Paper yarns are classified by the paper they start from and by tape width and twist. Traditional shifu yarn is hand-cut washi made from kozo, mitsumata or gampi; in Japan, elite paper mulberry strains used for washi have been propagated vegetatively and distributed nationally. Most commercial washi yarn is industrial: Oji Fiber, for example, states that its OJO+ yarn is made from Manila hemp (abaca) pulp formed into a long base sheet, slit into tapes about 1 to 6 mm wide and twisted. Wood-pulp paper yarns are also made, sometimes with finishing agents for knittability and wash stability. Paper yarn is sold as a single twisted tape, plied, or combined with cotton, linen or wool. Tape width, paper grammage and twist set thickness and stiffness.
paper-yarn.fabrics: Paper yarn is woven and knitted into summer shirts, jackets, knitwear, hats, bags and accessories, often blended with cotton or linen to soften the hand. In Japan, washi yarn fabrics are marketed for breathable summer clothing. Traditional shifu cloth is woven from hand-twisted washi strips. Paper yarn also makes crisp, structured hats and bags that resemble straw, and it is used in interior textiles. Experimental work has extended the shifu technique to yarns made from fungal sheets.
paper-yarn.quality: Check the label for the paper source (abaca, kozo or wood pulp) and the paper percentage in any blend. Good paper yarn is evenly twisted without flat, untwisted sections, and the fabric should feel crisp but not brittle when crushed in the hand. Ask whether the yarn is finished for wash durability: some modern finished yarns keep most of their strength after repeated washing, while unfinished yarn may soften, fuzz or break. Wash a swatch before committing to a large project. Dye evenness matters, because paper takes dye readily but unevenly if the sheet varies in density.
pros: Paper yarn fabrics are light, crisp and breathable, which suits hot weather.
Washing shrinkage is low compared with cotton and viscose yarns.
Producers state that paper yarn dries quickly and does not pill.
Yarns can be made from renewable pulps, including abaca and certified wood.
cons: Paper yarn loses much of its strength when wet, so rough washing can break it.
The hand is stiff at first, and some wearers find it papery.
Unfinished yarns may soften, fuzz or lose shape after washing.
Paper has no EU fiber name, so composition statements on labels vary.
paper-yarn.impact: A paper yarn's footprint follows its pulp. Abaca-based washi yarn inherits abaca's smallholder farming profile, kozo-based shifu relies on paper mulberry bast, and wood-pulp yarns depend on forestry and pulping, where FSC or PEFC chain-of-custody certificates can document sourcing. Pulping and papermaking use water, energy and, for bleached papers, oxidizing chemicals, and finishing agents added for wash stability may affect biodegradability. Conventional dyeing of paper yarn can generate colored, salty effluent; a 2024 Carbohydrate Polymers study reported salt-free dyeing with a cationic cellulose nanofiber and chitosan auxiliary, with dye uptake up to 97 percent. Oji Fiber's claims about abaca's carbon dioxide uptake are producer statements, and no independent comparative life cycle assessment against cotton yarn was found.
paper-yarn.care: Follow the label, because finishes vary. Hand wash, or use a delicate cycle in cool water inside a mesh bag, with mild detergent, and do not soak for long, since paper loses much of its strength when wet. Do not wring; press water out in a towel, reshape, and dry flat or on a hanger in shade. Paper yarn dries quickly. Avoid tumble drying and bleach. Iron on a medium setting through a cloth while slightly damp if needed. Hats and bags of paper yarn should be spot cleaned only and kept out of rain. Store garments dry and loosely folded, because sharp creases in paper yarn fabric can become permanent.
faq: Can clothes made of paper yarn be washed?

Usually yes, gently. Paper yarn weakens markedly when wet because water disrupts the hydrogen bonds between its fibers, so hand washing or a delicate cycle, no wringing and flat drying are safest. Finished yarns tested for clothing have kept most of their strength after repeated washes.
What is shifu?

Shifu is a Japanese craft of weaving cloth from yarn made of washi. The paper is cut into narrow strips, rolled and twisted while damp, and woven. It enjoyed a twentieth-century revival for clothing and has inspired recent paper yarn research, including yarns made from fungal sheets.
Is washi yarn made from traditional Japanese paper?

Sometimes, but not always. Traditional washi uses kozo, mitsumata or gampi bast fibers, while many commercial washi yarns use industrially made paper from abaca pulp; Oji Fiber describes its OJO+ yarn as Manila hemp paper yarn. Ask the seller which pulp is used.
notable: Oji Fiber states that it produces paper yarn base sheets at least 20,000 m long before slitting them into tapes 1 to 6 mm wide.
Abaca, the Philippine rope fiber, is the raw material of some Japanese washi yarns.
