barkcloth.types: Barkcloth is grouped by source tree, region and finish. Pacific tapa is made mostly from paper mulberry, Broussonetia papyrifera, with regional traditions such as Samoan siapo and Hawaiian kapa that differ in beating, joining of layers and decoration by rubbing, stamping, stenciling or freehand painting. Ugandan barkcloth, called olubugo or lubugo in Buganda, comes from the mutuba tree, Ficus natalensis. Colors range from pale cream to deep reddish brown depending on species, processing and dyes. Market forms include heritage cloths, contemporary art cloths, souvenirs and modern barkcloth panels for fashion and interiors. Separately, vintage barkcloth also names a textured woven cotton furnishing fabric that contains no bark.
barkcloth.fabrics: Barkcloth is a nonwoven sheet rather than a fabric woven from yarns. In the Pacific it is made into ceremonial and presentation cloths, gifts, clothing and wall hangings, with large pieces built up by pasting or felting sheets together. In Buganda, barkcloth is central to ceremonies, and the Kabaka, the king, wears it during coronation rituals. Contemporary Ugandan designers have brought barkcloth into fashion and accessories, sometimes backing it with fabric for strength. Tapa is also made today as art for sale and display.
barkcloth.quality: For heritage or art pieces, ask about the maker, community, date and provenance, including export permits where the country of origin regulates cultural property; museums increasingly consult source communities before acquiring. Good barkcloth has even thickness without thin spots or holes, a supple rather than brittle texture, and firm joins where sheets are pasted or felted. Painted designs should be crisp and stable, not flaking. Beware of imitations: printed paper, nonwoven synthetics and cotton fabrics are sold as tapa or barkcloth. Real barkcloth shows a felted network with beater marks and no yarns when viewed in raking light.
pros: Barkcloth comes from renewable inner bark, and Ugandan mutuba trees regrow bark after harvest when protected.
It is light and can be made into very large sheets by joining pieces.
It carries living cultural knowledge in Pacific and Ugandan communities.
Its plant and mineral colorants can be identified scientifically, which supports conservation of historic pieces.
cons: It has low wet strength and cannot be laundered like woven cloth.
It becomes brittle in dry air and grows mold in damp conditions.
Old folds can crack and tear aged cloth.
Provenance and cultural-property issues complicate buying historic pieces.
barkcloth.impact: Barkcloth production is low input: bark is stripped by hand, beaten with wooden tools and colored with plant and mineral colorants. In Buganda, bark is harvested from Ficus natalensis during the two rainy seasons, and the trunk is wrapped in green banana leaves so that it heals and regrows bark in about a year, allowing repeated harvests from the same tree. The social dimension is significant. UNESCO proclaimed barkcloth making in Uganda a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005, and craftsmen of the Ngonge clan, led by a hereditary chief craftsman, have long made barkcloth for the Buganda royal family. Modern laminates or synthetic backings can reduce the biodegradability of contemporary products.
barkcloth.care: Barkcloth is not washed. Dust it lightly with a soft brush, or vacuum on low suction through a protective screen. Keep it out of direct sun and strong light, which fade colorants and weaken fibers. Keep relative humidity stable and moderate: damp air invites mold, and very dry air makes barkcloth brittle; conservation guides commonly treat about 65 percent RH as the level above which mold becomes likely. Store flat, or rolled on a wide padded tube with acid-free tissue, rather than folded, since old fold lines crack; if a large cloth must be folded, pad the folds generously. Handle with clean, dry hands and support the full weight. Check for insects, and consult a conservator about tears, stains or flaking paint.
faq: Can barkcloth be washed?

No. Barkcloth is a beaten sheet of inner bark with limited wet strength, and water can soften it, distort it, move dyes and encourage mold. Dust it gently instead, and consult a textile or paper conservator about stains or damage on valuable or historic pieces.
Is vintage barkcloth fabric made from bark?

Usually not. In vintage furnishings, barkcloth names a textured woven cotton fabric, often printed, that imitates the rough surface of beaten bark. True barkcloth, such as Pacific tapa or Ugandan olubugo, is a nonwoven sheet beaten from inner bark and contains no yarns.
How should I store a tapa cloth?

Store it flat or rolled on a wide, padded tube interleaved with acid-free tissue, in a dark place with stable, moderate humidity. Avoid new sharp folds, since old fold lines crack, and keep it away from damp walls, insects and direct sun. The University of Glasgow's tapa project publishes care guidelines.
What is Ugandan barkcloth?

Olubugo is barkcloth from the mutuba tree, Ficus natalensis, made by the Baganda of Uganda. Bark is harvested in the rainy seasons and the trunk is wrapped in banana leaves to regrow. UNESCO recognized barkcloth making in Uganda in 2005, and the Kabaka wears it in coronation rituals.
notable: Ugandan barkcloth makers wrap the stripped mutuba trunk in green banana leaves so that it regrows its bark in about a year.
UNESCO proclaimed barkcloth making in Uganda a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005.

lotus.types: Lotus textiles come in three main forms. Pure lotus cloth is woven entirely from the fine filaments drawn from Nelumbo nucifera stems. Lotus blends, most often with silk or cotton, are cheaper and more common. A third category is products merely named after lotus or printed with lotus motifs. The best-known production is in Myanmar around Inle Lake, in villages such as Kyaing Khan and In Paw Khone, and lotus fiber is also made in Cambodia and Vietnam. Sellers often call it lotus silk, but it is a plant cellulose fiber, not silk. Published accounts disagree widely on how many stems a square meter of cloth requires, from about 8,000 to more than 20,000, so such figures are estimates.
lotus.fabrics: Lotus fiber is woven mainly into scarves, shawls and stoles, with smaller output of ties, jackets and robes. Weaves are usually plain, and colors range from the natural beige of undyed fiber to plant-dyed shades. Blended fabrics combine lotus with silk for sheen and strength or with cotton to lower cost. Research groups have also spun lotus fiber into humidity-responsive yarn actuators and cross-linked composite fibers, which are laboratory products rather than consumer textiles.
lotus.quality: Ask for the exact composition and the workshop. Pure lotus cloth is matte to softly lustrous, slightly uneven, light and somewhat crisp, with a linen-like texture and a natural beige tone, and it softens with wear. A very smooth, shiny, uniform scarf sold cheaply as lotus is likely silk, cotton or synthetic. Reported prices for a pure lotus scarf at the source run to hundreds of US dollars, so bargains deserve suspicion. A loose thread of pure lotus should burn and char like cotton; silk smells of burnt hair, and synthetics melt. Reputable sellers name the village or workshop and state the lotus percentage.
pros: Lotus cloth is light and breathable, with a soft, linen-like texture.
The fiber is drawn and rolled by hand, with little or no chemical processing.
The craft provides income to lake communities in Myanmar and elsewhere in Southeast Asia.
Lotus fiber yarns respond strongly to humidity, a property researchers are exploring for smart textiles.
cons: Output is tiny and labor intensive, so pure lotus cloth is very expensive.
Independent data on strength, abrasion and colorfastness are scarce.
Fraud risk is high, because silk and cotton scarves are easily passed off as lotus.
The fabric is delicate and wrinkles easily.
lotus.impact: Lotus fiber is drawn by hand from cut stems, rolled into thread without chemical degumming and woven on hand looms, so energy and chemical inputs are low and the dominant input is labor. Lotus is also cultivated as a food and ornamental plant, so the stems can be a secondary use of an existing crop. Labor per piece is large: published accounts from Inle Lake report that a small scarf can take thousands of stems and about a day of skilled work. A 2024 data paper from Hanoi University of Science and Technology published an open design for an automatic lotus fiber extractor, aiming to raise productivity and improve working conditions for the laborers. No life cycle assessment of lotus textiles was found.
lotus.care: Treat lotus cloth like fine linen. Hand wash in cool water with a mild, neutral detergent, or use a cleaner experienced with delicate natural fibers; blends with silk need a silk-safe detergent. Do not wring or scrub; press water out in a towel and dry flat in shade. Iron while slightly damp on a low to medium setting through a pressing cloth, keeping the heat lowest for silk blends. Store clean and dry, loosely folded with acid-free tissue or rolled, in a breathable bag, since plant fibers can mildew when stored damp. Avoid prolonged sun, which can yellow undyed cloth. Lotus yarns twist and contract with moisture, so expect some shape change while wet.
faq: Is lotus silk real silk?

No. Lotus silk is a trade name for cloth woven from fine filaments drawn from lotus stems, a plant cellulose fiber. Real silk comes from silkworm cocoons. Some lotus scarves are blended with silk, so the label should state the percentage of each fiber.
Why is lotus fabric so expensive?

Each stem yields only a trace of fiber, drawn and rolled by hand, and published accounts estimate thousands of stems for a single scarf and tens of thousands for a square meter of cloth. The work is slow, output is tiny, and pure lotus scarves have been reported selling for hundreds of dollars.
Where is lotus fabric made?

The best-known production is in Myanmar, around Inle Lake in villages such as Kyaing Khan and In Paw Khone. Lotus fiber textiles are also reported from Cambodia and Vietnam. Asking for the named village or workshop is the best way to check a product's origin.
notable: A coiled lotus fiber yarn has been made into an artificial muscle with a reversible tensile stroke of 38 percent when exposed to water or humidity.
Published estimates of the stems needed per square meter of lotus cloth range from about 8,000 to more than 20,000, a spread that shows how little the craft has been measured.

milkweed.types: Milkweed floss is sold mainly as loose fill or as an ingredient in blended insulation. Commercial North American floss comes from cultivated common milkweed, Asclepias syriaca, grown in Quebec, and it is usually blended with other fibers because pure floss is fragile. Forms include loose floss, airlaid nonwoven batting with binder fibers, insulation for outdoor jackets and bedding, and experimental oil sorbent mats. Floss from Calotropis procera and Calotropis gigantea in Asia and Africa is also called milkweed but comes from a different genus. Grades are informal, so buyers should ask for the species, the cleaning method and the percentage of milkweed in any blend, since milkweed insulation may contain only a minority of floss.
milkweed.fabrics: Milkweed is used mostly where textiles need loft: insulation for outerwear, duvets, pillows and sleeping bags, usually blended with polyester or other binder fibers for durability, and building insulation and acoustic panels in nonwoven form. Spinning trials blend small percentages of floss with cotton or other fibers, because floss alone lacks cohesion. During the Second World War, floss filled life vests in place of kapok. Researchers also make oil sorbent pads from the hollow, waxy fibers.
milkweed.quality: For fill products, check the fiber content line for the milkweed share, binder fibers and any polyester or down. Good floss is silky, white to cream and free of seeds and pod fragments. Because the hollow fibers can collapse under pressure, ask how the product performs after compression and washing; loft retention data, where available, are more informative than warmth adjectives. Pure-milkweed claims are rare and should be supported by composition data. Claims about monarch butterfly habitat describe how the plants were grown, not how the garment performs, and should be backed by farm-level information.
pros: Hollow, wax-coated fibers give very low density and good thermal insulation.
Common milkweed is a perennial native to eastern North America and the main larval host plant of the monarch butterfly.
Floss absorbs oil strongly while repelling water, which suits spill cleanup.
Researchers report that the Quebec crop is grown without irrigation, pesticides or fertilizers.
cons: Fibers are short, slippery and fragile, so floss cannot be carded or spun well alone.
Hollow fibers can collapse under pressure, reducing loft.
Supply is small and concentrated in Quebec, so products are niche and relatively expensive.
It is flammable like other light cellulosic floss.
milkweed.impact: Common milkweed is the primary larval host plant of the monarch butterfly, whose eastern North American population fell by about 80 percent over the two decades before 2019, a decline linked in part to the loss of milkweed from farmland after herbicide-tolerant crops were adopted. Growing milkweed as a fiber crop could therefore add breeding habitat, but no study was found that measured monarch outcomes on commercial floss farms. Field studies add caveats: egg predation in grasslands reached up to 90 percent within 72 hours, and pesticide residues on milkweed near cropland produced mostly sublethal effects on monarchs in a 2020 experiment. Researchers report low input needs for the Quebec crop, but farm-scale life cycle data are lacking.
milkweed.care: Follow the label: many milkweed-insulated jackets and duvets are designed for gentle machine washing, but the floss itself is fragile. Wash cold or lukewarm on a gentle cycle with a mild detergent suited to technical outerwear, rinse thoroughly, and skip fabric softener, which can coat fibers and reduce loft. Dry on low heat with dryer balls to break up clumps, or dry flat in shade, turning and shaking the item often until completely dry, because damp fill can mildew. Do not iron or press the insulated areas, since compression flattens hollow fibers. For storage, keep insulated items loose in a breathable bag rather than compressed in a stuff sack for long periods.
faq: Is milkweed insulation as warm as down?

Tests of milkweed nonwovens found low thermal conductivity, and makers present it as an alternative to down and synthetics, but warmth depends on fill weight, blend and construction. Independent side-by-side tests of finished jackets are scarce, so compare fill weight and loft data rather than fiber names.
Does milkweed farming help monarch butterflies?

Possibly. Common milkweed is the monarch's main larval host plant, and loss of milkweed from farmland is one suspected cause of the eastern population's decline. However, no study was found measuring monarch benefits on commercial floss farms, and predation and pesticide exposure also affect monarch survival.
Why did Americans collect milkweed pods in World War II?

Imported kapok used to fill life vests became unavailable after Japan seized the East Indies. In 1944 schoolchildren and youth groups collected milkweed pods to supply floss as a substitute, under slogans such as 'Two bags save one life', and collectors were paid for each bag.
notable: A 1944 slogan urging American schoolchildren to gather milkweed pods for life vests was 'Two bags save one life'.
In a field experiment, up to 90 percent of monarch eggs on potted common milkweed in perennial grasslands were lost within 72 hours, much of it at night.

henequen.types: Henequen fiber is sorted by cultivar, length and cleanliness. Commercial plantations in Yucatan rely on clonally propagated cordage cultivars, chiefly Sac Ki and Yaax Ki, while the finer textile cultivar Kitam Ki is nearly extinct. Because each cultivar is essentially one clone and the plant's long life cycle makes breeding very slow, researchers at the Centro de Investigacion Cientifica de Yucatan have developed micropropagation and somatic embryogenesis protocols to multiply elite clones. Trade forms include long line fiber for rope and twine, shorter tow, spun yarn, woven rugs and mats, and chopped strands or ground flour for composites. Henequen is sometimes called Mexican sisal, but it is a different species from sisal.
henequen.fabrics: Henequen's main products are agricultural binder and baler twine, rope and cordage, rugs, mats and coarse woven goods, and craft items such as bags and hats made in Yucatan. It is also a composite reinforcement: chopped henequen with a maleic-anhydride coupling agent has been compounded with polypropylene into injection-molded parts, henequen fabrics have been infused with bio-based epoxy, and ground henequen has been added to 3D printing filament. Fine henequen textile fiber once came from the Kitam Ki cultivar, which is now nearly lost.
henequen.quality: For twine and rope, look for uniform diameter, tight twist, a pale straw color and no musty smell or dark mildew spots, and ask the supplier for breaking load and length per kilogram. Henequen is harsher and coarser than sisal, so a soft, pale fiber sold as henequen may be sisal or a blend. For rugs, check the label: henequen, sisal and maguey are separate EU fiber names and should not be interchanged. Plastic twines imitating natural fiber are common; they melt rather than char. For composites, specify fiber length, moisture content and any surface treatment or coupling agent.
pros: Henequen is strong and stiff, which suits twine, rope and heavy cordage.
In polypropylene composites, 50 percent henequen by weight matched the tensile strength of 20 percent glass fiber when a coupling agent was used.
Henequen raised the stiffness of polypropylene more than fourfold at high loading in one study.
The plant is long lived and grown as a perennial, so fields are not replanted each year.
cons: It is coarser and harsher than sisal, which limits textile uses.
Cultivars are genetically uniform clones, which leaves the crop vulnerable to pests and disease.
The long life cycle makes breeding improvements slow.
Its plantation history involved coercive labor, and the industry has shrunk greatly since its boom years.
henequen.impact: Henequen is a long-lived agave whose leaves are decorticated mechanically with water washing, so the main environmental questions concern decortication energy, water use and the handling of wet leaf residues, which also yield fermentable juice. By analogy with sisal, where a 2017 life cycle assessment found that residue disposal and fertilizer use drive greenhouse gas results, henequen's footprint likely depends on local practice, but no henequen-specific textile life cycle assessment was found. Clonal propagation of a few cultivars has left the crop genetically narrow, which reduces resilience. Socially, the crop carries the legacy of the Yucatan hacienda system of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, which relied on Maya labor under coercive conditions.
henequen.care: Care for henequen rugs as for sisal: vacuum often, blot spills at once, and avoid steam cleaning or wet shampooing, which can shrink, distort and stain agave fibers; use dry-extraction cleaning or a professional instead. Keep rugs out of bathrooms and other damp areas. Store henequen twine and rope dry, off the ground and out of sunlight, since moisture promotes rot and UV weakens the fiber. Bags and hats should be spot cleaned with a barely damp cloth, reshaped and air dried. Avoid bleach, which weakens and blotches the fiber. Brush rugs occasionally to lift embedded grit, which otherwise abrades the stiff fibers.
faq: Is henequen the same as sisal?

No. Henequen is Agave fourcroydes, domesticated in Yucatan, and sisal is Agave sisalana. The fibers look alike, but henequen is generally coarser and harsher. EU Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists them as separate fiber names, so labels should use the correct one even though henequen is sometimes called Mexican sisal.
Can henequen replace glass fiber?

In some composites, partly. In a 2022 Polymers study, polypropylene containing 50 percent henequen by weight plus a coupling agent matched the tensile strength of polypropylene with 20 percent glass fiber. Moisture sensitivity and natural variability still limit henequen in demanding structural parts.
Can a henequen rug be cleaned with water?

Not safely. Like sisal, henequen absorbs water and can shrink, distort and develop brown stains as it dries. Blot spills immediately, use dry-extraction products for spots, and hire a professional familiar with natural fiber rugs for deep cleaning.
notable: Micromechanical models and corrected single-filament tests put henequen's intrinsic Young's modulus at roughly 30 to 35 GPa.
Henequen's long life cycle makes conventional breeding very difficult, so Yucatan researchers use tissue culture methods such as somatic embryogenesis to multiply elite clones.

llama.types: Andean herders and researchers separate two main llama fleece types. The ccara or q'ara llama is double-coated, with more guard hair and less undercoat, while the ch'aku or th'ampulli type is woolly, single-coated and heavier-fleeced. A study of a llama population in southern Bolivia reported th'ampulli fleeces with a staple of about 155 mm and a mean diameter near 21 microns, against about 120 mm and 25 microns for the kara type, whose individual fibers spanned roughly 10 to 150 microns. Medullation, not coat type alone, drives handle: a Peruvian study found medullated fibers in similar proportions (around 46 to 47 percent by its classification) in both types. Commercial yarn is therefore graded by measured micron and dehairing quality rather than animal type.
llama.fabrics: Dehaired llama undercoat is spun into knitting yarns, often blended with wool or alpaca, and woven into blankets, throws and scarves. Natural colors (white, fawn, brown, grey and black) are frequently sold undyed. The coarse guard hair, which is unsuitable for next-to-skin wear, goes into rugs, saddle blankets, braided rope and cordage, uses with long Andean precedent. Woolly ch'aku fleece is also hand spun in highland communities for local textiles. Because much llama yarn comes from small herds, lots vary in grist and color from batch to batch.
llama.quality: Ask for a measured mean fiber diameter and, ideally, a medullation or comfort-factor figure; fine dehaired llama undercoat sits in the low 20s of microns, while unsorted fleece can be far coarser. Rub the fabric against the inside of your wrist: stiff, straight hairs standing out of the surface signal poor dehairing and will prickle. Terms such as baby llama are not defined in US or EU fiber-labeling law, so they do not substitute for a micron value. Llama and alpaca are hard to tell apart by eye, and cheap llama may be blended with wool or acrylic, so read the percentage label carefully.
pros: Well-dehaired undercoat gives warm, lofty yarn without the lanolin content of sheep wool.
A wide range of natural colors lets makers sell undyed yarn.
The coarse fraction has practical uses in rugs and rope, so less of the fleece is wasted.
Fiber is shorn from living animals that are also kept for pack work and meat.
cons: Guard hair left in the yarn causes prickle and visible stray hairs.
Fineness and medullation vary widely between animals, so quality is inconsistent between suppliers.
Heavily medullated fibers can dye unevenly and feel stiffer.
Supply is small and fragmented, which makes provenance hard to verify.
llama.impact: Llamas are raised mainly by smallholder and pastoral households in the Andes of Peru, Bolivia and Argentina, often on high grassland unsuitable for crops, and fiber is only one of several products alongside transport and meat. Camelids are often described as gentler on pasture than hard-hoofed livestock because of their padded feet, but no product life cycle assessment for llama yarn was found in this review, so claims of a lower footprint than sheep wool are unquantified. Shearing is annual or less frequent. Processing impacts resemble other specialty hair fibers: scouring water, energy for dehairing, and dyeing when fiber is not left natural. Fair payment to herders is a social question buyers can only check through supplier documentation.
llama.care: Hand wash in cool to lukewarm water (about 30 C or below) with a pH-neutral wool or hair detergent, keeping temperature constant to avoid felting. Do not wring; press out water, roll in a towel and dry flat away from direct heat and sunlight. Machine washing is only safe on a true wool cycle when the label permits it. Steam or iron on a low wool setting through a pressing cloth. Remove pills with a comb or fabric shaver. Store clean and dry with cedar or lavender as a deterrent, and inspect for clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae in spring and autumn. Chlorine bleach and alkaline detergents damage the keratin. The product label governs.
faq: Is llama wool itchy?

It depends on processing. Dehaired llama undercoat in the low 20s of microns is soft enough for scarves and many sweaters. Itch comes from residual guard hairs and coarse fibers above about 30 microns, so poorly dehaired llama yarn can prickle while a well-sorted one does not.
What is the difference between llama and alpaca fiber?

Both are South American camelid fibers. Llamas descend from the guanaco and have historically been bred more for pack work, so their fleece averages coarser, with more guard hair and medullation. Alpaca has been selected for fiber. A fine, dehaired llama yarn can overlap with alpaca in feel.
Does llama yarn contain lanolin?

Camelid fleece carries little of the wool grease that sheep produce, which is why llama is often suggested for people who react to lanolin. Sensitivity to the keratin itself, to dyes or to finishing chemicals is still possible, so test a small item first.
Can llama be machine washed?

Only if the label says so. Untreated llama is a keratin fiber that can felt with heat, agitation and sudden temperature changes. Hand washing in cool water with a wool detergent and drying flat is the safe default.
notable: In a Bolivian study, woolly th'ampulli llamas averaged about 21 microns, close to many commercial alpaca grades.
Andean llama types are often named by herders' terms, ccara (with little wool) and ch'aku (woolly), rather than formal breed registries.
A Peruvian study found similar overall medullation in both llama fleece types, showing that coat type alone does not predict yarn softness.

bison.types: Commercial bison fiber comes almost entirely from plains bison (Bison bison bison) on private ranches. Trade forms are graded by how much guard hair has been removed: raw shed fiber, dehaired down, carded roving or batts for hand spinners, and finished yarn. Yarns are sold as 100 percent bison down or as blends. Blends with silk, merino or cashmere are common because the short down spins more easily with a longer partner; one small US producer, for example, sells a laceweight of 50 percent bison down and 50 percent mulberry silk. Most bison yarn is lace, fingering or sport weight, sold in small skeins.
bison.fabrics: Bison down is used mainly in hand-knitting yarns and in small runs of knitted accessories such as scarves, hats, gloves and socks, plus some woven scarves and throws. Lace and fingering weights suit shawls and lightweight accessories where the down's warmth per gram matters most. Blends with silk add strength, luster and drape; merino blends add elasticity and memory; cotton or nylon may be added to sock yarns for abrasion resistance. Undyed natural brown is the norm, and dyed bison is usually overdyed in dark shades because the base is brown.
bison.quality: Look for stated 100 percent bison down or a clear blend percentage, and ask whether the fiber was dehaired commercially. Good yarn feels soft against the neck with no stiff, dark guard hairs poking out; if you can see coarse hairs, the dehairing was incomplete. A slight halo is normal, but yarn that sheds heavily when rubbed between fingers may be under-twisted. Reported down diameters of roughly 15 to 22 microns put it near cashmere, so prices well below cashmere are a red flag for a low bison percentage. Because Bison fiber is not a Wool Act specialty fiber, the label should name bison fiber or bison hair with its percentage.
pros: Fine dehaired down is soft enough for next-to-skin accessories.
Fibers hold still air, giving good warmth for their weight.
Fiber is a by-product of ranch herds kept for meat and conservation, not a separate harvest.
Natural brown color allows undyed yarns.
cons: Short staple makes 100 percent yarns prone to shedding and pilling.
Supply is small and depends on individual ranches, so price is high and color lots vary.
Natural brown limits pale dyed shades.
Species claims are hard to verify without laboratory testing.
bison.impact: Bison fiber is a minor co-product of ranching for meat and of conservation herds; ranch managers and conservation groups argue that bison grazing can support prairie ecosystems, but no life cycle assessment of bison yarn was found in this review, so any carbon or land-use comparison with other fibers is unquantified. Collection of shed fiber in spring adds little direct burden on the animals. The main processing inputs are water and energy for scouring and mechanical dehairing, often done by small mills. Most plains bison carry some cattle ancestry and descend from a small founder population, so conservation value varies by herd; claims that a purchase supports bison conservation should name the herd or program.
bison.care: Treat bison as a delicate, felting-prone keratin fiber. Hand wash in cool water (about 30 C or below) with a wool or hair detergent, soak briefly, and avoid rubbing or sudden temperature changes. Rinse at the same temperature, press out water in a towel and dry flat in shape, away from heaters and sun. Do not tumble dry. Steam lightly rather than ironing; if ironing is needed use a low wool setting and a pressing cloth. Remove pills gently with a fine comb. Store clean in breathable bags with a moth deterrent, and check for insect larvae periodically. Avoid chlorine bleach and alkaline detergents. The product label governs.
faq: Is bison wool warmer than cashmere?

Producers often claim so, but no standardized comparative test was found. Dehaired bison down has fiber diameters overlapping cashmere, so warmth per gram is likely similar; knit structure, yarn thickness and blend partner affect warmth more than the species difference.
Are bison harmed to collect the fiber?

Commercial bison fiber is collected as shed fiber in spring or recovered from hides of animals raised for meat, depending on the supplier. Bison are not routinely shorn. Ask the seller which method applies to the product.
Why is bison yarn so expensive?

Each animal gives a small amount of usable down, the down must be separated from guard hair on specialized dehairing equipment, and production runs are tiny. These costs resemble those of qiviut and cashmere.
Can bison yarn be dyed?

Yes. Bison down takes acid dyes and other protein-fiber dye classes, but the natural brown base limits results to darker or muted shades. Bleaching can lighten it but weakens the keratin, so most bison yarn is sold undyed or overdyed in deep colors.
notable: Bison down yarns are commonly sold in lace and fingering weights because the short down suits fine, well-twisted yarns.
At least one US producer sells a 50 percent bison down and 50 percent mulberry silk laceweight, using silk to add strength and drape to the short down.
Bison is not a specialty fiber under the Wool Products Labeling Act, so US labels name it as bison fiber or hair rather than wool.

possum.types: Textile possum fiber is the underfur of the brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula) from New Zealand, sold almost only in blends. The main trade forms are plucked fur, possum-merino knitting yarns and knitwear, and dressed possum pelts used for fur trims and throws, a separate product. Blends are defined by the possum share. Zealana, a New Zealand yarn brand, lists its Kauri worsted as 60 percent merino, 30 percent possum and 10 percent mulberry silk, and its Air range as 40 percent possum, 40 percent cashmere and 20 percent silk. Retail knitwear typically uses merino as the majority fiber with possum as a substantial minority, and silk or nylon added for strength and luster.
possum.fabrics: Most possum fiber ends up in knitted garments: jerseys, cardigans, beanies, scarves, gloves and socks, plus hand-knitting yarns from lace to worsted weight. Possum-merino socks and gloves are sold for outdoor and travel use. Silk-containing blends give drape and sheen for lighter shawls and fine-gauge knits. The possum share produces a soft halo on the knit surface. Fabrics are almost always knitted rather than woven, because the short, slippery fur needs the loft and give of a knit structure.
possum.quality: Read the percentage label: a higher possum share gives more halo and softness but can shed more early in wear, and very low percentages add little. Feel for a light, soft, fuzzy surface with no harsh fibers. Check that labels say possum or brushtail possum, not opossum, rabbit or generic fur fiber, since cheaper haloed yarns can imitate the look. Ask whether the yarn was made in New Zealand, as most possum processing happens there. Claims of extra warmth or pill resistance are producer statements; pilling can be tested by standard methods such as ISO 12945-2 if a buyer needs data.
pros: Possum adds a light, soft halo and loft to merino without much added weight.
Blends are commonly described by producers as warm for their weight.
The fiber comes from an introduced pest that New Zealand already controls to protect native forest.
Merino in the blend supplies elasticity and shape retention.
cons: Pure possum yarn is impractical, so the fiber is always blended and the possum share varies.
Short fibers can shed from the surface, especially in the first wears.
Supply depends on pest control and would shrink if eradication goals succeed.
Fiber comes from killed animals, which some buyers reject regardless of the pest context.
possum.impact: Possums are culled in New Zealand to protect native forest and birds and to control bovine tuberculosis, and fur recovery adds value to part of that control. An Envirolink report for regional councils estimated about 30 million possums after control efforts, lower than earlier estimates of 50 to 70 million. Whether commercial fur harvest aids conservation is contested: a 2012 study in Biological Conservation found that harvesting for economic return and controlling possums for biodiversity outcomes can pull in different directions, because hunters target accessible, high-yield areas rather than sites with the highest ecological priority. Animal welfare depends on trapping and poisoning methods. Processing impacts are mainly those of merino scouring and spinning.
possum.care: Hand wash in cool water with a gentle wool detergent unless the label states machine washable; some producers treat blends for machine washing on a wool cycle. Avoid hot water, agitation and wringing, which felt both the merino and the possum fibers. Rinse at the same temperature, roll in a towel and dry flat in shape. Do not tumble dry. Light shedding in the first few wears is normal; a lint roller or gentle brushing removes loose fibers. Press only with a cool iron through a damp cloth or use steam. Store folded, not hung, with a moth deterrent. The product label governs.
faq: Is possum fur the same as opossum?

No. Textile possum comes from the Australian brushtail possum, Trichosurus vulpecula, introduced to New Zealand in the nineteenth century. The American opossum, Didelphis, is a different marsupial whose fur is a separate, minor product.
Why is possum always blended with merino?
Brushtail possum underfur is short and slippery, so it does not hold together in a yarn by itself. Merino provides fiber length, crimp and cohesion, and silk or nylon may be added for strength.
Is buying possum merino good for the environment?

Possums damage New Zealand's native forests and are controlled for that reason. Using their fur adds value to control work, but research has found that commercial harvest and conservation goals do not always coincide, so treat blanket conservation claims cautiously.
Does possum merino shed?

Some shedding is common in the first wears as loose, short possum fibers work free from the yarn surface. It usually settles down after a few wears and gentle washing. Heavy, continuing shedding suggests a loosely spun yarn or a high possum share.
notable: An Envirolink report estimated New Zealand's possum population at about 30 million, down from earlier estimates of 50 to 70 million.
Commercial possum hunting has been called a mixed blessing for conservation because hunters seek fur where it is easy to take, not where native forest is most at risk.
Possum-merino yarns are among the few mainstream knitting yarns made from the fur of an animal officially classed as a pest.

rabbit.types: Generic rabbit hair divides into several trade forms. Rex rabbits are a fur breed whose short, plush coat is judged by hair density, length, fineness and hide area; research on Rex rabbits in China found winter-slaughtered pelts of better quality than summer ones. Meat-breed pelts supply lower-grade fur and loose hair. Hat felt uses rabbit fur, European hare fur (a different genus, Lepus) and beaver, alone or blended. Hatters' X ratings describe such blends, but there is no industry standard for what an X value means, so each brand's scale stands alone. Angora rabbit wool is a separate, long-haired product and is labeled differently in the EU.
rabbit.fabrics: Rabbit fur is felted into hat bodies for fedoras, trilbies and western hats, where it gives a smooth, dense surface. Loose rabbit hair is blended, usually as a minority share, with wool, nylon or other fibers in knitwear and yarns to add a soft halo. Dressed Rex and other rabbit pelts are used for fur trims, linings, throws and accessories; lapin is a French-derived trade term for rabbit fur in the fur trade. Short rabbit hair is also used in some flocked and felted craft products.
rabbit.quality: For hats, fur felt should feel dense, smooth and springy, and hold its shape when the brim is flexed; hatters state that pure rabbit felt is less dense than beaver and more prone to losing shape in rain. Because X ratings are not standardized, compare fur content statements rather than X counts across brands. For knitwear, check the fiber label for a rabbit hair percentage and avoid confusing it with angora. Heavy shedding when the fabric is rubbed indicates loosely held short fibers. In the US, fur products must name the animal, so rabbit should be stated even when trim is marketed as lapin.
pros: Rabbit fur felts readily into dense, smooth hat bodies.
Medullated hair is light and warm and adds a soft halo to blends.
Rabbit pelts and hair are largely by-products of rabbit meat production.
Fur felt hats cost less than beaver felt of similar appearance.
cons: Short, smooth fibers shed from knitwear and cling to other clothes.
Rabbit felt is less water resistant and shape-stable than beaver felt, according to hatters.
Hat X ratings are brand-specific marketing scales, not a standard.
Welfare of caged rabbits in meat and fur farming is a recognized concern.
rabbit.impact: Most rabbit fur and hair is a by-product of meat production, with some farms breeding Rex rabbits specifically for pelts. Welfare concerns center on cage housing, space and slaughter, which are the subject of EU policy debate on caged farming. Pelt dressing uses tanning and finishing chemicals, and historical hat felting used mercury compounds, now replaced in regulated industries. No life cycle assessment specific to rabbit hair textiles was identified in this review. Fur-trim claims such as by-product or humane need documentation of the farm system, because the finished fiber reveals nothing about how the animal was kept.
rabbit.care: For fur felt hats, brush with a soft hat brush in the direction of the nap, handle by the brim rather than the crown, and store upside down on the crown or in a hat box away from heat. If a hat gets wet, shake off water and let it dry naturally at room temperature with its shape supported; never use direct heat. For rabbit-blend knitwear, hand wash cool with a wool detergent, avoid agitation, and dry flat; shedding reduces with wear. Fur trims should be professionally cleaned by a fur specialist. Keep all rabbit products away from moths and carpet beetles. The product label governs.
faq: Is rabbit hair the same as angora?

No. Angora is the long, fine wool of Angora rabbit breeds and, in EU labeling, the name angora is reserved for it. Generic rabbit hair is shorter fur from other breeds, often recovered from pelts, and is mainly used in felt and as a minority blend fiber.
What does 4X or 10X mean on a felt hat?

X ratings describe the fur blend and density of a felt hat, with higher numbers usually meaning more beaver or finer fur. There is no industry standard for the scale, so a rating is only meaningful within one maker's line.
Why does my rabbit-blend sweater shed?

Rabbit hairs are short and smooth, so they hold weakly in a yarn and work loose with friction. Shedding usually lessens after early wear. Washing gently and avoiding rubbing against dark, fuzzy fabrics helps.
Is rabbit fur felt better than wool felt?

Fur felt is generally finer, smoother, lighter and more durable in shape than wool felt, and costs more. Wool felt hats are cheaper and heavier. Beaver felt is typically the most weather resistant of the three.
notable: There is no industry-wide definition of the X rating printed inside many fur felt hats.
Rex rabbit fur quality is studied genetically, with markers associated with hair density identified in Rex populations.
European hare, a different genus from the domestic rabbit, is a traditional ingredient in fine hat felt.

horsehair.types: Horsehair is graded by source, length and color. Tail hair is longer and is used for weaving and bows; mane and body hair is shorter and goes into curled upholstery stuffing and brushes. Weavers report white tail hair at roughly 20 inches (about 50 cm) and black or brown hair up to about 25 inches, which sets the width of woven haircloth. Bow makers prefer tail hair from stallions in cold climates such as Mongolia and Siberia, dressed repeatedly to remove kinked or thick hairs; white hair is standard for violin, viola and cello bows. Curled hair is sold by grade and hair content, and synthetic monofilament horsehair braid is a separate, non-hair product.
horsehair.fabrics: Haircloth is woven with a single horse tail hair as each weft pick on a cotton, silk or linen warp, so fabric widths are limited to roughly 70 cm or less. It comes in plain, satin and patterned weaves for chair seats, headboards, wall panels and luxury upholstery. Hair canvas interlinings stiffen the chests and lapels of tailored jackets. Curled mane hair fills traditional sprung upholstery and mattresses. A violin bow carries a flat ribbon of roughly 150 to 200 tail hairs, rosined to grip the string. Horsehair also appears in brushes, fishing lines, jewelry and millinery.
horsehair.quality: Genuine haircloth has a crisp, slightly glossy surface where individual hair ends are visible at the selvedges, and a burn test on a loose weft end gives a hair smell and brittle ash rather than a melted bead. Width is a cue: horsehair fabric wider than the longest tail hairs is suspect. For bow hair, look for even, straight hairs without kinks and ask whether it is stallion hair and from which region. For upholstery, curled hair should spring back strongly when compressed; hair mixed with plant fiber or synthetic fill is cheaper. Millinery braid labeled horsehair is usually nylon or polyester.
pros: Haircloth is extremely durable and resists crushing and wear on seats.
Stiff, springy hairs give tailored interlinings and upholstery lasting shape.
Bow hair has a scale structure that holds rosin and grips strings.
Tail hair can be collected from living horses without harm.
cons: Haircloth widths are narrow, which limits pattern layout and raises cost.
Stiff hair ends can poke through covers and scratch skin.
Bow hair wears and stretches, so regular players need rehairing every few months.
Old horsehair stuffing attracts moths and carpet beetles and can harbor dust.
horsehair.impact: Horsehair is a by-product: tail hair is trimmed from living horses or recovered at slaughter, depending on the supply chain, and haircloth weavers such as the long-established English mill John Boyd Textiles state that they use tail hair from live horses. Volumes are small and published environmental data are scarce, so no quantified footprint is available. Processing uses washing, degreasing, sometimes bleaching, and dyeing. Welfare questions concern trimming practices and slaughter conditions in supplying countries, which buyers can only check through supplier information. Curled hair stuffing is durable and can be reclaimed and re-curled by upholsterers, extending product life compared with foam.
horsehair.care: Vacuum haircloth upholstery with a soft brush attachment and wipe with a barely damp cloth; avoid soaking, which can loosen hairs and stain the warp. Test any spot cleaner on a hidden area. Keep furniture out of strong sun, which fades dyed hair and dries the warp. Hair canvas in tailored jackets should be dry cleaned or professionally pressed, not washed. Bows need rosin, loosened hair after playing, and clean hands; avoid touching the hair. Store bows away from heat and humidity swings and watch for bow bugs (carpet beetle larvae) in cases. The product label governs.
faq: Is horsehair braid in hats real horsehair?

Usually not. Most millinery braid sold as horsehair is nylon or polyester monofilament. A burn test on a single strand separates them: synthetic melts to a hard bead, while real hair chars with a burning-hair smell.
Why are violin bows strung with horsehair?

Horse tail hair has a scaled surface that holds rosin, which makes the hair grip and release the string to set it vibrating. A bow uses roughly 150 to 200 hairs, and bow makers favor stallion hair from cold climates for strength.
How often should a bow be rehaired?

String shops commonly advise about every 6 to 12 months for regular players and more often for daily professional use. Signs include lost hairs, poor grip even after rosining, and uneven hair tension.
Why is horsehair fabric so narrow?
Each weft pick is a single tail hair, so the cloth can be no wider than the usable length of the hair, roughly 70 cm or less. Wider fabrics labeled horsehair usually contain other fibers.
notable: John Boyd Textiles has woven horsehair fabric in Castle Cary, England, since 1837, using mechanical looms developed around 1870 that pick one hair at a time.
In hand weaving of haircloth, a child traditionally sat in the loom to pass single hairs to the weaver.
White tail hair tends to be shorter than black or brown hair, so white haircloth is narrower.

chiengora.types: Chiengora has no formal grades; spinners sort it by breed, coat type and how cleanly the undercoat was separated. Double-coated breeds with long, dense undercoats, such as Samoyed, Siberian Husky, Great Pyrenees and Newfoundland, give the most spinnable fiber, while short, stiff single coats are generally unsuitable. An academic comparison of five breeds found similar chemistry but large differences in diameter and linear density, with only Lhasa Apso and Pomeranian hair fine enough for machine spinning. Trade forms are raw brushings, washed and carded batts, and finished yarn, which is either 100 percent dog undercoat or a blend with wool or silk.
chiengora.fabrics: Most chiengora is hand spun into knitting or crochet yarn and made into scarves, hats, mittens and shawls, often as keepsakes from a household pet. Blends with wool add elasticity and reduce shedding; silk adds strength and sheen. Plied yarns are preferred because they shed less than singles. Woven items are uncommon, though some weavers use dog-hair yarn as weft in blankets. The historical parallel, Coast Salish blankets woven with woolly-dog fiber, belongs to a distinct Indigenous tradition and should not be confused with modern pet yarn.
chiengora.quality: Good chiengora starts with clean, guard-hair-free undercoat brushed during shedding; stiff, straight hairs in the yarn signal poor sorting and will prickle. Wash quality matters: well-scoured yarn smells neutral even when damp. Plied, moderately twisted yarn sheds less than loosely spun singles. Because processing is small-scale, ask a mill or spinner about minimum fiber weight, blend options and whether batches are kept separate if you want your own dog's fiber back. Commercial sale of dog-hair products in the US raises unresolved questions under the Dog and Cat Protection Act, so most chiengora is custom spun rather than sold at retail.
pros: Uses fiber that would otherwise be discarded after grooming.
Medullated undercoat gives a warm, lofty, haloed yarn.
Keepsake yarn has personal value that commercial fiber cannot offer.
No animal is harmed when fiber is brushed out during natural shedding.
cons: Yarn sheds and can develop a wet-dog smell if not thoroughly washed.
Dog allergens are present in hair, and so-called hypoallergenic breeds are no exception.
Quality varies strongly by breed and collection, and quantities per dog are small.
Commercial sale of dog-hair products is legally uncertain in the US and banned in the EU for dog fur.
chiengora.impact: Chiengora is a waste-recovery craft: fiber comes from routine grooming of companion animals and needs no land, feed or animals raised for the purpose. Environmental inputs are limited to washing water, detergent and the energy of small-scale carding and spinning, and no life cycle data exist. Animal welfare concerns are minimal when fiber is brushed out during shedding. The main social issue is legal and ethical: the US Dog and Cat Protection Act and the EU ban on cat and dog fur address dog fur products, and how they apply to yarn from shed hair is not settled, so commercial sellers should get legal advice.
chiengora.care: Hand wash in lukewarm water, about 30 C, with a wool or pet-safe mild detergent, and rinse thoroughly, since residual skin oils cause odor. A vinegar rinse is sometimes used by spinners to reduce smell. Do not agitate or change water temperature abruptly, as the fiber can felt, especially in wool blends. Press out water in a towel and dry flat, away from heat. Do not tumble dry or iron directly; steam lightly if needed. Store clean and dry with a moth deterrent, because dog hair is keratin and attracts clothes moths and carpet beetles. Expect some shedding; plied yarns shed less.
faq: Can I make yarn from my dog's hair?

Yes, if your dog has a soft, reasonably long undercoat. Brush during shedding, keep the undercoat separate from guard hairs and debris, and store it dry. Several ounces are usually needed for a small project, and many spinners blend it with wool.
Will chiengora smell like dog?

Properly washed yarn should not. Odor comes from skin oils and dander left in the fiber, so thorough scouring before spinning and a careful wash of the finished item are important. A lingering smell when damp suggests incomplete cleaning.
Is dog hair yarn safe for people with dog allergies?

Not necessarily. A 2012 study found the major dog allergen Can f 1 in hair and coat samples of all breeds tested, with higher levels in so-called hypoallergenic breeds. Washing may reduce allergen, but it has not been shown to remove it.
Is dog hair yarn warmer than wool?

Craft sources often say so, attributing warmth to the air-filled medulla of dog hair, but no standardized test supports a specific figure. Warmth in a finished item depends mostly on yarn thickness, spinning style and knit structure.
notable: A 2012 study found higher Can f 1 allergen levels in the hair and coats of so-called hypoallergenic dog breeds than in Labrador retrievers.
The medulla that makes dog hair lofty also makes the fiber less resistant to bending, one reason chiengora sheds.
In a five-breed study, only the finer Lhasa Apso and Pomeranian hair was slender enough for machine spinning.

down.types: Down is sold by species, composition and loft. Goose and duck down dominate; mature birds give larger clusters. Fill power, the volume one ounce occupies under a standard test, is the main loft class: duck down commonly tests around 550 to 750, while goose down reaches higher values, and fills above about 800 are mostly mature goose. Composition is stated as a down to feather ratio such as 90/10 or 80/20, meaning percent down cluster and percent feather. In US industry practice a product labeled down needs at least 75 percent down cluster, and species labels such as goose down must be nearly all that species. European EN 12934 uses different thresholds and categories.
down.fabrics: Down fills puffer jackets, vests, sleeping bags, quilts, comforters (duvets) and pillows. It is held in down-proof shells: tightly woven cotton cambric, batiste or sateen in bedding, and calendered or coated nylon or polyester ripstop in outdoor gear. Construction matters as much as fill: sewn-through quilting is light but creates cold spots at seams, while baffle-box walls let down loft fully. Hydrophobic down, treated with a durable water repellent finish, is used in some outdoor products. Blends with polyester fiber or feathers are used in cheaper bedding.
down.quality: Check four label items: species, down to feather ratio, fill power and fill weight. Fill power sets loft per ounce, but warmth depends on fill weight too, so a heavier 650 fill can be warmer than a light 850 fill. Fill power figures from US and European methods are not directly comparable. Quills poking through or a crunchy feel indicate feather content; a musty smell when damp suggests poorly washed down. Look for test reports from recognized labs and welfare certification such as the Responsible Down Standard. Very high fill power at a low price is a red flag. The FTC treats overstated down percentages as deceptive.
pros: Down gives more warmth for its weight than most fiber insulations when dry.
It compresses small and recovers loft many times, suiting packable gear.
Well-cared-for down products can last for decades and down can be recycled.
Down is a by-product of poultry meat production.
cons: Wet down clumps and loses most of its insulation, and dries slowly.
Live plucking and force-feeding for foie gras are welfare risks unless the supply chain is certified.
Species, fill power and down percentage are easy to overstate and hard to check without lab testing.
Washing and drying need care to avoid clumping and odor.
down.impact: Down is mostly a by-product of duck and goose meat production, and how its footprint is allocated is contested. The EU Product Environmental Footprint database gives about 4.15 kg CO2e per kg of virgin down including bird raising, a figure the processor ALLIED Feather + Down cited in 2026 when reporting its own audited processing at about 0.48 kg CO2e per kg. An LCA commissioned by the International Down and Feather Bureau from Long Trail Sustainability reported 85 to 97 percent lower impacts per ton for down than polyester fill; it is industry-funded. Welfare is the main social issue: the Responsible Down Standard, launched in January 2014 by The North Face, Textile Exchange and Control Union, prohibits live plucking and force-feeding.
down.care: Wash down products only when needed, in a large front-loading machine without an agitator, on a gentle cycle at about 30 C or as labeled, with a down-specific detergent; ordinary detergents and fabric softener strip natural oils and reduce loft. Rinse twice to remove residue. Tumble dry on low heat with clean dryer or tennis balls, for several hours, until no clumps remain; damp down left in clumps can mildew and smell. Spot clean shells with mild soap. Store lofted in a large breathable bag, never compressed in a stuff sack. Air comforters in the sun occasionally. The product label governs.
faq: What does 90/10 mean on a down comforter?

It means about 90 percent down cluster and 10 percent feathers by weight. Higher down ratios usually mean lighter, loftier fill. In the US, a product labeled down needs at least 75 percent down cluster, and labels below that must state both down and feather percentages.
Is goose down better than duck down?

Goose down clusters are often larger, so the highest fill powers are usually goose. But a mature duck down can outperform immature goose down. Compare stated fill power and fill weight rather than species alone.
What fill power do I need?

About 550 to 650 suits everyday bedding and casual jackets, 700 to 800 gives lighter, more packable warmth, and 800 or more is used where weight matters most, such as ultralight sleeping bags. Fill weight determines total warmth.
How do I know down was not live-plucked?

Look for a recognized welfare certification such as the Responsible Down Standard, which prohibits live plucking and force-feeding and tracks certified down through the supply chain. Live plucking cannot be detected by testing the finished fill.
Can a down duvet be washed at home?

Often yes, if it fits loosely in a large front-loading machine. Use a down detergent, a gentle cycle and a long, low-heat tumble dry with dryer balls. Oversized comforters are better sent to a professional cleaner.
notable: US industry labeling requires at least 75 percent down cluster for a product called down, while EN 12934 in Europe uses a lower threshold defined differently.
The Responsible Down Standard began as a The North Face initiative and was handed to Textile Exchange, launching in January 2014.
One down processor reported in 2026 an audited footprint of about 0.48 kg CO2e per kg of down, far below the EU database value of about 4.15.

feather.types: Filling feathers are graded by species (goose or duck), size and curl. Small, curved body feathers give springier fill than flat or large feathers, and whole feathers are preferred over crushed or chopped ones. Feather fills are sold as blends labeled by composition: a pillow may be mostly feathers with a small share of down, stated for example as 95 percent feathers and 5 percent down. In US industry practice, blends with less than 75 percent down cluster must list both down and feather percentages. Decorative feathers form a separate trade, graded by species, length and color, and many wild species are legally protected.
feather.fabrics: Feathers and feather-rich blends fill pillows, sofa and seat cushions, featherbeds (mattress toppers) and budget comforters. Their spring suits cushions that must support weight rather than simply insulate. Casings use tightly woven, down-proof cotton ticking to stop quills from escaping. Decorative uses include millinery, costume, fly-fishing flies, trims and fans. Industrial poultry feathers, a far larger stream, are hydrolyzed into feather meal or researched as a keratin source for films, fibers and composites.
feather.quality: Squeeze a feather pillow: it should rebound readily and feel resilient rather than flat or crunchy. Many sharp quills poking through suggest large feathers or thin ticking. Check the label for species and the down and feather percentages, and look for disclosure of crushed feathers, which the FTC says must be stated when more than minimal. A clean, neutral smell indicates well-washed fill. Tight, down-proof ticking with a high thread density lasts longer. For decorative feathers, ask about species and legal origin, since trade in feathers of many wild birds is restricted.
pros: Curved feathers give firm, springy support that suits cushions and pillows.
Feather fill is cheaper than down and makes use of an abundant by-product.
Feather bedding has been found to accumulate less dust-mite allergen than some synthetic bedding.
Feather fillings can be washed, re-sorted and reused.
cons: Quills can poke through casings and prick the user.
Feathers insulate less than down per unit weight.
Fillings flatten over time and need regular plumping.
Wet feathers mat, dry slowly and can develop odor or mildew.
feather.impact: Filling feathers are a by-product of duck and goose meat production and share the welfare issues of down, including live plucking in some regions, which standards such as the Responsible Down Standard also cover because they apply to feathers. Processing uses water, detergent and heat for washing and sanitizing. The much larger chicken feather stream is often a disposal problem, and converting it to keratin materials is an active research area. For health, New Zealand studies from 1999 and 2002 measured markedly lower house dust mite allergen (Der p 1) in feather pillows than in synthetic ones, which a 2004 study linked mainly to the tighter weave of feather pillow covers.
feather.care: Plump feather pillows and cushions daily to redistribute the fill. Use a removable, washable protector and wash that often. Wash feather pillows only when needed, in a front-loading machine on a gentle cycle, about 30 C or as labeled, with a mild or down detergent, two at a time for balance. Dry thoroughly on low heat with dryer balls, checking that no damp clumps remain, since damp feathers mildew. Air in sunlight to freshen. Replace pillows when they no longer recover after plumping. Store decorative feathers flat or in boxes away from light, dust and pests. The product label governs.
faq: What is the difference between a feather pillow and a down pillow?

Feathers have a stiff central quill and give firmer, springier support; down clusters have no quill and give soft, light loft. Many pillows blend both, and the label must state the percentages when down is less than 75 percent in US practice.
Are feather pillows bad for dust mite allergies?

Not necessarily. New Zealand studies found lower dust-mite allergen in feather pillows than in synthetic pillows, largely because feather pillow covers are woven more tightly. Allergen-proof covers help with any pillow type.
Why do feathers poke out of my pillow?

Stiff quills work through gaps between the threads of the casing. Large or broken feathers and loosely woven ticking make it worse. A tightly woven, down-proof pillow protector reduces it, and pulling a quill out backward avoids enlarging the hole.
How often should a feather pillow be replaced?
When it stays flat after plumping or smells even after washing. A folding test helps: fold the pillow in half; if it does not spring open, the fill has lost resilience.
notable: A 1999 New Zealand study found new synthetic pillows accumulated about three times as much dust-mite allergen as new feather pillows over 12 months.
In lab tests, live dust mites passed through standard synthetic pillow covers within 24 hours but not through feather pillow covers.
The FTC says selling feather products with more than minimal crushed or damaged plumage without disclosure would be deceptive.

eri-silk.types: Eri silk, called endi or errandi in Assam, comes from the domesticated eri silkworm, Samia ricini. Cocoons are mainly white, with a red or brick-colored strain. Because the cocoon is open-ended, eri is not reeled but spun, and trade forms include degummed fiber or tops, hand-spun yarn, mill-spun yarn in counts suitable for weaving and knitting, and noil from short waste. Hand-spun yarn is thicker and more irregular; mill-spun is finer and even. Eri is often sold as peace or ahimsa silk when moths emerge before processing. India's Ministry of Textiles reports eri at roughly 7,900 tonnes, about 19 percent of the country's raw silk output, in its 2025-26 annual report.
eri-silk.fabrics: Eri is woven into shawls, stoles, chadars, blankets and jacket fabric in Assam and Meghalaya, and increasingly into scarves, suiting and knitting yarn for export. Meghalaya's Ryndia, a hand-spun, handwoven and often naturally dyed eri textile made by Khasi, Bhoi and Jaintia communities, received a geographical indication tag in 2025. Eri blends with cotton, wool or mulberry silk appear in stoles and suiting. Its matte, woolly texture suits winter wraps rather than lustrous evening wear.
eri-silk.quality: Genuine eri has a matte, slightly textured surface, a soft, warm hand and a mild natural sheen, unlike the glassy luster of reeled mulberry silk. Hand-spun cloth shows slubs and slight irregularity, which is expected; very uniform cloth may be mill-spun or a blend. Check the fiber label for 100 percent silk or for blend percentages, and look for the Silk Mark label on Indian products, which certifies pure natural silk. For Ryndia, look for authorized GI users. Peace silk claims should be backed by the producer's description of how cocoons were handled.
pros: Spun eri is warm and soft, making silk suitable for winter shawls and blankets.
Moths can emerge before processing, since the cocoon is spun rather than reeled.
Eri takes natural dyes well and is widely sold in natural colors.
Rearing on castor supports household livelihoods in northeastern India.
cons: Spun eri lacks the smooth luster that many buyers expect from silk.
Hand-spun cloth varies in thickness and can pill at slubs.
Peace silk claims are voluntary and often undocumented.
Like all silk, it is weakened by sunlight, alkali and chlorine bleach.
eri-silk.impact: Eri is reared indoors on castor or other host leaves, commonly as a small household activity in Assam and Meghalaya, and castor is also grown for oil, so land use is partly shared. Because cocoons are spun, moths can be allowed to emerge; pupae are also eaten locally, which matters for how ethical claims are framed. No peer-reviewed life cycle assessment of eri fabric was found in this review. Degumming uses soap or alkali and heat, and natural dyeing can use mordants with their own effluent concerns. Hand spinning and weaving provide rural income, but wages and conditions vary and are rarely documented.
eri-silk.care: Hand wash in cool water with a mild, pH-neutral silk or wool detergent, or dry clean if the label requires it, especially for naturally dyed pieces that may bleed. Do not soak for long, wring or rub. Roll in a towel to remove water and dry flat or on a padded hanger in shade, since sunlight yellows and weakens silk. Iron on a low silk setting on the reverse while slightly damp, or steam. Spot clean with cold water; avoid chlorine bleach and enzyme detergents. Store folded with acid-free tissue in breathable cloth and check for carpet beetles. The product label governs.
faq: Is eri silk really cruelty-free?

Eri cocoons are open-ended, so the moth can emerge before the silk is processed, and much eri is produced this way. It is not guaranteed: some producers process cocoons with pupae inside, and pupae are eaten locally. Ask how the cocoons were handled.
Why doesn't eri silk look shiny?

Eri is spun from short degummed fibers rather than reeled as continuous filament. Spun yarn has fiber ends on its surface that scatter light, so eri looks matte and feels more like fine wool or cotton.
Is eri silk warm?
Yes. Spun eri traps air in its structure and is traditionally used for winter shawls and wraps in northeastern India. It is warmer than smooth reeled silk of the same weight.
What is Ryndia?

Ryndia is the Khasi term for a hand-spun, handwoven eri silk textile from Meghalaya, often naturally dyed. It received a geographical indication tag in 2025, which reserves the name for authorized producers from the region.
notable: Eri makes up roughly a fifth of India's raw silk output, making it the country's largest non-mulberry silk.
Meghalaya's Ryndia eri textile received a geographical indication tag in 2025, following recognition of Umden-Diwon as the state's first eri silk village in 2021.
Because eri cocoons cannot be reeled, the moth's emergence does not destroy the commercial value of the silk, unlike most mulberry silk.

tussar-silk.types: Tussar covers several Antheraea silks: tropical tasar from A. mylitta in central and eastern India, Chinese oak tussah from A. pernyi, and Japanese A. yamamai. Indian yarns are named by how they are made. Reeled tasar is continuous filament from whole cocoons. Ghicha, from a Hindi word for pulled, is drawn by hand from unreelable cocoons and basin waste, giving a thick, slubby yarn. Katia is spun from waste left after reeling, and balkal is spun from cocoon peduncles after alkaline boiling. India's Ministry of Textiles reports tasar at roughly 1,900 tonnes, about 4.6 percent of Indian raw silk, in its 2025-26 annual report.
tussar-silk.fabrics: Indian tussar is woven into saris, dupattas, stoles, shirting, suiting and furnishing fabric, often in its natural beige or honey color. Bhagalpur in Bihar, sometimes called India's silk city, is known for tussar cloth with stripes and checks; Bhagalpur silk received geographical indication status in 2013. Ghicha and katia yarns give textured, rustic fabrics used as weft with reeled or cotton warps. Chinese tussah was historically woven into shantung and pongee. Tussar is also blended with cotton, linen or mulberry silk and used for hand-painted and block-printed textiles.
tussar-silk.quality: Real tussar has a dull, golden or beige natural color, a slightly coarse, crisp hand and visible texture; pure white or brilliantly dyed cloth may be bleached tussar or a different silk. Ghicha weft shows thick, irregular slubs, which are a feature, not a fault. Examine a torn weft thread: tussar filament is flat and ribbon-like under magnification. Ask for the Silk Mark label on Indian products and check blend percentages, since tussar-look fabrics may be cotton or polyester blends. Handloom pieces cost more than power-loom ones and show slight irregularities in weave and selvedge.
pros: Natural golden color means many fabrics need no dyeing.
The filament is strong and extensible, giving durable cloth.
Textured ghicha and katia yarns use cocoons and waste that cannot be reeled.
Forest-based rearing supports tribal livelihoods in central and eastern India.
cons: Tussar can water-spot and stiffen after washing, so it often needs dry cleaning.
It takes dyes less evenly than mulberry silk, limiting bright colors.
The trade name is used loosely and covers several species and blends.
Reeled tussar involves killing pupae, like most reeled silk.
tussar-silk.impact: Tropical tasar is reared outdoors on forest and planted host trees such as Terminalia and sal, so it needs no dedicated mulberry farms or irrigation, and it provides cash income to tribal households in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and neighboring states. Outdoor rearing exposes larvae to weather and predators, and yields can be low and unpredictable. Cocoons for reeling are stifled, killing pupae; ghicha and katia use pierced cocoons and waste. Cooking and degumming use alkali or enzymes, and reeling is often done in cottage settings where income and working conditions are rarely documented. No life cycle assessment of tussar fabric was found in this review.
tussar-silk.care: Dry cleaning is the safest choice for tussar saris, suits and structured garments. If hand washing is allowed, use cold water and a mild, pH-neutral silk detergent, wash quickly without soaking or rubbing, and rinse well; uneven wetting can leave water marks. Roll in a towel and dry flat in shade. Iron on the reverse at a low silk setting, with a pressing cloth, while slightly damp. Do not spray water directly on the fabric. Store folded in cotton or muslin, refolding periodically to prevent permanent creases, and protect from carpet beetles. Keep away from perfume and deodorant. The product label governs.
faq: What is the difference between tussar and mulberry silk?

Tussar comes from wild or semi-wild Antheraea silkworms that feed on forest trees; mulberry silk comes from the domesticated Bombyx mori fed mulberry leaves. Tussar filament is flatter and coarser, with a natural golden color and a textured, less lustrous look.
What is ghicha silk?
Ghicha is a tussar yarn drawn by hand from cocoons that cannot be reeled and from reeling waste. It is thick and irregular, and woven into fabric it gives a rustic, slubby texture often used as weft.
Can tussar silk be washed at home?

Some tussar can be hand washed in cold water with a gentle detergent, but it may water-spot, shrink slightly or stiffen. For saris and tailored garments, dry cleaning is safer unless the label says otherwise.
How can I tell if a tussar sari is real?

Look for the Silk Mark label, the natural golden tone, a slightly coarse hand and flat, ribbon-like filaments under magnification. A burn test on a loose thread should smell like burning hair and leave crushable ash rather than a hard bead.
notable: Ghicha yarn takes its name from a Hindi word meaning pulled, because it is drawn by hand from unreelable cocoons.
Bhagalpur silk from Bihar received geographical indication status in 2013.
Shantung cloth takes its name from Shandong province, where it was historically woven from wild tussah silk.

muga-silk.types: Muga silk comes from Antheraea assamensis reared outdoors on som and other host trees in Assam, and is the rarest of India's commercial silks: the Ministry of Textiles reports roughly 230 tonnes, about 0.6 percent of Indian raw silk, in its 2025-26 annual report. Trade forms are reeled raw muga yarn, spun muga from pierced cocoons and waste, and blends with mulberry (pat) silk or cotton. Assam's silk tradition groups muga with eri and pat. Muga Silk of Assam has been a registered geographical indication since 2007, and a GI logo followed in 2014, with the Assam Science Technology and Environment Council as its registered proprietor.
muga-silk.fabrics: Muga is woven mainly on handlooms around Sualkuchi and other Assamese weaving centers into the mekhela chador (a two-piece garment), riha, saris and stoles. It is usually left in its natural golden color, with woven motifs in contrasting threads. Muga is sometimes combined with pat or eri silk in the same garment. Small quantities go into ties, handbags and export accessories. Its stiffness and weight suit structured drape rather than soft, fluid garments.
muga-silk.quality: Genuine muga has a natural golden luster that deepens with age and washing, a firm, crisp hand and a relatively high price. Uniform bright gold at a low price suggests dyed mulberry silk, polyester or a blend; adulteration has damaged muga's reputation, according to Assamese reporting. Look for the GI logo, Silk Mark labeling and the seller's authorized-user status, and ask for a test certificate on high-value garments. The Sualkuchi silk testing laboratory and other certified labs test for muga content. Hand-reeled muga shows slight variations in thickness, while perfectly even yarn deserves scrutiny.
pros: The natural golden color needs no dyeing.
Muga is strong and durable, and garments are commonly kept for generations.
A registered geographical indication and GI logo help protect origin.
Outdoor rearing on host trees supports rural Assamese households.
cons: Supply is very small and restricted to one region, so prices are high.
Adulteration and imitation are widespread in the market.
The firm hand is less soft and fluid than mulberry silk.
Production is vulnerable to pollution, weather and disease affecting outdoor rearing.
muga-silk.impact: Muga rearing is an outdoor activity on som and other host trees, needing no irrigation or mulberry cultivation, but it exposes larvae to birds, insects, disease and weather, and research has linked air pollution near industrial sites to stress on host trees. Production is tiny, about 0.6 percent of India's raw silk, so the industry's footprint is small in absolute terms; no life cycle assessment of muga fabric was found. Reeling kills pupae, as with most reeled silk. Socially, muga sustains rearers, reelers and handloom weavers in Assam, and adulteration undercuts genuine producers, which is why the GI logo and testing projects at the Central Muga Eri Research and Training Institute matter.
muga-silk.care: Many Assamese owners hand wash muga in cool water with a mild, neutral soap or shampoo, which traditional accounts say brightens its luster; dry cleaning is an alternative for garments with mixed fibers or zari work. Do not soak for long, wring or scrub. Rinse, roll in a towel and dry in shade, as direct sun can weaken the silk. Iron on the reverse at a low silk setting while slightly damp. Store folded in soft cotton cloth, refolding occasionally to avoid crease breaks, with protection against carpet beetles and silverfish. Keep perfume and deodorant off the fabric. The product label governs.
faq: Why is muga silk golden?
The color is natural to the silk produced by Antheraea assamensis and is not dyed. It varies slightly with rearing season and host tree, and is often described as deepening with age.
How can I tell real muga from fake?

Buy from authorized GI users, look for the muga GI logo and Silk Mark label, and request a laboratory test for expensive pieces. Real muga has a natural, not glaring, gold and a firm hand; unusually low prices are a warning sign.
Why is muga silk so expensive?

It is produced only in Assam in small quantities, about 230 tonnes a year according to the Ministry of Textiles, by outdoor rearing that is exposed to weather and disease, and it is mainly hand-reeled and handwoven.
Can muga silk be washed?
Yes. Hand washing in cool water with a mild soap is traditional for muga, and it is known for tolerating washing well. Dry clean pieces with metallic zari or mixed fibers.
notable: Muga Silk of Assam received geographical indication status in 2007 and a registered GI logo in 2014.
Muga makes up well under 1 percent of India's raw silk output.
The Central Muga Eri Research and Training Institute has listed a project to develop a portable analyzer for muga purity in dyed fabrics.
