pbi.types: PBI in textiles is mostly a staple fiber sold for blending, rarely used alone. The best-known product is PBI Gold, which its producer describes as 40 percent PBI and 60 percent para-aramid, used as a firefighter turnout outer shell; later shell fabrics combine PBI with para-aramid in different weaves and finishes, such as TenCate's Flex7, which is marketed as 'powered by PBI'. Outside apparel, the PBI name also covers fuel-cell and battery membranes and electrospun mats, so specifications must state the product form. Because very few companies make textile PBI fiber, grades are identified by the fabric maker's style names rather than by public fiber grades.
pbi.fabrics: The main use is the outer shell of structural firefighting turnout coats and trousers, where PBI and para-aramid blends are woven in ripstop or twill constructions and treated with a water-repellent finish. The shell sits over a moisture barrier and a thermal liner to form the full ensemble. PBI blends also appear in some industrial and military protective garments and in specialty knits, but volumes are small, and price keeps PBI a minority component in most garments.
pbi.quality: For turnout gear, the certification label is the key document: shells are sold as part of ensembles certified to the NFPA standard for structural firefighting in North America or EN 469 in Europe, and the producer states PBI Gold meets NFPA and EN 469 requirements. Check the shell composition percentages, fabric weight, the certifying body, and the date of manufacture on the garment label. Compare thermal protective performance and total heat loss values across complete ensembles rather than shell fabrics alone. The natural gold color does not prove PBI content; para-aramid is similar in color.
pros: It does not melt and stays flexible after charring instead of turning brittle.
Blended with para-aramid, it resists shrinking and break-open under flame and heat.
It absorbs more moisture than most synthetics, which aids comfort.
It resists acids, bases and organic solvents.
cons: It is expensive and made by very few producers, which limits availability.
Its natural gold color is hard to dye over, restricting color options.
On its own it has moderate strength, so it relies on para-aramid blend partners.
The para-aramid partner in blends still suffers from ultraviolet degradation.
pbi.impact: PBI's footprint is poorly documented because output is small and production data are proprietary; the atlas found no independent life cycle figures. The polymer is made from aromatic petrochemical monomers and spun from strong polar solvents that must be recovered. Its environmental relevance lies more in the firefighting ensemble than in the fiber: debate has focused on PFAS in moisture barriers and fluorinated water-repellent finishes on shells. California's AB 1817 exempts firefighting protective equipment from its textile PFAS ban, so the composition of each layer must be checked through the maker. Used turnout gear is usually landfilled or incinerated.
pbi.care: Turnout gear care follows the maker's instructions and NFPA's standard for the selection, care and maintenance of firefighting ensembles, which sets routine and advanced cleaning, inspection and retirement rules. In practice, gear is cleaned after contamination in a front-loading extractor with detergents the maker approves, never with chlorine bleach, and dried away from direct sunlight because ultraviolet light degrades the para-aramid in PBI blends. Liners and shells are usually separated for cleaning. Inspect for char, thin spots, torn seams and failed reflective trim, and retire gear when the standard or the maker requires it.
faq: Why is some turnout gear gold?

Natural PBI fiber is gold, and para-aramid is yellow, so PBI and aramid shells are often left in their natural color. Other colors are harder to achieve because the fibers resist dyeing. Color alone does not show what the shell contains.
Is PBI better than Nomex?

They do different jobs. PBI blends keep flexibility and resist break-open after severe flame exposure, which suits turnout outer shells, while meta-aramid is cheaper and widely used in station wear and industrial FR clothing. The certified performance of the whole garment matters more than the fiber.
Does PBI melt?

No. PBI has no melting point in normal use; it chars and keeps its shape at temperatures that destroy most textile fibers. That is why it is used where fabric must not melt or drip onto skin under flame.
notable: PBI's producer describes PBI Gold as 40 percent PBI and 60 percent para-aramid, pairing PBI's char stability with para-aramid strength.
California's 2025 textile PFAS ban exempts firefighting protective equipment, one reason ensemble chemistry is still debated in the fire service.

carbon.types: Carbon fiber is specified by tow size and modulus class. 'K' counts thousands of filaments per tow, from 1K and 3K up to 12K, 24K and large tows of 48K to 50K; Toray lists its standard-modulus T300 in 1K, 3K, 6K and 12K tows and T700 in 6K, 12K and 24K. Standard-modulus fibers such as T300 have a tensile modulus near 230 GPa; intermediate- and high-modulus PAN grades and pitch-based ultra-high-modulus fibers trade strength or cost for stiffness. Product forms include continuous tow, unidirectional tape, woven fabric, non-crimp fabric, braided sleeve, prepreg with resin already applied, chopped and milled fiber, and nonwoven mats of recycled fiber.
carbon.fabrics: Small tows such as 3K are woven into the plain and twill fabrics seen on bicycle frames, car trim and consumer goods, where the pattern is visible under clear resin. Larger 12K to 50K tows go into unidirectional tapes, non-crimp fabrics and pultrusions for wind turbine spar caps, pressure vessels and civil strengthening, where cost matters more than appearance. Braided sleeves form tubes such as fishing rods and hockey sticks. Outside composites, carbon fiber makes heating elements and conductive textiles, and oxidized PAN, an intermediate stage, is blended into flame-resistant fabrics.
carbon.quality: Buyers of fabric should ask for fiber grade and tow size, weave, areal weight in grams per square meter, sizing compatibility with the intended resin, and, for prepreg, resin system, cure schedule and out-life. For finished parts, laminate test data and the layup matter more than the weave on the surface: a glossy 3K twill can be a cosmetic layer over fiberglass or foam. Look for dry spots, pinholes, resin-starved areas, wrinkles and fiber misalignment. Red flags include 'carbon' products that are vinyl wraps or printed polyester, and strength claims without test data. Large tows cost less per kilogram but give coarser surfaces.
pros: It gives very high stiffness per unit weight, which enables light, rigid structures.
It resists fatigue and does not corrode, unlike many metals.
It is electrically and thermally conductive, useful for heating and sensing.
Its thermal expansion along the fiber is very low, keeping precision structures stable.
cons: Parts fail in a brittle way and can hide internal damage after impact.
Production is energy-intensive and costly compared with glass fiber.
Conductivity causes galvanic corrosion with aluminum and steel if not insulated.
Cured thermoset composites are difficult to recycle, and recovered fibers lose some strength.
carbon.impact: Carbon fiber production is energy-intensive. A review of life cycle studies titled 'Bringing Light into the Dark' reported climate impacts of about 13 to 29 kg CO2e per kg of PAN-based carbon fiber in global scenarios and about 34 kg in a Chinese grid scenario, and estimated that renewable electricity plus process optimization could cut the impact by about 62 percent. In use, lighter vehicles and aircraft can offset some of this. End of life is the weak point: thermoset composites are mostly landfilled, and pyrolysis recovery works but reduced recovered fiber tensile strength by up to about 35 percent in one steam and air study.
carbon.care: Clean composite products with mild soap and water, and avoid strong solvents that can attack the resin or clear coat. Follow torque specifications for clamps and fittings, because overtightening crushes tubes. After a crash or hard impact, have critical parts such as bicycle frames, forks or climbing gear inspected, since damage may not show on the surface. Protect clear-coated surfaces from prolonged sunlight, which yellows and degrades resin. Store dry fabric flat or rolled in a clean, dry place; prepregs are usually kept frozen and have limited working time at room temperature. Do not sand or cut composites without dust control.
faq: What does 3K carbon fiber mean?

It means each tow contains about 3,000 filaments. The number describes the bundle size, not the grade or strength. Small tows like 3K make fine, even weave patterns favored for visible surfaces, while 12K and larger tows are cheaper per kilogram and used for thick structural parts.
Is carbon fiber stronger than steel?

Per unit weight, carbon fiber composites are far stiffer and stronger than steel in the fiber direction. Across the fibers and under impact they are weaker, and they fail without bending first, so good design orients fibers along the loads.
Can carbon fiber be recycled?

Yes, partly. Pyrolysis and solvent processes can remove the resin and recover fibers, which are usually chopped and reused in nonwovens, molding compounds or concrete. Recovered fibers are shorter and can be weaker than virgin fiber, so they rarely return to aerospace structures.
notable: Large-tow carbon fiber with 48,000 or more filaments per bundle was developed to cut cost for wind energy and industrial parts rather than to improve performance.
A review of carbon fiber life cycle studies found that where the fiber is made matters: the grid electricity mix shifted climate impact by several kilograms of CO2e per kilogram of fiber.

glass.types: Textile glass is graded by composition. E-glass, the general-purpose grade, is roughly 54 percent silica, 14 percent alumina, 22 percent calcium and magnesium oxides and 10 percent boron oxide, with pristine filament strength near 3.4 GPa and modulus near 69 to 72 GPa. S-glass and S-2 glass are magnesium aluminosilicates of roughly 65 percent silica, 25 percent alumina and 10 percent magnesia, reaching about 4.6 GPa and 86 GPa at higher cost. Alkali-resistant glass contains zirconia for cement reinforcement. Product forms include direct and assembled roving sold by tex, chopped strand, chopped strand mat, woven roving, fine woven fabrics, twisted yarns and glass wool insulation.
glass.fabrics: Chopped strand mat and heavy woven roving are laminated with polyester or vinyl ester resin into boat hulls, tanks and panels. Fine, tightly woven E-glass fabrics impregnated with epoxy form the base of printed circuit boards. Unidirectional and multiaxial non-crimp fabrics reinforce wind turbine blades. Coated glass fabrics make welding curtains, fire blankets, PVC-coated insect screening and PTFE-coated tensile roofs. Glass yarn also appears in cut-resistant glove cores and, as knit socks, in some mattress fire barriers.
glass.quality: For composite fabrics, specify glass type, areal weight in grams per square meter or ounces per square yard, weave or stitch architecture, roving tex, and a sizing compatible with the resin, since epoxy and polyester need different silane chemistry. S-glass should come with a certificate, because it is visually identical to cheaper E-glass. For finished laminates, check fiber content, voids and dry fibers, which show as white patches. For household items, read the content label: mattresses and upholstered goods may list glass fiber in a fire barrier layer. A red flag is a mattress with a removable zipped cover over a glass fiber sock.
pros: It is inexpensive compared with carbon and aramid for good strength.
It is nonflammable and an electrical insulator, useful for circuit boards and fire barriers.
It is dimensionally stable and does not absorb water into the fiber.
It is widely available in many product forms and resin-compatible sizings.
cons: Its lower stiffness makes glass composites heavier than carbon for equal rigidity.
Loose fibers and fragments irritate skin, eyes and airways.
It is brittle and abrades on itself, so it suits reinforcement rather than clothing.
Glass-reinforced thermosets are hard to recycle at end of life.
glass.impact: Glass fiber begins in large furnaces that melt sand and minerals at high temperature, so energy use and furnace emissions dominate production impacts; a basalt review in Polymers cites about 6 to 8 kWh per kilogram for glass fiber. Composites raise the end-of-life problem: retired wind blades, boats and panels are largely landfilled, ground into filler or co-processed in cement kilns. Pyrolysis is being piloted; a pilot plant study published in 2023 recovered fibers 6.2 to 8.05 micrometers across that did not meet the WHO respirable fiber definition, though residual coatings carried traces of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Fiber migration from mattress fire barriers is a newer consumer concern.
glass.care: When cutting or handling glass fabric, wear gloves, long sleeves and eye protection, and wash work clothes separately so fibers do not transfer to other laundry. Cut with sharp shears to limit fraying. Clean composite boats and panels with mild soap and water, and renew gel coat or paint to keep water and ultraviolet light out of the laminate. Replace fire blankets and welding curtains after use or damage. Do not remove the zipped cover of a mattress that contains a glass fiber barrier; if fibers have escaped, maker guidance and professional cleaning are the safer route.
faq: What is the difference between E-glass and S-glass?

E-glass is the general-purpose grade with boron oxide and calcium oxide in its composition. S-glass is a magnesium aluminosilicate with about a third more tensile strength and higher stiffness, used in aerospace, armor and pressure vessels. It costs considerably more and looks the same.
Is fiberglass in mattresses dangerous?

Glass fiber is used inside some mattress fire barriers. If it stays enclosed it is not usually a problem, but if the cover is removed or damaged, fibers can spread and irritate skin, eyes and airways. Keep the cover on and follow the maker's instructions.
Is fiberglass the same as glass wool?

Both are glass, but glass wool is a fluffy insulation made by centrifugal fiberizing, while textile glass is drawn into continuous filaments for yarn, fabric and composites. They differ in fiber diameter, form and health classification.
notable: Most printed circuit boards are built on a core of finely woven E-glass fabric impregnated with epoxy.
S-glass and E-glass cannot be told apart by eye; buyers depend on certificates or elemental analysis to confirm the grade.

basalt.types: Basalt fiber is sold in the same product forms as glass fiber: direct and assembled continuous roving, chopped fiber of set lengths for concrete and plastics, woven fabrics, stitched multiaxial fabrics, mesh and geogrid, pultruded basalt fiber reinforced polymer (BFRP) rebar, and short staple or 'superthin' fibers from flame or centrifugal blowing for insulation. Unlike glass there are no widely standardized composition grades such as E or S, because the melt comes from quarried rock; buyers distinguish products by filament diameter, linear density, sizing chemistry (epoxy-, polyester- or cement-compatible) and the producer's quarry and process. Performance data should therefore be checked batch by batch.
basalt.fabrics: Woven basalt fabrics are used for fire blankets, heat shields and welding protection, and as reinforcement in composite panels, pipes and sporting goods. Chopped basalt fiber is mixed into concrete and shotcrete to control cracking, while basalt mesh and BFRP bars replace steel in some slabs and precast elements where corrosion is a concern. Prepregs combine basalt fabric with resins; one study with bio-based furan resin reached the highest fire hazard classification required for large surfaces in railway vehicle interiors. Basalt also appears in cable, pipe and tank reinforcement.
basalt.quality: Ask for a batch-specific test certificate giving tensile strength, modulus, filament diameter and linear density, because properties scatter between producers and batches more than for E-glass. Confirm the sizing matches the resin or cement. For rebar and mesh, look for approvals under the relevant national construction codes and check long-term alkali durability data. The brown color suggests basalt but is not proof; elemental analysis is. Red flags include 'natural' or 'eco' claims without an environmental product declaration, and property figures copied from generic reviews rather than measured on the product.
pros: It usually has higher modulus and strength than E-glass at a similar weight.
It keeps a large share of its strength after exposure to high temperatures.
It resists alkali, suiting concrete reinforcement where steel would corrode.
It does not burn and is used in fire blankets and heat shields.
cons: Quality varies with the rock source and furnace, so data scatter between batches.
Its polar, inert surface bonds poorly to resins without suitable sizing or treatment.
Production volumes are small, limiting supply chains and design codes.
Brittle filaments shed and itch like glass fiber when cut or abraded.
basalt.impact: Basalt fiber avoids the boron-containing batch minerals used in E-glass and melts quarried rock directly, so its production impacts center on quarrying, crushing and furnace energy. Independent life cycle assessments comparing basalt with glass are few, and energy figures in reviews depend on furnace type. Its best-documented environmental benefit is durability: a 2023 review in Materials concluded that adding basalt fiber improved concrete durability measures across many studies, though it flagged research gaps before routine structural use. Non-corroding BFRP rebar may extend service life in marine structures. End-of-life options mirror glass composites and remain limited.
basalt.care: Handle basalt fabric and roving with gloves, long sleeves and eye protection, since broken filaments irritate skin like glass fiber, and control dust when cutting or grinding composites. Store fabric and roving dry and away from contamination that would weaken resin bonding. Basalt fire blankets should be kept in their container, inspected for holes or brittleness, and replaced after use. Composite parts are cleaned with mild soap and water and protected from ultraviolet light by coatings, as with glass-reinforced parts.
faq: Is basalt fiber better than fiberglass?

It is stiffer and more heat and alkali resistant than E-glass, but it usually costs more per kilogram, has less consistent properties and fewer design standards. For most boats and panels E-glass is still the default; basalt suits heat exposure and some concrete uses.
Is basalt fiber natural?

The raw material is natural rock, but the fiber is a manufactured glass drawn from a melt at high temperature, much like glass fiber. 'Natural' claims describe the feedstock, not the product, and do not imply safety or biodegradability.
Is basalt fiber safe to work with?

Continuous basalt filaments are generally too thick to be respirable, but cutting and grinding can create dust and fragments that irritate skin, eyes and airways. Treat it like glass fiber and follow the safety data sheet.
notable: Basalt fiber's brown color comes from its iron oxide content, which also makes the melt harder to heat evenly in furnaces.
A basalt and furan resin prepreg in a 2022 study met the highest fire hazard class for large surfaces inside railway vehicles.

metal.types: Modern metal textile fibers fall into several groups. Stainless steel is drawn into fine filament bundles or cut into staple and blended with cotton or polyester; suppliers commonly cite 316L grade for conductive blends. Silver-plated nylon or polyester yarns carry a thin metal skin on a polymer core. Fine copper and silver-copper wires are wrapped or plied with textile yarns. Decorative metallic yarns are mostly metallized or colored polymer film slit into narrow strips, which contain very little metal. Historic metal threads, from gilt silver strip to copper wire wrapped on silk or cotton, form a separate conservation category.
metal.fabrics: Conductive yarn knitted into the thumb and fingertips of gloves lets them work touchscreens, which sense the capacitance of a finger. Stainless steel blend yarns form grids in antistatic workwear, cleanroom garments and conveyor fabrics, and cores in some cut-resistant glove yarns. Silver-plated knits make electrodes in heart rate straps and wearable sensors, and radio frequency shielding pouches, curtains and garments. Stainless multi-ply thread is sewn as circuits in e-textile projects. Metallic film yarns add sparkle to lame, brocade and knitwear, and metal fiber felts serve as industrial filters.
metal.quality: For touchscreen gloves, check that conductive yarn is knitted through the fingertip, including the side of the finger, rather than a painted or printed patch, which wears off quickly. For conductive thread or fabric, ask for resistance per meter or per square and whether it is stable after washing. For shielding products, look for attenuation figures in decibels with the frequency range and test method. Red flags include 'copper-infused' or 'silver' claims without a content label or test report, and metallic-look yarns sold as solid metal.
pros: Stainless and silver-plated yarns conduct electricity for touchscreen, antistatic and sensor uses.
Stainless steel fibers tolerate heat and many chemicals.
Blending a small share of metal fiber can give durable static control.
Metallic film yarns give sparkle at low cost and weight.
cons: Metal fibers add stiffness and weight, and broken filaments can prick skin.
Silver and copper coatings tarnish and wear, reducing conductivity over time.
Silver-treated textiles release silver into wash water.
Mixed metal and polymer yarns complicate textile recycling.
metal.impact: Metal fibers carry the footprint of mining and refining, although the mass used in textiles is small. The better-studied concern is release during use: silver-treated textiles shed silver particles in laundering, adding to wastewater loads, which is why antimicrobial silver claims are regulated as biocides or pesticides in some jurisdictions. Metallized film yarns are mainly polyester or nylon with thin aluminum or colored coatings, and they behave like other plastic yarns in waste. Garments with metal yarns, sensors or conductive tracks are hard to sort and recycle, and e-textiles add small electronics to the textile waste stream.
metal.care: Hand wash or use a gentle cycle in a laundry bag for touchscreen and conductive gloves, with mild detergent and no bleach, which can corrode silver and copper. Avoid fabric softeners that can coat conductive fibers. Air dry or tumble on low. For e-textile garments, remove batteries and electronics before washing as the maker directs. Metallic film yarns can melt or dull under a hot iron, so iron on low from the reverse side with a press cloth if the label allows. Historic metal threads should not be cleaned or polished at home; a textile conservator should assess them.
faq: How do touchscreen gloves work?

Most phone screens are capacitive: they detect the small change in electric field when a conductive finger touches them. Touchscreen gloves knit conductive yarn, usually stainless steel blends or silver-plated nylon, into the fingertip so the charge passes from the skin through the glove.
Why did my touchscreen gloves stop working?

Painted or printed conductive patches wear off, silver coatings can tarnish or abrade, and stiff metal yarns can break. Very thick glove linings can also insulate the fingertip. Gloves with conductive yarn knitted through the fingertip tend to last longer.
Is Lurex real metal?

Most modern metallic yarns, including many sold under familiar trade names, are thin polymer film coated with aluminum or colored layers and slit into narrow strips. They contain little metal and behave like plastic yarns in washing and ironing.
notable: Touchscreen gloves work by conducting the charge of the wearer's own finger through the glove rather than generating any signal themselves.
Most decorative 'metallic' yarns carry only a thin metal or colored coating on polymer film, so a sparkly knit can be almost entirely plastic.

ceramic.types: Industrial ceramic fiber products are grouped by fiber type and form. Refractory ceramic fiber (RCF, aluminosilicate wool), alkaline earth silicate (AES) wool and polycrystalline wool (PCW) are each sold as needled blanket, rigid board, paper, vacuum-formed shapes, modules, loose bulk fiber, rope, tape and cloth. Textile forms are usually reinforced with glass filament or metal wire to be woven or braided. Grades are named by classification temperature, the highest temperature at which shrinkage stays within a limit, and by density. Continuous oxide and silicon carbide fibers used in ceramic-matrix composites are a separate high-cost class. The safety data sheet names which fiber type a product contains.
ceramic.fabrics: Ceramic fiber cloth, tape and rope are used as furnace door seals, kiln and oven gaskets, expansion joint fillers, pipe wraps, fire stops and heat shields in industrial plants. Blankets and modules line furnaces, kilns and boilers; papers serve as gaskets and heat barriers in appliances and exhaust systems. Continuous ceramic fibers are woven or braided into preforms for aerospace composites. None of these are apparel, and the atlas does not recommend handling or processing them.
ceramic.quality: This is specification guidance for industrial buyers, not handling advice. Read the safety data sheet first to confirm whether the product is RCF, AES or PCW and its hazard classification, and prefer AES wool wherever its temperature and chemical limits suit the application, since it was developed as a less biopersistent substitute. Check classification temperature, density, shrinkage data and chemical compatibility. For removal or replacement projects, ask whether the old lining is after-service RCF that has converted to crystalline silica, which changes disposal and protection requirements. Unlabeled white 'ceramic' blankets from marketplaces are a red flag.
pros: It insulates at furnace temperatures far beyond organic fibers.
Low heat storage lets furnaces heat and cool faster, saving fuel.
It resists thermal shock and most chemicals and does not burn.
AES wool alternatives offer lower biopersistence for many applications.
cons: RCF is classified by IARC as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B).
Handling, cutting and removal release respirable fibers.
After long service above about 1,000 C, RCF partly converts to cristobalite, a crystalline silica.
It is brittle and wears when flexed or abraded.
ceramic.impact: Ceramic fiber insulation saves energy in industrial furnaces, but its hazards dominate its footprint. NIOSH recommends limiting workplace exposure to 0.5 fibers per cubic centimeter as a 10-hour time-weighted average, and the US National Toxicology Program lists respirable ceramic fibers in its Report on Carcinogens. NIOSH notes that RCF held above about 980 to 1,000 C for long periods partially devitrifies into cristobalite, so removed 'after-service' insulation can carry crystalline silica hazards as well as fiber hazards. Disposal follows local waste rules. Substitution by AES wools reduces biopersistence but not all dust concerns.
ceramic.care: The atlas gives no handling instructions for ceramic fiber. Installed insulation that is intact and enclosed should be left undisturbed. Repair, removal and disposal belong with trained contractors working under the product's safety data sheet and the occupational rules of the jurisdiction, which address exposure monitoring, respiratory protection and waste. Owners of kilns, furnaces or stoves with ceramic fiber linings should follow the equipment maker's service instructions and use qualified technicians for relining. Treat old, high-temperature linings as possible after-service fiber containing crystalline silica.
faq: Is ceramic fiber insulation as dangerous as asbestos?

They are different materials with different evidence. IARC classifies RCF as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), while asbestos is Group 1, a known human carcinogen. RCF is still hazardous when inhaled, and US workers with high exposure showed pleural changes, so exposure should be controlled.
What is after-service ceramic fiber?

It is RCF that has spent long periods above roughly 1,000 C and has partly crystallized into cristobalite, a form of crystalline silica. It is common in old furnace and kiln linings and brings a silica hazard in addition to the fiber hazard during removal.
What are AES or biosoluble wools?

Alkaline earth silicate wools are high-temperature insulation fibers based on calcium and magnesium silicates, designed to dissolve faster in lung fluid than RCF. They were developed as substitutes and are preferred where their temperature and chemical limits fit.
notable: NIOSH's recommended exposure limit for RCF is 0.5 fibers per cubic centimeter, averaged over a 10-hour shift.
Heating in service can transform amorphous RCF into crystalline cristobalite, so a lining's hazard can change over its working life.

asbestos.types: Asbestos minerals are classified for regulation, not for purchase. Regulators distinguish chrysotile, the serpentine form behind most historical use, from the amphiboles crocidolite, amosite, tremolite, anthophyllite and actinolite. Historically, the long fibers suited to spinning were graded for textiles, while shorter grades went into cement sheet, floor tile, friction products and insulation. In the United States, the EPA's 2024 rule addressed the last known ongoing uses of chrysotile: diaphragms in chlor-alkali plants, sheet gaskets, oilfield brake blocks, aftermarket automotive brakes and linings, and other vehicle friction products. This entry describes these categories only for historical and regulatory context.
asbestos.fabrics: Historical asbestos textiles included woven cloth, tape, rope, yarn, lagging and felt, used in fire blankets, heat-resistant gloves and aprons, theater safety curtains, boiler and stove door rope seals, pipe and duct wrap, electrical insulation and laboratory equipment. Asbestos was often blended with a carrier fiber such as cotton to make it spinnable. Such items can survive in old buildings, ships, workshops, laboratories and collections, which is why museums and property owners treat unknown vintage heat-resistant textiles with caution.
asbestos.quality: This atlas gives no buying, selling or handling advice for asbestos. Asbestos is banned or restricted in many countries; the International Ban Asbestos Secretariat lists national bans in roughly 70 countries, with 2025 totals varying by source and by how partial bans are counted. Legacy items are the realistic concern: old fire blankets, gloves, rope gaskets, lagging and lab mats that are gray-white, stiff or felt-like may contain asbestos, but appearance cannot confirm it. If an item is suspected, do not buy, sell, use or disturb it; only an accredited laboratory sample taken by a qualified professional can establish its content.
pros: Historically it resisted heat and fire, which drove its use in protective and insulating products.
It could be spun and woven like a textile fiber.
It resisted many chemicals and was cheap, which explains its once-wide adoption.
These historical properties do not justify any current use.
cons: IARC classifies all forms of asbestos as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1).
Inhaled fibers cause asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma, often decades after exposure.
Legacy material in buildings, vehicles and products still exposes workers and occupants when disturbed.
Removal and disposal are costly and must follow strict regulations.
asbestos.impact: Asbestos's footprint is measured in disease. Beyond the annual death toll estimates in the research profile, chrysotile is still mined and used in some countries while dozens of others have banned it. In the United States, the EPA published its Part 1 chrysotile rule under TSCA section 6 on 28 March 2024, effective 28 May 2024, banning the remaining known uses with phased compliance dates. Industry groups challenged it in the Fifth Circuit; in 2025 EPA sought time to reconsider parts of the rule, then withdrew that motion in July 2025, leaving the rule in place while litigation continued. Legacy asbestos in buildings and waste remains the main exposure route.
asbestos.care: Do not disturb. Suspected asbestos textiles or materials should not be cut, brushed, washed, vacuumed, repaired, moved, bagged or thrown out by an untrained person. Keep people away from damaged material and leave assessment, sampling, removal and disposal to licensed asbestos professionals working under the rules of the jurisdiction, such as EPA and OSHA requirements in the United States or national rules implementing EU directives. Museums and owners of historic collections should consult conservators and licensed assessors. This is general safety information, not legal or professional advice.
faq: Is asbestos banned in the United States?

The EPA's 2024 TSCA rule bans the remaining known uses of chrysotile asbestos, with phased deadlines, and was in effect as of the sources reviewed, though litigation continued. Older asbestos in buildings is not removed by the rule and is managed under separate abatement and workplace regulations.
Is asbestos banned worldwide?

No. Many countries, including all EU member states, have national bans, and the International Ban Asbestos Secretariat's list counted roughly 70 countries in 2025, with totals varying by source. Chrysotile is still mined and used elsewhere, so bans remain uneven.
How can I tell if an old fire blanket contains asbestos?

You cannot tell by look or feel. Only an accredited laboratory analyzing a sample taken by a qualified professional can confirm it. Leave the item undisturbed, keep people away if it is damaged, and contact a licensed asbestos assessor.
Is chrysotile safer than other asbestos?

Chrysotile is less biopersistent than amphiboles and less potent for mesothelioma, but IARC classifies all asbestos forms, chrysotile included, as carcinogenic to humans. Regulators treat it as a serious hazard, which is why the EPA's 2024 rule targeted it.
notable: The EPA's 2024 chrysotile rule was the first ban finalized under the agency's revised TSCA section 6 authority.
Among the last US uses of chrysotile were diaphragms in chlor-alkali plants that make chlorine and caustic soda.
In June 2025 EPA told the Fifth Circuit it planned to reconsider parts of its chrysotile rule, then withdrew that request the following month.

recycled-cotton.types: Recycled cotton is separated first by source. Pre-consumer (post-industrial) fiber comes from spinning waste, cutting-room scraps and off-cuts; it is clean, known in composition and often sorted by color. Post-consumer fiber comes from used garments and home textiles and is more variable, with dyes, finishes and blended fibers. Mechanically recycled cotton is shredded back to short fiber and respun; color-sorted inputs can give melange yarns with no redyeing. Chemically recycled cotton is not sold as cotton: cotton-rich waste is dissolved into pulp for regenerated fibers such as lyocell or viscose. The Swedish chemical recycler Renewcell, which made such pulp, entered bankruptcy and was acquired by the investment firm Altor in 2024, a reminder that the sector is still commercially fragile.
recycled-cotton.fabrics: Because mechanically recycled fibers are short, they are usually blended and rotor spun into coarser yarns for denim, sweatshirts and fleece, T-shirts, socks, towels, blankets and canvas. Recycled cotton is often combined with virgin cotton for fineness or with polyester, frequently recycled polyester, for strength. Studies have demonstrated ring-spun yarns with a quarter or so recycled content for finer knits. Heather and speckled melange effects come naturally from mixed pre-colored inputs. Lower grades go into mop yarns, wiping cloths, industrial felts, insulation batts and upholstery padding, which are common destinations for post-consumer cotton that cannot be respun.
recycled-cotton.quality: Expect recycled cotton fabric to feel slightly drier and hairier than premium virgin cotton, with more surface fuzz and occasional flecks from mixed inputs. Check the full fiber line: a garment described as recycled may contain only a minority share of recycled cotton, blended with virgin cotton or polyester. Pull the fabric gently and look at yarn evenness; very uneven, thin areas or high lint suggest short-fiber-heavy yarn. For denim, a firm, dense twill hides the shorter fibers well. Credible claims name a percentage and reference a chain-of-custody certificate such as the Recycled Claim Standard or Global Recycled Standard with transaction certificates. Because recycled and virgin cotton cannot be told apart by testing, documentation is the only proof.
pros: It reuses cotton already grown, avoiding new irrigation, fertilizer and pesticide inputs for that share.
Pre-colored inputs can skip dyeing and give melange effects.
It performs like cotton in absorbency, breathability and ease of care.
Pre-consumer scrap is a clean, well-characterized feedstock that is otherwise wasted.
cons: Shredding shortens fibers, so yarns are weaker, hairier and usually coarser.
It usually needs blending with virgin cotton or polyester, which dilutes the recycled share and can complicate later recycling.
Post-consumer inputs vary in color, finishes and hidden elastane or polyester.
Claims are hard to verify without certificates, because recycled and virgin cotton look the same in tests.
recycled-cotton.impact: Recycled cotton's benefit comes mainly from displacing virgin cotton farming, so it scales with the recycled share. A 2023 cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment comparing fabrics with 30% mechanically recycled and 70% virgin cotton against 100% virgin cotton found reductions that were real but modest, in the single digits for greenhouse gases in several scenarios; larger savings require higher recycled shares and clean energy. Textile-to-textile recycling is still marginal: Textile Exchange reports that pre- and post-consumer recycled textiles made up less than 1% of the global fiber market. Collection, sorting and transport add impacts, and blending with virgin polyester to restore strength shifts rather than removes the footprint. Evidence is highly dependent on system boundaries and allocation choices.
recycled-cotton.care: Care for recycled cotton as you would cotton, with a little extra gentleness. Wash at 30 to 40 C for everyday items, turning garments inside out to limit surface abrasion and lint; hotter washes up to the label limit suit towels and bedding. Use a normal or color detergent, and avoid chlorine bleach on melange colors. Short fibers make recycled fabrics lint and pill more at first, so wash with similar fabrics and clean the lint filter often. Tumble dry low to medium or line dry to limit shrinkage. Iron pure cotton hot (three dots, about 200 C) while slightly damp, but use two dots if polyester is blended in. Store dry and clean to prevent mildew.
faq: Is recycled cotton as good as new cotton?

It behaves like cotton in comfort and absorbency, but mechanical recycling shortens fibers, so fabrics can be weaker, hairier and coarser. Makers usually blend it with virgin cotton or polyester to compensate. For heavy fabrics such as denim and sweatshirts the difference is small; for fine shirting it is harder to use.
Why is recycled cotton often blended with polyester?

Shredded cotton fibers are short and give weaker yarn, so polyester, often recycled polyester, adds strength and spinning stability. The trade-off is that the resulting blend is harder to recycle again, because separating cotton from polyester requires chemical processes that are not yet widespread.
How can I tell if a recycled cotton claim is real?

Look for a stated percentage and a chain-of-custody certification such as the Recycled Claim Standard or Global Recycled Standard. Laboratory tests cannot distinguish recycled from virgin cotton, so documentation through the supply chain is the only verification. Vague phrases without percentages or certificates deserve skepticism.
Does recycled cotton save water?

It avoids the irrigation used to grow the cotton it replaces, so it can save substantial water per kilogram of fiber. At the garment level, savings depend on how much recycled fiber is used; with about 30% recycled content, one 2023 study found only modest overall reductions.
notable: Textile Exchange estimates that recycled textiles, pre- and post-consumer combined, make up less than 1% of the global fiber market.
Mixed-color cotton scraps can be respun into heathered yarns with no new dyeing at all.
The Swedish cotton-to-pulp recycler Renewcell went bankrupt and was bought by the investment firm Altor, showing how fragile chemical recycling economics still are.

recycled-nylon.types: Recycled nylon differs by input and route. Pre-consumer material includes polymer purge, off-spec chip, yarn waste and fabric offcuts, usually mechanically reprocessed by remelting clean, single-polymer scrap; it is widely used because it is clean and consistent. Post-consumer inputs include fishing nets, carpet fluff and used garments, which need sorting and cleaning. Chemically recycled nylon 6 is depolymerized to caprolactam, purified and repolymerized, so it can match virgin quality; Aquafil's ECONYL is the best-known branded example and, according to the producer, mixes pre- and post-consumer inputs. Nylon 6,6 is harder to depolymerize commercially, so much recycled 6,6 is mechanically recycled. Mass-balance claims allocate recycled input across output rather than tracing each fiber, which should be disclosed.
recycled-nylon.fabrics: Recycled nylon serves the same markets as virgin polyamide. Chemically recycled nylon 6 appears in swimwear and activewear, usually as tricot or circular knits with elastane, and in hosiery, lingerie and fine linings where uniform dyeing matters. Mechanically recycled grades suit heavier textured yarns for bags, outerwear shells, ripstop and webbing. Carpet makers use recycled nylon 6, which also closes a loop because carpet is a major nylon waste stream. Fishing-net-derived yarn is marketed in swimwear and accessories, although nets are only one of several feedstocks. Blends with elastane are common and make the next round of recycling harder.
recycled-nylon.quality: Performance depends on polymer and process, not on the word recycled, so judge the fabric as you would virgin nylon: hand, weave or knit density, opacity and recovery for swimwear, denier and coating for bags. Ask which polymer it is and which route: chemically recycled nylon 6 should match virgin, while mechanically recycled grades can vary in dye uptake and strength. Credible products state the recycled percentage and hold a chain-of-custody certificate, such as the Global Recycled Standard, backed by transaction certificates through each step. Be cautious with vague ocean-plastic language; ask what share is post-consumer and what waste stream it came from. Producer environmental product declarations add useful context.
pros: Chemically recycled nylon 6 can match virgin nylon in strength, recovery and dyeability.
It diverts waste such as production scrap, carpet and fishing nets from landfill or the sea.
Life cycle studies report substantially lower greenhouse emissions than fossil caprolactam for some chemical routes.
It fits existing spinning, knitting and dyeing lines without new equipment.
cons: Garments shed microplastic fibers just as virgin nylon does.
Much recycled nylon comes from pre-consumer scrap, so it does little to reduce post-consumer garment waste.
Mechanically recycled grades can vary in color and strength and may not suit fine yarns.
Elastane blends and coatings make recycled nylon garments hard to recycle again.
recycled-nylon.impact: Recycled nylon's main benefits are avoided virgin monomer production and diversion of waste. For chemical recycling of nylon 6, a 2026 parametric life cycle assessment of real processes found the solvent-free alkaline route cut global warming potential by about 80% relative to fossil caprolactam, though results varied by route and energy supply. Aquafil publishes an environmental product declaration for ECONYL yarn, which is a producer document based on its own data. Mechanical recycling uses less energy but is limited to clean streams. Recycled content does not change use-phase behavior: nylon garments still shed fibers in washing, and a 2023 study found that lowering fiber surface friction cut shedding, showing that fiber design matters. Collection of post-consumer nylon remains limited outside carpets and nets.
recycled-nylon.care: Care is identical to virgin nylon. Wash at about 30 to 40 C with a mild detergent, separate from dark colors because nylon absorbs loose dyes, and use a mesh bag for swimwear and hosiery. Avoid chlorine bleach, which yellows nylon and degrades elastane. Rinse swimsuits in fresh water after use and dry them flat in the shade. Line dry or tumble on low, and iron only on the lowest setting (one dot, about 110 C) through a cloth if at all. Keep garments out of prolonged sunlight, which yellows and weakens polyamide. When the item wears out, check whether the brand or the producer runs a take-back program, since single-polymer nylon items are easier to recycle than blends.
faq: Is ECONYL really made from fishing nets?

Fishing nets are one of its feedstocks, but Aquafil describes ECONYL as regenerated from a mix of pre- and post-consumer nylon waste, including carpet fluff, fabric scraps and industrial plastic as well as nets. The yarn's share of each stream is not usually shown on a garment, so ask the brand for details.
Is recycled nylon as strong as new nylon?

Chemically recycled nylon 6, rebuilt from purified caprolactam, can match virgin nylon in strength and recovery. Mechanically recycled nylon, simply remelted, may lose some molecular weight and vary in color, which is why it is often used in heavier fabrics. The fabric's construction matters more than the recycled label.
Does recycled nylon shed microplastics?

Yes. Once spun, recycled nylon is the same polymer as virgin nylon and sheds fibers in washing and wear. Washing on cool, short, full loads, using a filter or wash bag, and choosing tightly constructed fabrics help reduce shedding.
What certification should recycled nylon have?

Look for the Global Recycled Standard or the Recycled Claim Standard, which track recycled material through the supply chain with transaction certificates. The Global Recycled Standard also adds social, environmental and chemical requirements. A brand name alone does not certify recycled content.
notable: Aquafil publishes an environmental product declaration for ECONYL yarn, giving buyers producer-reported life cycle data for a specific recycled textile yarn.
Carpet is both a major market for nylon 6 and a significant source of post-consumer nylon for chemical recycling.
Under Textile Exchange standards, transaction certificates document each shipment of certified recycled material between certified sites.

tencel.types: TENCEL is a family of product lines, and the generic fiber differs between them. TENCEL Lyocell is solvent-spun staple fiber, the workhorse for denim, shirting and bedding. TENCEL Modal is a viscose-route fiber that Lenzing makes from beech wood, prized for softness in underwear and loungewear. TENCEL Lyocell Filament and the TENCEL LUXE line are continuous lyocell filaments, which Lenzing says are spun with its Eco-Filament technology as a continuous parallel yarn for silk-like wovens. Lines marked TENCEL with REFIBRA technology contain recycled cotton pulp, which Lenzing puts at 30% or more. Carbon-zero TENCEL fibers are, per Lenzing, the same lyocell sold with an added climate claim based on emission reductions and offsetting, not a different polymer.
tencel.fabrics: Lyocell staple appears in denim (often blended with cotton and elastane), twills, chambray shirting, sateen and percale sheets, towels and jersey knits. Modal is spun into fine yarns for underwear, T-shirts, sleepwear and brushed knits, frequently blended with cotton or elastane. Lyocell filament is woven into fluid satins, crepes and linings that compete with silk and cupro. Peached or sanded lyocell twills exploit the fiber's controlled fibrillation for a suede-like face.
tencel.quality: First read the content label: it must say lyocell or modal, and a label that shows only TENCEL is incomplete. Genuine branded fabric can carry a TENCEL hangtag, which fabric mills obtain by applying for a product license through Lenzing's E-Branding Service; the tags are free to licensed customers, so a missing tag is not proof of fakery, but a tag on unlicensed goods is misuse. Lenzing states it has built a physical fiber identification technology into TENCEL lyocell and modal that can confirm origin at fabric and garment level. Good lyocell wovens feel cool, heavy and drapey; look for even color without white, fuzzy abrasion lines at seams and folds, a sign of fibrillation.
pros: Lenzing's lyocell keeps most of its strength when wet, so it tolerates laundering better than standard viscose.
Staple, filament and recycled-content lines let one documented source cover fabrics from denim to silk-like satins.
Licensing and a built-in fiber identification system give brands a route to check authenticity that most commodity cellulosics lack.
Lyocell's closed-loop solvent recovery is well documented in the technical literature, not only in marketing.
cons: The single brand name covers different fibers, so shoppers can buy modal believing it is lyocell.
Lyocell fibrillates under wet abrasion, producing white streaks and a fuzzy surface if washed roughly or finished poorly.
Branded fiber usually costs more than generic lyocell or viscose, and the premium is not always reflected in fabric construction.
Environmental comparisons on TENCEL materials are the producer's own and use Lenzing's chosen baselines.
tencel.impact: Lenzing's claims center on wood from certified forests, NMMO solvent recovery above 99.8%, and lower emissions than generic cellulosics; these are producer figures tied to its own plants and life-cycle boundaries. Independent evidence mostly concerns the end of life. In a 2019 laboratory study at North Carolina State University (Zambrano and colleagues), cellulose-based knit fabrics shed more microfiber mass in accelerated laundering (about 0.2 to 4 mg per g of fabric) than polyester (0.1 to 1 mg per g), but rayon and cotton microfibers degraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester persisted. That supports the general case that regenerated cellulose fragments are less persistent than plastic ones, though dyes, finishes and blends with elastane or polyester complicate both biodegradation and recycling. Plant-level energy and water data should be requested for the specific site.
tencel.care: Treat woven TENCEL lyocell like a delicate cotton: wash at 30 to 40 C on a gentle cycle with a mild liquid detergent, turned inside out, and avoid overloading, because wet abrasion causes fibrillation and white fold marks. Modal knits wash similarly and handle warm washes but pill if tumbled hot and long. Line dry or tumble on low and remove promptly. Iron lyocell at a medium setting (the two-dot range, about 150 C) while slightly damp, on the reverse for dark colors. Store dry, since all cellulose can mildew. Chlorine bleach weakens cellulose and strips reactive dyes. Follow the garment label, which reflects the whole blend and finish.
faq: Is TENCEL the same as lyocell?

Not exactly. TENCEL is Lenzing's trademark and covers both lyocell and modal, plus filament and recycled-content lines. Lyocell is the generic fiber name. The fiber content label, which must list the generic name, tells you which one is in the garment.
Is TENCEL a natural fiber?

No. It is a manufactured regenerated cellulose: wood pulp is dissolved and spun into new fiber. The raw material is plant-based, but the fiber does not exist in nature, and US and EU labeling law treat it as a manufactured fiber with a regulated generic name.
Why does my TENCEL shirt have white streaks?

That is usually fibrillation: wet abrasion splits fine fibrils from the lyocell surface, which scatter light and look pale, especially on dark dyes. Washing inside out, on a gentle cycle with a smaller load, and avoiding hard tumble drying reduces it.
Is TENCEL Modal better than generic modal?

The chemistry is the same fiber class. What the brand adds is Lenzing's sourcing documentation, licensing and fiber identification. Softness and durability depend more on yarn count, knit structure and finishing than on the brand name itself.
notable: Lenzing states that TENCEL lyocell and modal carry a built-in physical identification feature that lets it confirm fiber origin in finished fabric and garments.
TENCEL hangtags are issued free to licensed customers through Lenzing's online E-Branding Service, which ties each tag to a specific licensed fabric.
The TENCEL LUXE line is a continuous lyocell filament, which puts the brand in competition with silk and cupro rather than only with cotton.

ecovero.types: LENZING ECOVERO is sold as viscose staple fiber in the usual textile deniers and cut lengths for ring, open-end and air-jet spinning; the brand is defined by sourcing and process documentation rather than by a new chemistry. The main variants Lenzing promotes are standard ECOVERO viscose, ECOVERO black, a spin-dyed (dope-dyed) fiber in which black pigment is added to the dissolved pulp before extrusion so the color runs through the fiber, and ECOVERO made with REFIBRA technology, which adds recycled cotton pulp to the wood pulp. Lenzing presents ECOVERO as a viscose brand, so the generic name on an ECOVERO label should be viscose (rayon in the US).
ecovero.fabrics: ECOVERO goes wherever ordinary viscose goes: fluid challis and crepe for dresses and blouses, printed rayon wovens, viscose jersey for T-shirts and tops, and blends with cotton, polyester, linen or elastane. Spun viscose yarns made from it are used in knitwear and in soft suiting blends. Spin-dyed ECOVERO black targets knits and wovens where deep, wash-stable black is the selling point. Because the fiber is chemically ordinary viscose, the fabric's hand, drape and shrinkage depend on the mill's yarn and finishing, not on the brand.
ecovero.quality: The label must say viscose or rayon; ECOVERO may appear only in addition. Lenzing states that the fiber carries an identification system that lets it detect ECOVERO in finished products long after spinning and dyeing, so brands can ask for verification. Genuine branded hangtags are issued through Lenzing's E-Branding Service against a licensed fabric. For the fabric itself, look for a dense, even weave that does not slip at the seams, since viscose seams fray easily. Ask whether the fabric was preshrunk; rayon wovens can shrink several percent on first wash. Very low prices for 'ECOVERO' fabric sold by the meter without documentation are a red flag.
pros: It keeps the drape, luster and absorbency that make viscose popular while adding documented sourcing.
Lenzing's built-in fiber identification allows the brand to be checked in finished goods, unlike generic viscose.
Lenzing reports an EU Ecolabel license for the fiber, a third-party scheme with published criteria.
The spin-dyed black variant resists fading because the pigment sits inside the fiber rather than on it.
cons: It is still viscose: weak when wet, prone to shrinkage and creasing, and easily distorted by wringing.
The xanthate route still uses carbon disulfide, so the brand improves rather than removes the chemistry concerns of viscose.
Environmental savings are quoted against a generic viscose baseline chosen by the producer.
The brand gives no information on fabric weight, weave density or finishing, which decide durability.
ecovero.impact: Lenzing's headline claims are that ECOVERO production causes about half the emissions and water impact of generic viscose and that the wood comes from FSC or PEFC certified sources; these are producer comparisons against its own definition of generic viscose. For the spin-dyed black version, trade reporting quotes Lenzing as saying that dyeing in the dope can roughly halve water use and cut the dyeing stage's carbon footprint by about 60% compared with conventional dyeing. Independent evidence at the end of life favors cellulose over plastics: a 2019 study by Zambrano and colleagues found rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester microfibers persisted, although cellulose fabrics shed more microfiber mass in washing. Social and pollution risks in the wider viscose industry (carbon disulfide exposure, effluent) are the reason site-level data matter.
ecovero.care: Wash viscose gently: cold to 30 C, delicate or hand-wash cycle, mild detergent, and a mesh bag for fluid wovens. Do not wring or twist, because wet viscose loses much of its strength; roll in a towel to remove water, then dry flat or on a padded hanger. Tumble drying invites shrinkage and seam distortion. Iron on a medium setting (the two-dot range, about 150 C) on the reverse while slightly damp, or steam, to avoid shine. Store clean and dry to prevent mildew. Dark prints can bleed at first wash, so wash separately. Check the label; many rayon challis garments are safer dry cleaned.
faq: Is ECOVERO better than regular viscose?

It is the same fiber type with different sourcing, process controls and documentation. Performance in wear is essentially that of good viscose. What differs is the producer's reported environmental data, certification and the ability to verify the fiber in finished goods, all of which should be checked for the product.
Does ECOVERO shrink?

It can, like any viscose. Shrinkage depends on how the fabric was woven or knitted and whether it was preshrunk or resin finished. Wash cool, avoid the dryer, and expect some relaxation shrinkage on the first wash of untreated fabric.
Is ECOVERO biodegradable?

Viscose is regenerated cellulose and in laboratory tests rayon microfibers biodegrade in aerobic aquatic conditions. Real garments contain dyes, finishes, threads and often synthetic blend fibers, which change the outcome, so biodegradability claims should be read as applying to the fiber under stated test conditions.
notable: ECOVERO black is colored in the spinning dope, so the black pigment is locked inside each fiber rather than dyed onto the surface afterward.
Lenzing says ECOVERO can be detected in a finished garment by its fiber identification system, which it later extended to TENCEL fibers.

refibra.types: REFIBRA is not sold as a fiber on its own; it is a technology tag applied to other Lenzing fibers. The two product families are TENCEL Lyocell with REFIBRA technology, where Lenzing now describes recycled cotton pulp content of 30% or more, and LENZING ECOVERO viscose made with REFIBRA technology. The recycled share has risen since the 2017 launch (from about 20%) and the input mix has shifted from pre-consumer cutting scraps toward including post-consumer cotton garments. There are no separate grades by strength or denier beyond those of the host fiber, so a buyer specifies the lyocell or viscose type first and the REFIBRA content second.
refibra.fabrics: REFIBRA lyocell appears in the same places as TENCEL lyocell: denim, shirting, knit tops, bedding and towels, often in blends with cotton or recycled cotton. REFIBRA viscose is used in fluid dress fabrics, jersey and printed wovens. Because the recycled content is inside the fiber and the finished fabric is often blended, a garment that says 'made with REFIBRA' may contain a modest overall recycled share. Brands have used it mainly in capsule collections and denim lines that advertise circular content.
refibra.quality: Check that the label gives the generic fiber (lyocell or viscose) and, if a recycled claim is made, a percentage for the whole product. Ask the brand what share of the lyocell or viscose is recycled pulp and what share of the garment that fiber represents; a garment of 30% REFIBRA lyocell with 30% recycled pulp contains only about 9% recycled cotton. Documentation such as transaction certificates under a recycled-content standard and Lenzing's fiber identification can support the claim. Fabric quality is judged exactly as for lyocell or viscose: even surface, low pilling, clean seams.
pros: It returns cotton cutting scraps and some post-consumer cotton to fiber production instead of landfill or incineration.
The finished fiber behaves like standard lyocell or viscose, so mills can use it without changing processes.
It reduces the wood pulp needed per tonne of fiber by the recycled share.
Lenzing's fiber identification allows branded content to be checked in finished goods.
cons: Most of the fiber is still wood pulp, so 'recycled' claims can overstate the circular share.
Recycled share is diluted again when the fiber is blended with other materials in the garment.
Cotton waste with polyester, elastane or heavy finishes is hard to use, which limits the feedstock.
Recycled content cannot be detected chemically; buyers rely on documentation.
refibra.impact: Lenzing presents REFIBRA as reducing virgin wood demand and diverting cotton waste, which follows logically from replacing part of the pulp; the size of any net benefit depends on the energy and chemicals used to purify colored, finished cotton waste, which Lenzing reports in its own life-cycle data. No independent peer-reviewed life-cycle study specific to REFIBRA was found for this entry. General evidence for regenerated cellulose applies: a 2019 NC State study found rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester microfibers persisted. Recycled-content claims in the US fall under the FTC Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260), which expect claims to be qualified and substantiated. Chain-of-custody standards such as Textile Exchange's Content Claim Standard exist to carry such claims through the supply chain.
refibra.care: Care follows the host fiber. For REFIBRA lyocell: wash at 30 to 40 C on a gentle cycle, inside out, with mild detergent, avoid overloading to limit fibrillation, and iron at medium heat (about 150 C) while slightly damp. For REFIBRA viscose: wash cold to 30 C, do not wring, dry flat or hanging, and iron on medium on the reverse. Both are cellulose, so avoid chlorine bleach and store dry to prevent mildew. Recycled content does not change care needs. Where the garment is a blend with elastane or polyester, the most heat-sensitive component and the label set the limits.
faq: Is REFIBRA a fabric?

No. It is Lenzing's name for a technology that puts recycled cotton pulp into its lyocell and viscose fibers. The garment label still has to name the fiber, such as lyocell or viscose, and any recycled claim should state a percentage.
How much recycled content does REFIBRA contain?

Lenzing started at about 20% recycled cotton pulp in 2017 and now describes 30% or more for TENCEL lyocell with REFIBRA, the rest being wood pulp. The share in a finished garment is lower if the fiber is blended with other materials.
Can REFIBRA garments be recycled again?

In principle, cellulose fiber can be pulped again, and the same route that uses cotton waste could use lyocell waste. In practice, blends with polyester or elastane, dyes and finishes make recycling harder, and collection systems for post-consumer textiles are still limited.
notable: A garment with 30% REFIBRA lyocell whose fiber holds 30% recycled pulp contains only about 9% recycled cotton overall.
REFIBRA started with pre-consumer cotton scraps from garment cutting rooms and later added post-consumer cotton textiles.

econyl.types: ECONYL is a regenerated nylon 6 sold in several product forms. The main textile line is nylon textile filament (NTF) yarn, supplied in fine deniers for hosiery, swimwear, activewear and lingerie, with flat and textured variants. A second major line is bulked continuous filament (BCF) yarn for carpets, which Aquafil also makes in its own carpet-yarn business. Aquafil publishes separate Environmental Product Declarations for its textile filament yarns, so specifications and impact figures should be matched to the exact product and EPD version.
econyl.fabrics: Textile ECONYL yarns go into swimwear and bikinis (usually warp-knit with elastane), leggings and sports bras, hosiery, lingerie, lightweight windbreakers, backpacks and bags, and tricot linings. Carpet yarns are tufted into commercial carpet tiles and broadloom. In most apparel, ECONYL nylon is combined with a substantial share of elastane or with other fibers, which affects the recycled share and end-of-life recyclability of the product.
econyl.quality: The content label must say nylon or polyamide; ECONYL appears only alongside it. Ask the brand for the ECONYL share of total fiber content, since swimwear often contains a significant elastane fraction. Aquafil's EPDs and any recycled-content certificate should name the yarn. Physically, good nylon swim fabric feels dense and springy, recovers quickly after stretching and is opaque when stretched; thin fabric that goes see-through or bags out is a construction issue, not a fiber issue. Be skeptical of claims that a product is 'made from fishing nets' without a stated share, as Aquafil uses several waste streams.
pros: Depolymerization to purified caprolactam gives nylon that Aquafil says matches virgin nylon 6 in quality, unlike many mechanically recycled plastics.
It uses post-consumer and post-industrial nylon waste, including carpet fluff and fishing nets, as feedstock.
Aquafil publishes third-party verified EPDs, giving auditable impact data.
The same route can in principle regenerate ECONYL products again at end of life if they are collected and are nylon 6.
cons: It is still a synthetic that sheds microplastic fibers in washing, like virgin nylon.
Most apparel uses blend it with elastane, which makes the finished garment hard to recycle.
Marketing emphasis on ocean fishing nets can overstate that feedstock's share.
Only nylon 6 can be regenerated this way; nylon 6,6 and mixed waste are excluded.
econyl.impact: Aquafil states that ECONYL nylon can reduce the global warming impact of nylon by up to 90% compared with nylon from oil, and that for every 10,000 tonnes of ECONYL raw material about 65,100 tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions are avoided; it attributes part of this to renewable electricity at its plant. These figures come from Aquafil and its EPDs, which are third-party verified within the EPD system but use Aquafil's functional units and baselines. Chemical depolymerization itself needs heat and steam, so gains depend on the energy mix. At the use stage, nylon sheds microfibers in laundering like other synthetics; a 2021 review in Heliyon (Gaylarde and colleagues) summarizes evidence that laundering synthetic textiles is a major source of microfibers. Recycled origin does not change that persistence.
econyl.care: Swimwear and activewear in ECONYL nylon should be rinsed in cool fresh water soon after use to remove chlorine, salt and sunscreen, then hand washed or machine washed cold on a gentle cycle with mild detergent. Avoid fabric softener, which clogs knit structures and holds odor. Do not wring; press out water and dry flat in the shade, since UV degrades both nylon and elastane. Never tumble dry hot or iron swimwear; nylon softens on heating and elastane loses recovery. For other nylon garments, iron only on a low to medium setting. A wash bag reduces snagging and fiber shedding.
faq: Is ECONYL made from ocean plastic?

Partly, sometimes. Aquafil uses several nylon waste streams, including discarded fishing nets, carpet face fiber and industrial scrap. The share of fishing nets varies, so a product claim should state the specific content rather than implying all the nylon came from the sea.
Is ECONYL as strong as regular nylon?

Aquafil says yes, because the waste is broken down to caprolactam, purified and repolymerized into nylon 6, the same polymer as virgin nylon 6. Durability of a garment still depends on yarn denier, knit construction and elastane content.
Does ECONYL shed microplastics?

Yes. Regenerated nylon is chemically nylon 6 and sheds fibers in washing like virgin nylon. Washing cold, using full but not overloaded machines, wash bags or filters, and washing less often reduce release.
notable: Aquafil states that every 10,000 tonnes of ECONYL raw material avoids about 65,100 tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions compared with oil-based caprolactam.
Nylon 6 suits this closed loop because it depolymerizes cleanly back to a single monomer, caprolactam, which can be distilled to high purity.

repreve.types: REPREVE is a platform rather than one fiber. Its core products are recycled polyester filament yarns (flat and textured) and staple fiber, mostly from post-consumer PET bottles, plus REPREVE nylon. Unifi also markets REPREVE Takeback, which uses textile and yarn waste as feedstock, and REPREVE Our Ocean, promoted around plastic recovered before it reaches the sea; buyers should ask for Unifi's collection definition. Unifi states that all REPREVE products can be made with the CiCLO additive, sold as REPREVE with CiCLO technology, which it describes as making the polyester or nylon biodegrade faster in certain environments. Solution-dyed and functional variants exist, and deniers and filament counts follow ordinary polyester specifications.
repreve.fabrics: REPREVE polyester appears in performance tees, fleece, running shorts and leggings, jackets and insulation, socks, and home textiles such as upholstery, bedding and carpets; staple fiber is used in batting and fill. REPREVE nylon targets hosiery, swimwear and activewear. Many products are blends, for example REPREVE polyester with cotton in T-shirts or with spandex in leggings, so the recycled share depends on the blend.
repreve.quality: Look for a REPREVE hangtag or label naming the percentage of REPREVE fiber, and check that the content label states polyester or nylon with a total. Unifi's U-TRUST verification tests fabrics and garments for its FiberPrint tracer, which it says is embedded in every REPREVE strand, so brands can have claims checked at resin, yarn, fabric or garment stage. Recycled PET is chemically identical to virgin PET, so hand and durability depend on yarn and fabric construction: dense knits, even dyeing, and minimal pilling after a test rub indicate a better fabric. 'Contains REPREVE' without a percentage is a weak claim.
pros: It turns post-consumer bottles and some textile waste into fiber that performs like virgin polyester.
The FiberPrint tracer and U-TRUST testing let recycled content be verified physically, which is rare for recycled polyester.
The platform is large, so recycled options exist across many fabric types and price points.
It displaces some virgin PET made from petroleum feedstocks.
cons: Bottle-to-fiber recycling moves PET out of the bottle loop rather than closing a textile loop.
Recycled polyester still sheds persistent microfibers, and one study found more release than from virgin polyester.
Blends with cotton or spandex make the finished garment hard to recycle again.
Biodegradability claims for CiCLO-treated versions rest largely on producer-commissioned testing.
repreve.impact: Unifi reports cumulative figures of more than 46 billion bottles recycled and the equivalent of one billion T-shirts of textile and yarn waste turned into fiber; these are company figures. Mechanically recycled PET generally needs less energy than virgin PET, but most feedstock is bottles, so REPREVE is often described by critics as downcycling out of a food-grade loop. Microfibers are the main independent concern. In a 2024 study in Environmental Pollution (Akyildiz and colleagues), recycled polyester fabric released more microplastic fibers than comparable virgin polyester under the same 40 C washing conditions (about 1,193 versus 908 counted fibers). Claims of biodegradability for CiCLO versions should be read against the FTC Green Guides, which expect degradable claims to be qualified by conditions and timeframe.
repreve.care: Care is that of ordinary polyester or nylon. Wash at 30 to 40 C, inside out, with similar colors; cooler water, full loads and a wash bag or filter reduce microfiber release. Skip fabric softener on performance knits, as it blocks wicking and traps odor. Tumble dry low or line dry; high heat can glaze or distort thermoplastic fibers and damage any spandex. Iron polyester on a low to medium setting (about 110 to 150 C), never directly on printed or coated areas. Oil-based stains bind to polyester, so pretreat promptly with detergent. Pilling in staple fabrics can be removed with a fabric shaver.
faq: What is REPREVE made from?

Mostly post-consumer plastic bottles, which are washed, flaked and melted into recycled polyester. Unifi also makes REPREVE nylon and lines that use textile and yarn waste. The label must still say polyester or nylon, and the REPREVE percentage should be stated.
How can I tell if a product really contains REPREVE?

Unifi puts a proprietary tracer, FiberPrint, into REPREVE fiber and offers U-TRUST testing to detect it in fabrics and finished goods. As a shopper you rely on the brand's hangtag and claims; brands can ask Unifi for verification.
Is recycled polyester better for the ocean?

Not at the washing stage. Recycled polyester is chemically PET and sheds persistent microfibers like virgin polyester; one 2024 study found higher release from a recycled fabric. Its benefits lie in feedstock and energy, not in end-of-life behavior.
notable: Every REPREVE fiber is embedded with a proprietary tracer called FiberPrint, which Unifi uses to test products for genuine content.
Unifi reports having recycled more than 46 billion plastic bottles into REPREVE fiber.
