seaqual.types: The SEAQUAL INITIATIVE sells several related materials. SEAQUAL MARINE PLASTIC is the traceable raw material, made from litter collected from oceans, rivers and beaches. SEAQUAL YARN is recycled polyester filament that the initiative describes as 100% post-consumer recycled PET, of which 10% is SEAQUAL MARINE PLASTIC and 90% is land-sourced recycled PET such as bottles. SEAQUAL FIBER is the staple-fiber counterpart for spun yarns, nonwovens and fill. Licensed partners also make fabrics and finished products under the program. The practical differences between forms are filament versus staple and the documented marine share, not the polymer, which is ordinary PET.
seaqual.fabrics: According to the initiative's brand listings, SEAQUAL materials are used across apparel, footwear, accessories and home textiles, with swimwear, sportswear and casual knits prominent. Staple fiber suits spun yarns, fill and nonwovens. Filament yarns are knitted into jersey and tricot or woven into light shell fabrics. As with other recycled polyester, much of the finished product may be blended with elastane, cotton or virgin fibers, which lowers the program content of the item.
seaqual.quality: Check the product label for polyester and for a stated percentage of SEAQUAL content; the program is a licensing community, so licensed companies are listed on the initiative's website and can be looked up. The initiative states that its yarn contains a tracer that links material to collection projects, so a brand can ask for verification. Remember the arithmetic: a garment that is 50% SEAQUAL YARN contains about 5% marine plastic. Fabric quality is judged as for any polyester: dense construction, good recovery, even dyeing and low pilling. 'Ocean plastic' wording without percentages is a red flag.
pros: It creates a paid outlet for marine litter that fishing crews and clean-ups bring ashore, supporting collection.
The yarn is 100% post-consumer recycled PET, so it avoids virgin polymer entirely, according to the initiative.
A tracer and a public licensee list make claims easier to check than generic 'ocean plastic' marketing.
Performance is that of standard polyester, so it fits existing fabric specifications.
cons: Only about 10% of the yarn is marine plastic; most is bottle-derived PET like other recycled polyester.
It sheds persistent microplastic fibers when washed, which is the opposite of an ocean benefit at the use stage.
Blended garments are difficult to recycle again.
The initiative's life-cycle savings are self-reported comparisons with virgin PET.
seaqual.impact: The initiative reports that producing SEAQUAL YARN cuts CO2 emissions by about 37%, water use by about 34% and electricity by about 40% compared with virgin PET; these are producer figures whose study year and functional unit should be requested. The marine share is small, so the environmental case rests mainly on recycled PET in general plus the social value of funded litter collection. Independent research raises a use-phase issue: a 2024 study in Environmental Pollution (Akyildiz and colleagues) found that a recycled polyester fabric released more microplastic fibers than virgin polyester under identical 40 C washing (about 1,193 versus 908 counted fibers). Any 'ocean' claim should therefore be read alongside the product's own microfiber shedding.
seaqual.care: Treat SEAQUAL products as polyester. Wash at 30 C where possible, inside out, with similar colors, in a full but not packed machine; a microfiber-catching bag or filter reduces shedding. Use liquid detergent and skip fabric softener on performance knits. Line dry or tumble on low heat, because polyester is thermoplastic and elastane blends degrade with heat. Iron on a low to medium setting (about 110 to 150 C) if needed, avoiding prints. Pretreat oily stains quickly, since polyester holds oils. Remove pills with a fabric shaver rather than pulling them. Store away from direct sunlight to limit fading.
faq: Is SEAQUAL made from ocean plastic?

Partly. The initiative says SEAQUAL YARN is 100% post-consumer recycled polyester, of which about 10% is marine plastic and about 90% is other post-consumer PET such as bottles. A garment made partly of the yarn contains less still.
How do I know a SEAQUAL product is genuine?

Look for stated SEAQUAL content on the tag and check that the brand appears among the initiative's licensees. The initiative also says its yarn carries a tracer that links it to collection projects, which brands can use for verification.
Does buying SEAQUAL clean the ocean?

It helps fund and use litter brought ashore by fishing crews and clean-up projects, but the quantity per garment is small and the product still sheds microfibers when washed. It is a recycling and collection program, not an ocean remediation technology.
notable: SEAQUAL licensing is tiered, with licensees able to choose a license fee from zero up to 1,000 euros, according to the initiative's licensee portal.
A garment that is half SEAQUAL YARN contains only about 5% marine-derived plastic, because the yarn itself is about one tenth marine plastic.

spinnova.types: SPINNOVA is one fiber technology rather than a range of numbered grades. The standard product is a staple fiber made from wood pulp, and the producer has reported separate life-cycle results for fiber made from eucalyptus pulp. Spinnova also states that the same mechanical route can use waste streams, including leather, textile and agricultural residues, which would produce variants with different feedstock histories. Beyond apparel, the material has been tested in composites: a Finnish ski maker has published trials using SPINNOVA material in place of fiberglass. Because output volumes remain small and the Woodspin factory joint venture was put on hold, commercial availability should be checked before specifying it.
spinnova.fabrics: SPINNOVA fiber is blended with other fibers and spun into yarns for knitwear, T-shirts and other casual apparel shown in brand collaborations and limited collections. It is supplied as staple fiber for conventional spinning, usually as a blend component rather than as 100% SPINNOVA yarn. Composite applications, such as ski constructions, use the fiber as reinforcement in a resin matrix. Most consumer items have been capsule or collaboration products, so the blend ratio on the label is essential.
spinnova.quality: Because SPINNOVA is normally a minority blend component, read the content label for its percentage, and note that no generic fiber name for it has been publicly confirmed, so labels may vary. Ask the brand which regulatory fiber name was used and on what basis. Performance claims should be backed by test reports for the actual yarn: tensile strength, abrasion (Martindale or similar), pilling and wash durability. Ask specifically for wet strength, since the fiber is held together by hydrogen bonds that water can loosen. Expect a premium price and small runs; mass-market pricing with 'SPINNOVA' claims warrants a documentation request.
pros: Spinnova states the process uses no dissolving chemicals, forming fiber mechanically from microfibrillated cellulose.
The producer reports large reductions in water use and emissions compared with cotton in its own assessments.
The fiber keeps native cellulose I structure, a different route from viscose, lyocell or cupro.
Its feedstock range can in principle extend to waste streams, according to the company.
cons: Commercial scale is unproven; the Woodspin factory joint venture was halted in 2025.
Independent test data on strength, wet performance and durability are scarce.
It is almost always blended, so the environmental benefit per garment is diluted.
Regulatory labeling of this new fiber type is unsettled, which can confuse content labels.
spinnova.impact: Spinnova's own life-cycle statements compare its fiber with cotton: the company has said its wood-pulp fiber has about a 65% lower carbon footprint and uses about 99% less water than cotton, and a later figure for eucalyptus-pulp fiber put greenhouse gas emissions about 74% below the global average for conventional cotton. Reported percentages vary with the cotton baseline chosen (irrigated versus global average) and the pulp source, so they should not be compared across studies without checking the functional unit, usually one tonne of fiber. No independent peer-reviewed life-cycle assessment was found for this entry. Impacts of pulp production, including forestry and energy, sit upstream and depend on the pulp supplier. End-of-life behavior should resemble other cellulose, but blends with polyester change that.
spinnova.care: Care is governed by the blend partner and the garment label. For cotton or lyocell blends, wash at 30 to 40 C on a gentle cycle with mild detergent, inside out, and avoid long, hot tumble drying. Because independent data on wet strength are limited, do not wring and avoid harsh mechanical washing; dry flat or on a hanger. Iron on a medium setting only if the label permits. Avoid chlorine bleach, which attacks cellulose. Store dry to prevent mildew, as with any cellulose fiber. If the garment includes recycled polyester, follow the lower heat limits for that component.
faq: What is SPINNOVA made of?

Cellulose, mostly from wood pulp. The pulp is mechanically refined into a paste of fine fibrils, which a nozzle aligns into a fiber that dries without a chemical coagulation bath, according to the company. It is not paper and not viscose.
Is SPINNOVA better for the environment than cotton?

The company reports much lower water use and emissions than cotton, around 99% less water and 65 to 74% lower emissions depending on the study and baseline. These are producer assessments; independent comparisons are not yet available, and garment-level benefit depends on blend share.
Can I buy SPINNOVA clothing?

Mostly through limited collaborations and capsule collections. Spinnova's planned large-scale factory joint venture was put on hold in 2025, so supply is small and availability varies. Check the content label for the percentage used.
notable: Spinnova fibers keep the native cellulose I crystal form because the cellulose is never dissolved, unlike viscose, lyocell and cupro.
A Finnish ski maker has published trials using SPINNOVA material as a reinforcement in place of fiberglass in ski composites.

infinna.types: Infinna is marketed as a single staple fiber made from recycled textile waste by the cellulose carbamate route, rather than as a family of grades. The producer presents it as a cotton-like fiber for spinning in blends or alone. What varies between batches is the feedstock history (mostly cotton-rich post-consumer textiles) and the cut length and fineness chosen for a spinning system; these should be confirmed with the company for any order. Treat Infinna as a pre-commercial material until the Kemi factory is built.
infinna.fabrics: Infinna is intended for cotton-like apparel uses, where it can be spun alone or blended with cotton, lyocell or other fibers. Because the fiber is regenerated cellulose, it spins on standard staple systems and dyes with cellulose dye classes, so mills can treat it much like viscose or lyocell staple. Volumes so far have come from pilot output, so finished products have been small collections rather than mainstream lines, and the percentage of Infinna in each item should be read from the label.
infinna.quality: Expect small volumes and premium pricing, because commercial production awaits the Kemi factory investment decision. The content label should list a generic fiber name; since the regulatory name for a carbamate fiber could not be confirmed for this atlas, ask the brand which name it used and why. Recycled-content claims should come with documentation such as transaction certificates under a recycled-content chain-of-custody standard. Ask for test data on tensile strength, pilling and colorfastness for the actual fabric. Judge the fabric as you would a viscose or lyocell blend: even surface, stable dimensions after washing, and clean seams.
pros: It uses post-consumer textile waste, a feedstock that mostly goes to landfill or incineration today.
The carbamate route avoids carbon disulfide, the most criticized chemical of the viscose process.
The fiber is regenerated cellulose, so its microfibers are expected to biodegrade more readily than polyester fibers.
The process is designed to separate out polyester and elastane, which are common contaminants in textile waste.
cons: Commercial-scale supply does not yet exist; the first factory has a permit but no final investment decision as of March 2026.
Independent performance and life-cycle data are limited.
Pricing and availability are uncertain for designers and buyers.
The correct generic fiber name for labeling is not settled in public guidance.
infinna.impact: Infinited Fiber's case rests on replacing virgin cotton or wood pulp with textile waste, and on a chemistry based on urea and alkali rather than carbon disulfide; the company's life-cycle figures are producer claims and no independent peer-reviewed assessment specific to Infinna was found for this entry. The environmental balance will depend on the energy source at Kemi, the yield from mixed textile waste, and what happens to the separated polyester and other residues. General evidence favors cellulose over plastic at end of life: in a 2019 study (Zambrano and colleagues), rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester microfibers persisted. Recycled-content marketing in the US is subject to the FTC Green Guides, which expect claims to be specific and substantiated.
infinna.care: Care is expected to follow viscose-type regenerated cellulose and the blend partner. Wash cool (30 C) on a gentle cycle with mild detergent, turn garments inside out, and avoid wringing, since regenerated cellulose is typically weaker wet than dry. Dry flat or on a hanger, or tumble on low only if the label allows. Iron on a medium setting (about 150 C) while slightly damp. Avoid chlorine bleach and store dry to prevent mildew. For denim blends, wash sparingly and inside out to limit abrasion and fading. The garment label takes precedence, since independent care testing is limited.
faq: What is Infinna made from?

Cotton-rich textile waste, mainly discarded clothing. The cellulose is recovered, reacted with urea to form cellulose carbamate, dissolved in alkali and spun into new fiber, according to Infinited Fiber Company.
Is Infinna the same as viscose?

It is also regenerated cellulose, but it is not made by the viscose process, which uses carbon disulfide. The carbamate route is different chemistry. The name used on a US or EU content label should be confirmed with the brand.
Can I buy Infinna clothes now?

Only in small quantities from pilot production. The company's planned Kemi factory of about 30,000 tonnes per year had an environmental permit but no final investment decision as of March 2026, so availability is limited.
notable: Infinna's chemistry swaps the carbon disulfide of viscose for urea, forming cellulose carbamate that dissolves in dilute alkali.
The planned Kemi factory would reuse the site of a closed paper mill in Finnish Lapland.

circulose.types: CIRCULOSE itself is a dissolving pulp in sheet form, made from cotton-rich textile waste; it becomes a fiber only in a partner's viscose or lyocell plant. Fiber products made with it have been sold as CIRCULOSE viscose with about 30% or 50% recycled pulp content and CIRCULOSE lyocell with about 30%, the remainder being wood pulp, according to the producer. In 2025 Circulose announced a partnership with Jilin Chemical Fiber for viscose filament yarn and, later, a partner-only supply model in which pulp goes to brands with direct partnerships. Specifications such as viscosity and alpha-cellulose content matter to fiber makers; for shoppers the key figure is the recycled share.
circulose.fabrics: Fibers containing CIRCULOSE pulp go into the usual viscose and lyocell products, such as dresses, blouses, knit tops and denim blends, and the Jilin partnership targets viscose filament yarn for smooth wovens. The producer reports that more than 250 styles have been made with brands including H&M, Levi's, Tommy Hilfiger, COS, Zara and Calvin Klein, and has since announced partnerships with EILEEN FISHER, Marimekko, Samsoe Samsoe and King Louie. Because the pulp is mixed with wood pulp and the resulting fiber is often blended with cotton or elastane, garments usually contain a minority of recycled cellulose.
circulose.quality: The garment label will list viscose, lyocell or rayon, never CIRCULOSE as a fiber. Ask the brand for two numbers: the recycled pulp share in the fiber and the fiber's share in the garment. Circulose announced in 2025 that it would trace material from pulp to finished apparel through TextileGenesis, a digital system that issues a token for each kilogram of pulp to prevent double counting, so brands can request that record. Fabric quality follows the fiber type: viscose from recycled pulp should be judged like any viscose for drape, seam strength and shrinkage.
pros: It makes dissolving pulp from discarded cotton garments, not only from production scraps.
Downstream fiber makers can use it in existing viscose and lyocell lines without new equipment.
Digital traceability through a token system is designed to stop the same recycled pulp being claimed twice.
It reduces the wood pulp needed for the share it replaces.
cons: The original company, Renewcell, went bankrupt in 2024, and supply has depended on restarting the plant.
Recycled share in fibers is typically 30 to 50%, and lower again in blended garments.
A partner-only model limits who can buy it and how widely it is available.
Independent life-cycle data are limited; most figures come from the producer.
circulose.impact: Circulose presents its pulp as replacing wood pulp and diverting cotton waste; the balance depends on energy use, bleaching chemistry and yields at Ortviken, and on the viscose or lyocell plant that later dissolves the pulp. The fiber stage carries the usual impacts of viscose, including carbon disulfide handling, or of lyocell. No independent peer-reviewed life-cycle study specific to CIRCULOSE was found for this entry. At end of life, regenerated cellulose behaves better than polyester in one respect: a 2019 study (Zambrano and colleagues) found rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester microfibers persisted. The commercial history matters to impact too: a plant that sits idle for lack of orders diverts no waste.
circulose.care: Care follows the fiber made from the pulp. For viscose garments: wash cold to 30 C on a delicate cycle, do not wring, dry flat or hanging, and iron on medium (about 150 C) on the reverse while slightly damp. For lyocell: wash at 30 to 40 C, gentle cycle, inside out, avoid overloading to limit fibrillation. Avoid chlorine bleach with both. Store dry to prevent mildew. Recycled pulp does not change care needs. When the garment is a blend with elastane or polyester, use the most heat-sensitive fiber's limits and follow the care label.
faq: Is CIRCULOSE a fabric?
No. It is a recycled dissolving pulp that fiber producers turn into viscose or lyocell. The garment label will show that generic fiber, and the brand may add that it contains CIRCULOSE pulp.
How much recycled material is in CIRCULOSE garments?

Fibers made with it have typically contained about 30% or 50% recycled pulp, with wood pulp making up the rest. If the garment also includes cotton or elastane, the overall recycled share is lower. Ask the brand for the exact figure.
What happened to Renewcell?

Renewcell, which developed CIRCULOSE, was declared bankrupt in February 2024. The investment firm Altor bought the business and plant later that year and renamed it Circulose, which announced plans to restart production in the fourth quarter of 2026.
notable: Circulose's traceability partner issues a digital token for every kilogram of pulp to record each processing step and prevent double counting.
The producer reports that more than 250 garment styles have been made with CIRCULOSE across well-known fashion brands.

naia.types: Naia comes in three main forms. Naia filament yarn, the original 2017 product, is continuous cellulose acetate for wovens and knits with a silk-like luster. Naia staple fiber, which Eastman showed at Premiere Vision in 2020, is cut fiber for blending with other fibers in spun yarns, mainly for knitwear. Naia Renew, available as filament and staple, is described by Eastman as 60% wood pulp and 40% certified recycled waste plastics, with the recycled content allocated by an ISCC-certified mass balance method; Naia Renew ES is a version Eastman says carries increased recycled content. Within each form, deniers, filament counts and luster levels distinguish specific yarns.
naia.fabrics: Naia filament is used in satins, crepes, charmeuse-like wovens, jacquards and linings, in blouses, dresses and eveningwear, and in fluid knits. Staple Naia blends appear in sweaters, cardigans and T-shirt knits, where Eastman highlights softness and reduced pilling. Acetate's classic role as a lining persists alongside cupro and viscose. Eastman announced H&M as the first brand to adopt Naia Renew, in a Conscious Exclusive collection. Because acetate is thermoplastic, it is also used where heat-set pleats or moire effects are wanted.
naia.quality: The label must say acetate, not Naia alone and not 'silk'. For filament wovens, look for a dense, smooth weave with no seam slippage and even luster; acetate satins with loose weaves slip at seams under stress. Test a hidden spot before using nail polish remover or perfume nearby: acetone dissolves acetate, and a genuine acetate fabric is marked by it. For Naia Renew, ask how the 40% recycled content is allocated: under mass balance, the recycled molecules are credited on paper across production, not physically traceable in each fiber. Eastman lists ISCC and GRS-related certifications; confirm the certificate covers the product.
pros: Acetate filament gives a silk-like luster and drape at a lower price than silk.
It dries faster and wrinkles less than viscose because acetylation reduces water uptake.
Eastman reports TUV AUSTRIA 'OK biodegradable' marks for soil and freshwater and 'OK compost' for industrial composting.
Naia Renew uses recycled waste plastics as a feedstock for acetyl chemicals, according to Eastman.
cons: Acetone, some nail polish removers and some solvents dissolve or mark acetate.
It is weaker than viscose or polyester and loses strength when wet, so it abrades and tears more easily.
Heat can glaze or melt it, making ironing risky.
Mass balance allocation means recycled content in Naia Renew is an accounting credit rather than a measurable share of each fiber.
naia.impact: Eastman's claims are that Naia production recovers its solvents in a closed loop, and that Naia Renew has a lower carbon footprint than standard Naia; it also cites a study with the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution showing Naia disintegrating and biodegrading in the ocean within months. Independent evidence adds context. In a 2019 washing study (Yang and colleagues, Environmental Pollution), acetate fabric released the most microfibers of the three fabrics tested, up to about 74,800 per square meter per wash. A 2023 study (Tan and colleagues) found cellulose acetate tow and film lost under 3% of weight after 16 weeks in river water or seawater, showing that degradation depends strongly on degree of substitution, form and microbial conditions. Biodegradability claims should therefore be read against their stated test conditions.
naia.care: Hand wash in cool water or use a delicate cycle at 30 C in a mesh bag, with mild detergent; many acetate garments are labeled dry clean only, and linings in tailored garments should be dry cleaned with the outer fabric. Never wring or twist. Roll in a towel and hang or dry flat, away from heat; do not tumble dry. Iron at the lowest setting (the one-dot range, about 110 C) on the reverse with a press cloth, because acetate glazes and can melt. Keep acetone, nail polish remover and some perfumes and alcohol-based sprays away. Store on padded hangers to avoid shoulder marks.
faq: Is Naia natural or synthetic?

Neither exactly. It is made from wood pulp cellulose that is chemically modified with acetyl groups, so it is a manufactured cellulose ester. Labels call it acetate. It behaves partly like a cellulose and partly like a thermoplastic.
Is Naia the same as silk?

No. Acetate imitates silk's luster and drape, but it is a wood-derived manufactured fiber. It is weaker than silk, especially when wet, and is damaged by acetone and high heat. Content labels must say acetate.
Is Naia biodegradable?

Eastman reports certifications for biodegradation in soil and freshwater and composting in industrial facilities, plus a marine study. Independent research shows acetate degradation varies strongly with conditions, and garments with dyes, blends or threads may behave differently, so check the stated test conditions.
What does 'mass balance' mean for Naia Renew?

Eastman feeds recycled plastic into its chemical production and allocates the recycled share to certain products through ISCC-certified bookkeeping. The recycled content is real at site level but cannot be measured in any individual fiber.
notable: A drop of acetone on a hidden seam allowance is a classic home test: acetate softens or dissolves while viscose, cotton and silk do not.
Eastman cites a Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution study in which Naia disintegrated and biodegraded in seawater within months.

sorona.types: Sorona is sold as PTT polymer to licensed fiber makers, who turn it into several product forms. Continuous filament yarns, flat or textured, go into apparel fabrics; bicomponent filaments can pair PTT with another polyester so the two shrink differently and the yarn coils, giving mechanical stretch without elastane. Staple fiber is used in spun yarns, fill and insulation. Bulked continuous filament goes into carpets, which in the US may be labeled triexta. Covation also markets Sorona for faux fur. Its Common Thread program certifies fabrics from partner mills, and it has introduced apparel sub-brands for specific performance claims.
sorona.fabrics: In apparel, Sorona appears in stretch wovens for trousers and outerwear, suiting and shirting that aims for wrinkle recovery, activewear knits, swimwear, and faux fur and fleece piles. Staple and fill versions are used in insulated jackets and bedding. In home furnishings, PTT carpet fiber is valued for resilience and stain resistance. Sorona is often blended with cotton, wool, nylon, polyester or spandex, so the stretch and hand of a fabric depend on the blend and construction.
sorona.quality: US labels may say polyester or triexta; EU labels say polyester. Look for the Common Thread certification on fabrics from partner mills, which Covation uses to identify certified fabrics made with its polymer, and for the stated Sorona percentage. In stretch wovens, pull the fabric widthwise and watch recovery: a good bicomponent Sorona fabric should snap back without bagging. Because PTT melts at a lower temperature than PET, poor finishing can leave a harsh or shiny surface; inspect for glazing. Claims that Sorona is 'plant-based' should say 37% bio-based by weight.
pros: About 37% of the polymer by weight comes from corn-derived 1,3-propanediol, according to the producer.
PTT's spring-like chain gives stretch and recovery, allowing some stretch fabrics without elastane.
It dyes at lower temperatures than PET, which can save energy in dyehouses.
Carpet fibers show good resilience and stain resistance.
cons: About 63% of the polymer is still petroleum-derived terephthalic acid.
It is not biodegradable and sheds microfibers like other polyesters.
Its lower melting point means less tolerance of hot irons than PET.
Mechanical stretch from bicomponent yarns is usually lower than from elastane blends.
sorona.impact: Sorona's brand materials state that producing the polymer uses about 30% less energy and releases about 63% fewer greenhouse gas emissions than producing nylon 6, per unit of polymer; the comparison is the producer's own and uses nylon 6 rather than PET as the baseline. The bio-based share depends on corn grown for fermentation, bringing agricultural land use, fertilizer and pesticides into the footprint, which the headline figures do not describe. No independent peer-reviewed life-cycle study of Sorona fiber was found for this entry. At the use stage, PTT is a polyester and, like PET, releases persistent microfibers in laundering; a 2021 review in Heliyon (Gaylarde and colleagues) summarizes evidence that synthetic textile laundering is a major microfiber source. PTT carpet and apparel waste is rarely recycled at present.
sorona.care: Wash at 30 to 40 C with like colors; Sorona blends generally tolerate machine washing, but follow the label for wool or elastane components. Skip high dryer heat: tumble low or line dry, since PTT softens at lower temperatures than standard polyester. Iron at a low to medium setting (about 110 to 150 C) with a press cloth on the reverse; excess heat can flatten texture or glaze the surface. Faux fur in Sorona should be shaken out, brushed gently when dry, and never ironed. Pretreat oily stains promptly. Carpets in PTT fiber resist many water-based stains but should be blotted quickly.
faq: Is Sorona spandex?

No. Sorona is a polyester, poly(trimethylene terephthalate), partly made from corn-derived 1,3-propanediol. Its molecular shape gives stretch and recovery, and bicomponent yarns coil like springs, but it is not a polyurethane elastomer.
Is Sorona plant-based?

Partly. The producer states that 37% of the polymer by weight comes from renewable plant sugars; the rest is petroleum-derived terephthalic acid. It is not biodegradable and behaves like other polyesters at end of life.
What does triexta mean on a label?

Triexta is a US generic name the FTC adopted in 2009 for a polyester subclass based on 1,3-propanediol, which covers PTT such as Sorona. It appears mostly on carpets. Polyester is also an allowed name.
notable: Sorona's producer compares it against nylon 6, not PET, when claiming about 30% less energy and 63% fewer greenhouse gas emissions.
Bicomponent Sorona yarns get their stretch from two polymers that shrink differently, which makes the filament curl like a coil spring.

bemberg.types: Bemberg is made as continuous filament cupro yarn, available in a range of deniers and lusters, and sold to weavers and knitters rather than to consumers. Its traditional product is lining yarn, woven into taffeta, twill and satin linings for tailored jackets and coats. Asahi Kasei has been extending the brand into outer apparel fabrics, with knitted and woven Bemberg fabrics using new finishing, knitting and weaving methods. The same cuprammonium chemistry also produces Bemliese, a cupro nonwoven sold under its own name. Asahi Kasei states that Bemberg uses 100% cotton linter, a pre-consumer by-product of cottonseed oil production, and holds Global Recycled Standard certification on that basis.
bemberg.fabrics: Bemberg's best-known role is as suit, coat and jacket lining, where its smooth filaments slide over shirts and knitwear and its moisture uptake reduces static and clamminess compared with polyester linings. It is also woven into satins, georgettes and twills for blouses, dresses and trousers, and knitted into jersey for tops, underwear and sleepwear. Blends with polyester, wool, silk or elastane appear in fashion fabrics. Retailers often use 'Bemberg lining' as a quality cue in tailoring.
bemberg.quality: The label should say cupro (EU) or rayon (US) with Bemberg as a trademark; beware 'Bemberg' used as a generic word for any smooth lining. A good cupro lining feels cool, dry and slippery, with a soft sheen rather than the hard glint of polyester, and does not crackle with static. Check that lining seams are generously allowed and pleated at the back, because cupro is weaker than polyester and tears under strain. In fashion fabrics, even luster and no seam slippage are the key signs. Burn and microscopy tests can distinguish cupro from polyester but not the Bemberg brand from other cupro.
pros: Smooth, round filaments make it one of the most comfortable lining yarns, breathable and low in static.
Asahi Kasei states that its feedstock is 100% pre-consumer cotton linter, certified under the Global Recycled Standard.
The producer reports biodegradability and compostability, including certification for marine biodegradation of the filament.
Asahi Kasei describes a closed-loop system that recovers and reuses copper and ammonia.
cons: Cupro is much weaker when wet, so it can shrink, distort or tear with rough washing.
It water-spots and shows creases more readily than polyester.
Linings usually cost more than polyester alternatives.
Supply depends largely on a single producer, which concentrates risk.
bemberg.impact: Asahi Kasei's claims center on its feedstock and process: cotton linter, a by-product of cottonseed oil milling, is used instead of wood pulp, and copper and ammonia are recovered and reused in a closed loop. The company reports Global Recycled Standard certification and biodegradability certifications, including marine biodegradation for the filament. Plant-level data on energy, water and copper discharge should be requested from the producer, since public independent audits were not found for this entry. As regenerated cellulose, cupro's shed fibers are expected to behave like other cellulose; a 2019 study (Zambrano and colleagues) found rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester persisted. Replacing a polyester lining with cupro therefore removes one persistent microfiber source from a garment, though the effect has not been measured specifically.
bemberg.care: Most garments lined with Bemberg should be dry cleaned as a whole, because the lining and shell may shrink differently. Washable cupro garments should be hand washed or machine washed cold on a delicate cycle in a mesh bag, with mild detergent. Never wring; roll in a towel and hang to dry away from direct heat. Water drops can leave marks on cupro satins, so steam or press evenly rather than spot-dampening. Iron on a medium-low setting on the reverse with a press cloth. Store on padded hangers, clean and dry. Avoid chlorine bleach, which damages cellulose.
faq: What is Bemberg lining?

It is a lining woven from Bemberg, Asahi Kasei's brand of cupro, a regenerated cellulose made from cotton linter. It is smoother and more breathable than polyester lining and reduces static, which is why it is used in higher-end tailoring.
Is Bemberg the same as silk?

No. Cupro is regenerated cellulose, not a protein fiber. It shares silk's smooth, fine filaments and sheen, and is sometimes called 'vegan silk' in marketing, but it behaves like a cellulose: absorbent, weaker when wet, and prone to water spots.
Can I wash a Bemberg-lined jacket?

Usually not. Linings and shell fabrics can shrink at different rates, which distorts tailored garments. Follow the label; most jackets and coats with cupro linings are labeled dry clean. Unlined cupro garments may be washable by hand.
notable: Asahi Kasei says Bemberg's raw material is 100% cotton linter, the short fuzz left on cottonseed after ginning, which it classes as pre-consumer recycled material.
The same cuprammonium process that makes Bemberg yarn also makes Bemliese, a cupro nonwoven.

lycra.types: The LYCRA name covers two chemically different fiber families. LYCRA fiber proper is spandex (elastane), a segmented polyurethane supplied in many deniers for hosiery, swimwear, shapewear and blends. LYCRA XTRA LIFE fiber, marketed under the lastingFIT technology name, is a modified spandex that the company says resists fiber damage from external agents that wear out ordinary spandex; the same technology label can also use LYCRA T400 fiber. LYCRA T400 is not spandex at all but a bicomponent polyester, which the company labels elasterell-p (a US polyester subclass) or elastomultiester in the EU; LYCRA T400 EcoMade contains more than 65% recycled and plant-based content, per the company. LYCRA FiT400 targets knitwear.
lycra.fabrics: Spandex is almost never used alone: it is core-spun with cotton or wool, covered with nylon or polyester, air-entangled, or knitted bare alongside other yarns. Typical products are jeans and stretch chinos (a few percent spandex), T-shirts and knit tops, leggings and sports bras (with much higher spandex shares), swimwear, hosiery, bras and shapewear. T400 appears in stretch wovens, denim and trousers where moderate, comfortable stretch and wrinkle recovery are wanted without elastane's sensitivity to heat. The same company's portfolio also includes COOLMAX and THERMOLITE performance brands.
lycra.quality: The content label must show spandex or elastane for LYCRA fiber, and polyester (or elasterell-p or elastomultiester) for T400; a label saying only 'LYCRA' is incomplete. Genuine branded fabric carries a LYCRA hangtag: the company offers free printed or virtual hangtags for fabrics that pass its certification, which checks that they contain genuine LYCRA technologies and meet its performance standards. In the fabric, stretch it and watch recovery: good spandex fabrics snap back fully, while grinning (the spandex showing through when stretched) or bagging at knees and seat signals low content or poor construction. 'Lycra' as a common noun in listings does not mean branded fiber.
pros: Small percentages of spandex add stretch, fit and shape retention that no rigid fiber can match.
The company offers grade-specific options, such as durability-focused XTRA LIFE and polyester-based T400, for different use conditions.
Free, certification-backed hangtags give shoppers a way to identify genuine branded fabric.
T400 EcoMade offers a stretch option with more than 65% recycled and plant-based content, according to the producer.
cons: Spandex degrades with chlorine, heat, UV and body oils, which eventually causes baggy, stringy fabric.
Even a few percent of elastane makes garments much harder to recycle.
The brand name is often used loosely for any stretch fiber, confusing buyers.
The company's ownership has changed repeatedly, most recently through a 2026 Chapter 11 reorganization.
lycra.impact: Spandex production uses diisocyanates and, in the dry-spinning route, polar solvents such as dimethylacetamide that must be recovered; detailed, audited plant-level data for LYCRA grades were not found for this entry, and the company's EcoMade recycled and bio-derived claims are producer statements. The best-documented independent concern is end of life. Elastane is present in a large share of apparel at low percentages, and a 2026 review in Polymers (Plavec and colleagues) notes that post-consumer textiles containing elastane, dyes and finishes make selective recycling considerably more difficult, because the polyurethane responds differently from cotton or polyester to separation chemistry. Durability-focused grades such as XTRA LIFE can reduce impact indirectly if garments last longer, but that benefit has not been independently quantified.
lycra.care: Wash stretch garments cool (30 C), inside out, on a gentle cycle with mild detergent; avoid chlorine bleach entirely, since chlorine attacks spandex. Rinse swimwear in fresh water after pools or sea. Skip fabric softener, which can coat fibers and reduce recovery in performance knits. Heat is the main enemy: line dry or tumble on the lowest setting, and never leave stretch items on radiators or in hot cars. Iron only if the label allows, quickly and at the lowest setting (about 110 C), avoiding the stretch areas. Store flat or folded, not hung by stretched straps. Lotions and body oils shorten spandex life; wash activewear after each use.
faq: Is LYCRA the same as spandex?

LYCRA is a brand. Most LYCRA fiber is spandex (called elastane in Europe), but the company also sells LYCRA T400, which is a bicomponent polyester, not spandex. The fiber content label shows the generic name.
Why does my stretch fabric go baggy?

Spandex loses recovery after repeated exposure to heat, chlorine, UV and body oils, and when fibers break the fabric no longer snaps back. Cool washing, air drying, rinsing after swimming and avoiding bleach extend its life. Chlorine-resistant grades exist for swimwear.
How much spandex is in stretch jeans?
Usually only a small percentage, often in the low single digits, core-spun inside cotton yarns in the weft. Higher percentages give more stretch but can reduce durability and make recycling harder.
notable: LYCRA T400 fiber, despite the LYCRA name, is a bicomponent polyester and appears on labels as polyester, elasterell-p or elastomultiester rather than spandex.
The LYCRA Company certifies fabrics before issuing free hangtags, so a genuine tag indicates a certified fabric, not just the presence of fiber.

kevlar.types: Kevlar grades share the same PPTA polymer but differ in crystallinity, orientation and finish. Kevlar 29 is the basic high-tenacity grade used in ropes, cables, protective apparel and soft armor. Kevlar 49 is a high-modulus grade made by heat-treating the fiber under tension, favored for composites in aerospace, marine and sporting goods. Kevlar 129 offers higher tenacity for ballistic uses such as vests and helmets. Kevlar KM2 was developed for military fragmentation protection with high toughness and energy absorption. In April 2023 DuPont announced Kevlar EXO, described as a new aramid fiber platform made at Spruance, Virginia, that it said gives the highest ballistic performance among aramid fibers with more flexibility. Pulp and short-cut forms serve friction materials and gaskets.
kevlar.fabrics: Kevlar filament is woven into plain-weave ballistic fabrics layered in soft armor, laminated into helmets and hard panels, and woven or knitted into cut-resistant gloves, sleeves and chainsaw chaps. Kevlar is blended in small shares with meta-aramid, as in Nomex IIIA, to strengthen flame-resistant clothing. Composite fabrics reinforce canoes, kayaks, bicycle parts and aircraft panels. It also reinforces tires, belts, hoses, ropes, fiber-optic cables and motorcycle clothing. In each case the tested construction, not the fiber name, defines protection.
kevlar.quality: For protective products, buy on certification, not fiber content: body armor should be certified to the applicable ballistic standard (in the US, the National Institute of Justice standard), and gloves should show cut ratings under standards such as EN 388 or ANSI/ISEA 105. Check labels for panel manufacture date and model, and that certificates match the exact model. Undyed para-aramid is golden yellow; black or colored items may be solution-dyed. Beware 'Kevlar-lined' or 'Kevlar blend' claims without percentages, and counterfeit panels sold online without traceable certification. For composites, specify the grade (29, 49, 129) and fabric style.
pros: Para-aramid combines very high tensile strength and modulus with low density, making protective items light.
It does not melt and chars only at high temperature, so it is inherently flame resistant.
Distinct grades let engineers choose between toughness for armor and stiffness for composites.
Kevlar EXO is described by its developer as keeping the same protection after five years as on day one.
cons: UV light degrades it, so exposed fabrics lose strength unless covered or coated.
Its compressive strength is poor, and fibers split into fibrils when cut or abraded.
It absorbs some moisture, which can reduce ballistic performance unless panels are sealed.
It is hard to dye and hard to recycle, and costs far more than common fibers.
kevlar.impact: Public, independent life-cycle data for Kevlar were not found for this entry, so figures are not given here. Qualitatively, PPTA is made from p-phenylenediamine and terephthaloyl chloride, and the polymer is spun from concentrated sulfuric acid, which must be recovered or neutralized; these are energy- and chemical-intensive steps compared with commodity fibers. Against that, para-aramid items are often long-lived and used in small quantities for their function, and protective equipment has a safety benefit that is not captured by per-kilogram footprints. End-of-life options are limited: expired armor panels are generally discarded rather than reused, and aramid recycling is mostly limited to grinding into pulp or short fibers for fillers and friction materials. Ownership moved from DuPont to Arclin in 2026, so current environmental reporting should come from Arclin.
kevlar.care: Protective items need the manufacturer's instructions above all. Soft armor panels should be removed from carriers before washing the carrier; panels are usually wiped with a damp cloth and mild soap, never machine washed, soaked, dry cleaned or ironed. Keep panels flat and out of sunlight; do not fold or crush them. Replace armor according to the manufacturer's service life and after any ballistic hit. Kevlar gloves and sleeves can often be washed warm with mild detergent, but chlorine bleach damages aramid and should be avoided. Inspect cut-resistant gear for fraying, holes and thinning, and retire it when worn.
faq: Is Kevlar bulletproof?

No fabric is bulletproof on its own. Kevlar layers, in a certified design and number of plies, can stop specified threats at specified velocities. Protection depends on the tested panel, and certified vests are rated for particular threat levels, not all bullets.
What is the difference between Kevlar 29 and Kevlar 49?

Both are para-aramid, but Kevlar 49 is heat-treated under tension to raise orientation and stiffness, so it suits composites. Kevlar 29 is tougher and more flexible, suited to ropes, armor and protective fabrics.
Who makes Kevlar now?

DuPont created Kevlar and sold its Aramids business, including Kevlar and Nomex, to Arclin, a US chemical company; the deal closed on 1 April 2026. DuPont retained a minority stake in Arclin, so check current reporting for the latest ownership.
notable: Kevlar 49 is made by heat-treating Kevlar 29 under tension, which raises chain alignment and stiffness without changing the polymer.
DuPont announced Kevlar EXO in April 2023 as its most significant aramid fiber innovation in more than 50 years, made at its Spruance plant in Virginia.

nomex.types: Nomex covers several product forms built on meta-aramid. The best-known textile blend is Nomex IIIA, which DuPont specified as 93% Nomex meta-aramid, 5% Kevlar para-aramid and 2% P-140, a carbon-based antistatic fiber; the para-aramid adds strength and break-open resistance, and the antistatic fiber reduces static discharge. Other Nomex fabrics use different blends and constructions, including those for firefighter turnout gear. Beyond textiles, Nomex paper, made from short fibers and binding fibrids, insulates motors and transformers, and Nomex honeycomb, made from that paper, forms light panels for aircraft interiors. Fabric weight also varies; some industrial coveralls use about 4.5 ounces per square yard, and heavier weights give more thermal insulation.
nomex.fabrics: Nomex fabrics are made into firefighter turnout gear and station wear, military aircrew and armored-vehicle crew coveralls, motorsport suits, gloves and balaclavas, and industrial flame-resistant coveralls and shirts for oil, gas, chemical and electrical work. Knit Nomex appears in hoods and underlayers. Some protective fabrics blend meta-aramid with flame-resistant cellulosics or modacrylic to improve comfort and moisture handling. Nomex paper and honeycomb serve electrical insulation and aerospace structures rather than apparel.
nomex.quality: Buy flame-resistant clothing on certification: garments should carry labels showing the standards they meet, such as NFPA 2112 for flash fire protection in industrial settings in the US or EN ISO 11612 in Europe, and an arc rating where electrical hazards exist. Check the fabric weight and blend on the label, since lighter fabrics give less thermal protection. Genuine Nomex fabric is labeled aramid with the percentage; 'FR' alone does not tell you whether flame resistance is inherent or a chemical treatment. Look for intact reflective trim, seams sewn with flame-resistant thread, and no contamination or holes on used gear.
pros: Flame resistance is inherent to the polymer and does not wash out.
It does not melt or drip and self-extinguishes when the flame is removed.
Under heat the fabric thickens and chars, forming an insulating barrier that buys escape time.
Standard blends such as Nomex IIIA are widely specified, so certified garments are easy to source.
cons: Meta-aramid is expensive compared with treated cotton flame-resistant fabrics.
It yellows and loses strength under UV exposure.
It is hard to dye, and colors can fade or shift with use.
Protection is lost if garments are contaminated with oil, grease or fuel, which can burn.
nomex.impact: Independent life-cycle data specific to Nomex were not found for this entry. Meta-aramid is made from m-phenylenediamine and isophthaloyl chloride in polar amide solvents, releasing hydrochloric acid that is neutralized, and spinning and hot drawing are energy intensive, so per-kilogram impacts are likely higher than commodity fibers, though not quantified here. Garments are durable and inherently flame resistant, which avoids the flame-retardant chemical finishes used on treated cotton and their wash-out over time. At end of life, used protective clothing may be contaminated with combustion products, and aramid recycling mostly means mechanical shredding for lower-value uses. Current environmental reporting should come from Arclin, which has owned the business since April 2026.
nomex.care: Home or industrial laundering is usually allowed, but follow the garment label and, for firefighter gear, the manufacturer's instructions and the fire department's cleaning program. Wash contaminated gear separately from household laundry, promptly, to remove oils, grease and fuels that can ignite. Use regular detergent at moderate temperatures; avoid chlorine bleach, which weakens aramid and fades color. Tumble dry at low to moderate settings and remove promptly to limit shrinkage. Inspect for holes, thin areas, damaged reflective trim and seam failure, and retire garments that no longer meet the standard. Store away from sunlight.
faq: What is Nomex IIIA?

It is a flame-resistant fabric blend specified as 93% Nomex meta-aramid, 5% Kevlar para-aramid and 2% P-140 antistatic fiber. The Kevlar adds strength so the fabric resists breaking open in a flash fire, and the antistatic fiber reduces static sparks.
Does Nomex's flame resistance wash out?

No. The flame resistance comes from the meta-aramid polymer itself, not a finish, so it lasts the life of the garment. Protection can still be compromised by contamination with flammable soils, wear, holes or UV damage, so inspection matters.
Is Nomex fireproof?

No fabric is fireproof. Nomex resists ignition, does not melt and self-extinguishes, which reduces burn injury and gives escape time. Protection depends on the garment design, fabric weight, layers underneath and the exposure time.
notable: Nomex IIIA includes 2% of a carbon-based antistatic fiber, P-140, to reduce the risk of static discharge in hazardous environments.
Nomex paper, made from meta-aramid short fibers and fibrids, is folded into honeycomb cores used in aircraft interior panels.

dyneema.types: Dyneema fiber is sold in numbered grades that trade off strength against creep, the slow permanent elongation under sustained load. SK75 was long the standard high-strength grade. SK78 offers similar strength with markedly better creep resistance and has become a common rope grade. SK99, launched in 2013, is reported by rope makers to be about 20% stronger than SK78 with similar creep behavior. DM20 has slightly lower tenacity but very low creep, which rope makers quote at about 0.00007% per day at 30 C and 300 MPa, suiting standing rigging and other static loads. Beyond fiber, the brand covers unidirectional sheets for armor and Dyneema composite fabrics, laminated membranes used in ultralight tents, packs and sails.
dyneema.fabrics: Dyneema is braided into mooring lines, winch lines, running and standing rigging, climbing slings and fishing lines, where its strength per weight and low stretch are decisive. Woven and knitted fabrics use it in cut-resistant gloves and sleeves, abrasion-resistant motorcycle jeans and patches in packs and luggage. Laminated composite fabrics make ultralight shelters, backpacks and sails. Unidirectional cross-plied sheets are pressed into ballistic helmets and panels. It is often blended with nylon, polyester or elastane in gloves and apparel to add comfort and stretch.
dyneema.quality: Ask for the grade (for example SK78, SK99 or DM20) and the construction, since strength, creep and price differ sharply; 'HMPE' or 'UHMWPE' without a brand may be another producer's fiber, which is not necessarily worse but should be specified. Check rope certification and breaking-strength data from the rope maker, and for slings the rated load marked on the product. Gloves should show EN 388 or ANSI/ISEA 105 cut ratings. For composite fabrics, specify weight in ounces per square yard or grams per square meter. A practical check: the fiber floats in water and feels waxy and slippery.
pros: It gives very high strength per weight with low stretch, and the fiber floats.
It resists UV, moisture and many chemicals better than aramids.
Excellent abrasion and cut resistance suit gloves, ropes and packs.
Grade choice lets users trade strength against creep for static or dynamic loads.
cons: It melts at a low temperature for a high-performance fiber, roughly 145 to 155 C, so friction heat can damage it.
It creeps under sustained load unless a low-creep grade is used.
Its slippery, nonpolar surface makes knots, splices, coatings and dyeing difficult.
Low stretch means it absorbs little shock energy, so it must not be used as dynamic climbing rope.
dyneema.impact: Independent life-cycle data for Dyneema were not found for this entry, so no figures are given. Gel spinning dissolves the polymer in a hydrocarbon solvent that is recovered, and ultra-drawing is energy intensive, but the fiber's strength means much less material is needed than with steel or polyester for the same load, a trade-off that producer life-cycle studies typically emphasize. Polyethylene is not biodegradable, and fragments from worn ropes, nets and lines persist in water; the 2021 Heliyon review by Gaylarde and colleagues describes how synthetic microfibers are ingested by aquatic organisms more readily than larger plastic particles. Long service life can offset production impact. Recycling routes for UHMWPE products remain limited.
dyneema.care: Keep Dyneema away from heat: never tumble dry hot or iron, avoid friction such as rope running fast over rope, and store away from heaters and hot vehicles. Rinse ropes and gear in fresh water after salt exposure, wash gently with mild detergent if soiled, and air dry out of direct sun. Inspect slings and ropes for glazing, cuts and flattened areas, and retire items per the maker's guidance. Knots can greatly reduce strength in slippery fiber, so use splices or knots the manufacturer recommends. Composite fabric shelters should be packed loosely, not tightly creased repeatedly, and patched with compatible tape.
faq: Is Dyneema stronger than Kevlar?

Weight for weight, UHMWPE fibers such as Dyneema are generally stronger in tension and more abrasion and UV resistant, and they float. Kevlar tolerates much higher temperatures and does not melt, so the better choice depends on heat, load and environment.
What is Dyneema composite fabric?

It is a laminated sheet in which thin layers of Dyneema fibers are sandwiched between polyester films, making a very light, strong, waterproof fabric used in ultralight tents, backpacks and sails. It does not stretch much and is repaired with tape.
Why do climbers worry about Dyneema slings?

They are strong but static and have a low melting point. They absorb little energy in a fall, so shock loading can generate high forces, and friction from a moving rope can melt them. Use them within the manufacturer's guidance.
notable: Rope makers quote DM20 creep at about 0.00007% per day at 30 C and 300 MPa, low enough for permanent standing rigging.
Dyneema fiber is less dense than water, so ropes made from it float.

nuyarn.types: Nuyarn is a yarn-making method rather than a set of fiber grades. As trade reporting describes it, superfine merino fibers are drafted along a continuous high-performance nylon filament that acts as a carrier, without twisting the wool, producing a two-ply style yarn with more volume and air than a twisted ring-spun yarn. Brand and retailer materials describe it as developed in New Zealand in the mid-2010s. Yarns differ mainly by the merino fineness used, the filament's denier and the wool-to-nylon ratio, which is typically wool-dominant; the exact percentages appear on each garment's label. Weights range from light base-layer jerseys to heavier midlayer and sock yarns.
nuyarn.fabrics: Nuyarn yarns are knitted into merino base layers, T-shirts, leggings, midlayers, hunting and outdoor layers, activewear and socks. Several New Zealand outdoor and activewear brands use it for technical merino ranges, often presenting it as an alternative to merino blended with elastane. Brands pitch it for garments where fine merino alone wears quickly, such as socks, active layers and pieces worn under pack straps. Knit structures are the usual single jersey, rib and interlock of merino apparel, so fabric weight and gauge still decide warmth and durability.
nuyarn.quality: Read the label for the wool and nylon percentages and for the merino micron if given; a Nuyarn garment will not be '100% merino'. Brands using the technology typically name it on hangtags or in product descriptions; ask the brand if unsure. The company reports independent testing by Intertek and AgResearch showing seams about 120% stronger than in conventional ring-spun 100% merino; ask the garment brand for its own fabric test results on pilling, abrasion and dimensional stability. Handle the fabric: it should feel lofty and soft, recover when stretched, and show no twisting of side seams after washing. Check for mulesing-free or certified wool claims separately, since Nuyarn does not cover wool sourcing.
pros: The nylon carrier adds strength and abrasion resistance to fine merino, which is weak on its own.
Twist-free construction keeps the wool lofty, which the brand links to warmth for weight and faster drying.
The producer reports test results showing much stronger seams than conventional ring-spun merino.
Garments resist spirality, the twisting of side seams that can occur with twisted yarns, according to the brand.
cons: The nylon filament makes garments a wool-synthetic blend that is harder to recycle and not fully biodegradable.
Public, independent technical data beyond brand-reported tests are limited.
Wool sourcing and animal welfare are not covered by the technology name.
Garments usually cost more than conventional merino of similar weight.
nuyarn.impact: Nuyarn's environmental profile is essentially that of its components: merino wool, with the grazing land use, enteric methane and animal welfare questions of sheep farming, plus a nylon filament made from fossil feedstocks unless recycled nylon is specified. No life-cycle assessment of Nuyarn yarn was found for this entry. The blend has an end-of-life cost: wool alone can biodegrade and can be mechanically recycled, but an intimate wool-nylon construction complicates both. If the stronger yarn lets garments last longer, that could offset some impact, but this has not been independently quantified. For animal welfare, buyers should look for wool sourcing claims such as mulesing-free or certified standards, which research on flystrike control shows matter to the animals: alternatives to surgical mulesing have measurably smaller welfare effects on lambs.
nuyarn.care: Care follows merino with a synthetic core. Machine wash on a wool or gentle cycle at 30 C or cooler, inside out, with a wool-safe detergent that contains no protease enzymes or bleach, which attack keratin. Avoid fabric softener, which coats fibers. Dry flat or line dry in the shade; tumble drying risks felting and shrinkage of the wool component unless the label allows it. Iron rarely, on a wool setting with steam and a press cloth. Air garments between wears, since merino resists odor. Store clean and dry with cedar or sealed bags, because clothes moths and carpet beetles still attack the wool fraction.
faq: Is Nuyarn 100% merino?

No. Nuyarn yarns combine merino wool with a continuous nylon filament that carries the wool. The garment label will list both, usually with wool as the majority. The technology changes how the yarn is built, not the fibers themselves.
Why do brands use Nuyarn instead of merino with elastane?

The brands say the nylon-carrier, twist-free yarn gives durability, loft and some shape retention without elastane, while keeping the wool feel. Whether it performs better for a given use depends on the fabric, so compare test data and reviews.
How do I wash Nuyarn merino?

Like fine merino: cool gentle wash with a wool detergent, no bleach or enzyme detergents, and flat or line drying. The nylon adds strength, but the wool can still felt with heat and agitation, and moths can still damage it.
notable: Nuyarn drafts wool fibers along a nylon filament without twisting them, the opposite of conventional spinning, which relies on twist to hold staple fibers together.
The brand reports tests by Intertek and AgResearch finding seams about 120% stronger than in conventional ring-spun merino garments.

zq.types: ZQ is a set of wool sourcing standards, now run by Zentera, the company formerly called The New Zealand Merino Company, which has worked with growers under the ZQ name since 2007. The base ZQ standard is a third-party audited farm standard covering animal welfare, environmental integrity and social responsibility; it prohibits mulesing. ZQ+, formerly called ZQRX (the ZQ Regenerative Index), builds on ZQ with a regenerative agriculture program that measures and improves farm outcomes over time. Zentera also supplies wool certified to Textile Exchange's Responsible Wool Standard. None of these grades the fiber itself: micron, staple length and strength are specified separately, and ZQ is best known for fine merino.
zq.fabrics: ZQ merino goes into the same products as other fine wool: base layers, T-shirts, socks, knitwear, activewear, outdoor midlayers and suiting. Outdoor and performance apparel brands have been prominent users; Helly Hansen, for example, has described bringing ZQRX (now ZQ+) wool into base layers. Because the standard concerns farms and supply, the fabrics are ordinary wool constructions: worsted jersey, interlock and rib knits, woollen-spun sweaters and worsted suiting, sometimes blended with nylon or elastane.
zq.quality: The ZQ or ZQ+ mark on a hangtag indicates the wool came from audited growers, but it says nothing about fineness, so read the label for wool percentage and, if given, micron. For merino next to skin, fibers finer than about 20 microns generally feel soft, while coarser wool can prickle. Ask the brand whether the whole wool content is ZQ or only part of it, and check whether blends include nylon or elastane. Genuine program participation can be confirmed with the brand or Zentera. Quality signs are the usual ones for wool: dense, even knitting, clean seams, low pilling on a rub test, and shrink-resist information for machine-washable items.
pros: The base standard prohibits mulesing, according to the program.
Farms are audited by a third party against published animal welfare, environmental and social requirements.
The ZQ+ regenerative program adds measured farm-level outcomes beyond a pass or fail audit.
Traceability links wool to participating growers, mainly in New Zealand.
cons: The mark does not specify fiber quality, so ZQ wool can still be coarse or prickly if the grade is wrong.
Program standards are set by the commercial company that sells the wool, not by an independent standards body.
Regenerative outcomes are program-defined metrics whose independent verification is still developing.
Certified wool usually costs more than conventional wool.
zq.impact: Wool's footprint is dominated by the farm: land use, enteric methane from sheep, fertilizer and pasture management, with scouring water and energy downstream. ZQ addresses farm practices through audited standards and ZQ+ through regenerative metrics, but no independent comparison of ZQ farms against conventional farms was found for this entry, so claimed benefits are program statements. Animal welfare is where the standard is most specific: it bans mulesing, the removal of skin strips from the breech to prevent flystrike. Peer-reviewed Australian research supports the idea that alternatives to surgical mulesing reduce harm; a 2012 study in the Australian Veterinary Journal (Hemsworth and colleagues) found behavioral effects on lambs of plastic breech clips were smaller than those of surgical mulesing. Flystrike control without mulesing still needs breeding and management.
zq.care: ZQ does not change care; follow merino guidance and the label. Machine-washable merino (shrink-resist treated) can go on a wool or gentle cycle at 30 C or cooler, inside out, with a wool detergent free of protease enzymes and bleach. Untreated wool should be hand washed in lukewarm water with minimal agitation, since heat plus friction causes felting. Dry flat in the shade, reshaping while damp; do not tumble dry unless permitted. Steam or iron on the wool setting with a press cloth. De-pill with a comb. Store clean and dry with cedar or in sealed bags, as moth and carpet-beetle larvae eat keratin.
faq: What does ZQ mean on a wool label?

It means the wool came from growers audited under the ZQ standard, run by Zentera (formerly The New Zealand Merino Company), covering animal welfare, environment and social responsibility. It does not describe the wool's fineness or quality.
Is ZQ merino mulesing-free?

Yes, according to the program, which states that mulesing is not permitted on properties supplying ZQ wool. Growers manage flystrike through other strategies. This is a program claim verified through its farm audits.
What is the difference between ZQ and ZQ+?

ZQ is the base audited farm standard. ZQ+, formerly called ZQRX, is a regenerative program that builds on it by measuring and working to improve farm outcomes such as soil and biodiversity over time. Both are run by Zentera.
Is ZQ the same as the Responsible Wool Standard?

No. The Responsible Wool Standard is a Textile Exchange standard; ZQ is a company-run program. Both prohibit mulesing, but they differ in governance and detail. Zentera also supplies RWS-certified wool alongside ZQ.
notable: The company behind ZQ renamed itself Zentera, and its regenerative program ZQRX was renamed ZQ+.
The program describes ZQ as the first accredited wool fiber to guarantee that mulesing does not occur, a claim based on its farm audits.

seacell.types: SeaCell is essentially one fiber concept: lyocell with powdered seaweed incorporated during spinning, sold as staple fiber for spinning into yarn. Producer and secondary sources name the seaweed as knotted wrack (Ascophyllum nodosum), a brown alga harvested in Icelandic fjords. Published figures for the seaweed share are inconsistent, ranging from about 4% by weight to figures near 19%, and one description gives a volume ratio of 69% cellulose, 15% water and 16% seaweed; buyers should ask smartfiber for the current specification. A variant named SeaCell LT appears in producer literature. In finished fabrics, SeaCell is typically a minority blend component, so the seaweed share of the garment is lower still.
seacell.fabrics: SeaCell yarns, usually blended with other fibers, are used mainly in underwear, sleepwear, loungewear, T-shirts and other next-to-skin knits. Hand-knitting yarn companies have offered SeaCell blends for sweaters and shawls. Knit mills use it in fine-gauge jersey for its lyocell softness and drape. Because the base fiber is lyocell, fabrics behave like lyocell blends, with a smooth hand and good moisture uptake.
seacell.quality: The label should say lyocell (or rayon in the US), with SeaCell as a trademark. Ask for the SeaCell percentage in the garment and the seaweed share in the fiber; retail copy that calls a product 'seaweed fabric' or 'made from seaweed' overstates the content. Skin-benefit claims (vitamins, minerals, antioxidants) should be backed by test data showing effects from the actual fabric after washing; such evidence is limited. Judge the fabric as for lyocell: smooth even surface, no white fibrillation marks at seams, and good recovery in knits. Genuine SeaCell supply can be confirmed with smartfiber.
pros: It inherits lyocell's softness, drape, moisture handling and closed-loop solvent spinning.
Seaweed is a renewable additive that requires no irrigation or fertilizer.
It is suitable for next-to-skin knits and blends.
The fiber remains cellulose-based, so its microfibers are expected to be less persistent than synthetic ones.
cons: The seaweed share is small and inconsistently reported, making claims hard to evaluate.
Evidence that seaweed in the fiber benefits skin after washing is limited.
It is more expensive than plain lyocell for similar performance.
Wild seaweed harvesting needs management to avoid local ecological effects.
seacell.impact: SeaCell's footprint is mostly that of lyocell: wood pulp sourcing, energy for dissolution and spinning, and NMMO solvent recovery. The seaweed, reported as Ascophyllum nodosum from Iceland, is a wild-harvested resource; its sustainability depends on harvest rates and regeneration, and no independent assessment specific to SeaCell's supply was found for this entry. Producer claims of skin benefits are separate from environmental claims and are not supported by independent studies located here. At end of life, the cellulose matrix should behave like other regenerated cellulose; a 2019 study (Zambrano and colleagues) found rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester persisted. Blends with synthetic fibers change that outcome.
seacell.care: Care as for lyocell blends: machine wash at 30 C on a gentle cycle, inside out, with mild liquid detergent, and avoid overloading to limit fibrillation. Skip bleach and optical brighteners. Line dry or tumble on low and remove promptly; dry flat for knits to hold shape. Iron on a medium setting (about 150 C) while slightly damp if needed. Store dry, as cellulose can mildew. The producer's own care guidance should be followed if it claims that seaweed components persist through washing, since harsh detergents or hot washes would be expected to reduce any surface additive.
faq: Is SeaCell made from seaweed?

Only partly. It is lyocell, made from wood pulp, with powdered seaweed incorporated into the fiber. Reported seaweed shares vary from a few percent to under a fifth, and garments usually blend SeaCell with other fibers, so the seaweed content is modest.
Does SeaCell benefit the skin?

The producer promotes seaweed's minerals and antioxidants, but independent evidence that these transfer from a washed textile to skin in useful amounts is limited. Treat skin-benefit claims as unproven unless backed by tests on the actual fabric.
What seaweed is in SeaCell?

Sources describe knotted wrack, Ascophyllum nodosum, a brown alga harvested in Icelandic fjords, milled to a powder and added to the lyocell spinning solution. Confirm the current specification with the producer.
notable: The seaweed in SeaCell is reported to be knotted wrack (Ascophyllum nodosum) from Icelandic fjords, a brown alga of North Atlantic rocky shores.
Published figures for SeaCell's seaweed content disagree by several-fold, from about 4% by weight to about 19%.

coolmax.types: COOLMAX is a family of polyester moisture-management technologies licensed to fiber, yarn and fabric makers. The core COOLMAX technology uses polyester fibers with engineered, non-round cross-sections and fine filaments that move liquid sweat by capillary action. COOLMAX EcoMade versions, introduced by The LYCRA Company with ITOCHU in 2021 for the textile-waste route, are made from either 100% recycled PET bottles or 100% pre-consumer textile waste from cutting rooms, the latter processed by depolymerization and refining into polyester with properties the company says match virgin fiber. Different fabric programs are certified for specific constructions, so COOLMAX denotes a tested fabric specification as much as a fiber.
coolmax.fabrics: COOLMAX fabrics are used in running and cycling shirts, sports bras and underwear, socks (often blended with nylon, wool or spandex), workwear, and bedding and mattress covers marketed for cooling. Constructions are typically single jersey, pique and mesh knits, and two-faced knits that pull moisture from the skin side to the outer face. It is often blended with cotton or wool to combine wicking with a softer hand.
coolmax.quality: Check the content label for polyester and any blend fibers, and look for a COOLMAX hangtag or sewn-in label, which licensed fabrics carry. Wicking can be compared using standardized tests such as AATCC TM197 (vertical wicking) and TM195 (liquid moisture management), so ask brands for results. At home, drip water on the inside face: good wicking fabric absorbs and spreads it within seconds. Hydrophilic finishes can wash out, so treat claims of permanence skeptically. Many unbranded 'wicking' polyesters work similarly; the brand indicates a licensed specification, not a unique physics.
pros: Engineered fiber cross-sections move sweat to the fabric surface where it evaporates quickly.
Polyester keeps its strength when wet and dries fast, suiting sport and hot conditions.
EcoMade versions made from recycled bottles or textile waste reduce reliance on virgin polymer, according to the producer.
Licensing and fabric certification give some consistency across mills.
cons: Polyester retains body odor more than wool or cotton, especially in synthetic-only fabrics.
It sheds persistent microfibers, and recycled polyester may shed more than virgin.
Wicking finishes can degrade with washing and fabric softener.
The brand is one of many similar wicking polyesters, so the premium buys certification rather than unique performance.
coolmax.impact: COOLMAX is polyester, so its footprint follows PET production: fossil feedstocks for virgin fiber, or recycled bottles and textile waste for EcoMade versions, which the producer presents as keeping waste out of landfill. The textile-waste route uses chemical depolymerization, which can return polyester to near-virgin quality but requires energy; comparative figures are producer-reported. The main independent concern is microfiber shedding during laundering. A 2024 study in Environmental Pollution (Akyildiz and colleagues) found recycled polyester fabric released more microplastic fibers than virgin polyester under identical 40 C washes (about 1,193 versus 908 fibers counted). Durable, well-constructed knits and cooler, fuller washes reduce shedding over a garment's life.
coolmax.care: Wash inside out at 30 to 40 C with liquid detergent; odor-control or sport detergents help because polyester holds body oils. Never use fabric softener or dryer sheets, which coat fibers and block wicking. Wash soon after use rather than leaving damp gear in a bag. Line dry or tumble on low; high heat can damage spandex blends and set creases. Iron rarely, on a low setting (about 110 C). For stubborn odor, a pre-soak in water with a little white vinegar or an enzyme detergent often helps. A microfiber-catching bag or filter reduces shedding.
faq: What is COOLMAX made of?

Polyester with specially shaped fiber cross-sections and fine filaments that move sweat by capillary action. EcoMade versions use 100% recycled polyester from bottles or pre-consumer textile waste, according to The LYCRA Company.
Is COOLMAX better than merino for running?

They work differently. COOLMAX polyester wicks and dries quickly and is durable, while merino absorbs vapor and resists odor better. For hot, high-sweat activity many prefer wicking polyester; for multi-day wear without washing, merino often wins.
Why does my COOLMAX shirt still smell after washing?

Polyester binds body oils and odor-causing bacteria. Wash soon after use, turn inside out, skip fabric softener, and use a sport or enzyme detergent. An occasional soak with a little white vinegar can help.
notable: The LYCRA Company and ITOCHU introduced COOLMAX EcoMade fiber made from 100% textile waste in 2021, using depolymerization to recover polyester from cutting-room scraps.
COOLMAX's wicking depends on fiber shape: channeled, non-round cross-sections create capillaries that move liquid along the yarn.
